course: INFO 7375: Prompt Engineering for Generative AI

scoring.rule: Short essay scored against a rubric of five items, 1 point each.

chapters.6: Chapter 6: Claude Code and diff review

questions.prompt: Put these four in chronological order and give the year of each: the Transformer paper, Rosenblatt's Perceptron, Turing's "Computing Machinery and Intelligence", backpropagation popularized for multi-layer networks. Then explain in one or two sentences why "AI was founded in 1943" is a mix-up.

rubric.text: Turing's paper is placed first and dated 1950.
The Perceptron is placed second and dated 1958.
Backpropagation popularized is placed third and dated 1986.
The Transformer paper is placed fourth and dated 2017.
Explains that 1943 is the artificial neuron model while AI as a named field dates to 1956 (Dartmouth).

questions.section: 2. What is a model? What is a language model?
questions.prompt: Trace what happens between typing a prompt and receiving the first generated token, naming each stage. Then explain why sending a prompt does not change the model's weights.

rubric.text: Text is split into tokens and mapped to integer token IDs.
Token IDs are looked up as embeddings.
Transformer layers produce logits, one score per vocabulary token.
Softmax converts logits to probabilities and one token is sampled.
States that a prompt is input to inference, not training, so weights stay fixed.

questions.prompt: Compare how an RNN and a Transformer handle a long sequence. Cover how each carries information, whether training can be parallelized, and what happens to long-range dependencies.

rubric.text: RNN passes information through a hidden state, one step at a time.
RNN training is hard to parallelize because steps are sequential.
RNN long-range dependencies suffer from vanishing or exploding gradients.
Transformer uses attention so every position can look at every other position directly.
Transformer training runs in parallel; notes LSTM/GRU only reduce the RNN problem.

questions.prompt: A model has a vocabulary of 50,000 tokens and an embedding size of 768. A prompt is tokenized into 12 tokens. Give (a) the size of the token ID array, (b) the size of the embedded input matrix, and (c) the size of the logits vector for the next-token prediction. Explain why (c) does not depend on the prompt length.

rubric.text: (a) The token ID array has length 12.
(b) The embedded input is 12 × 768.
(c) The logits vector has length 50,000.
Explains logits give one score for every vocabulary token, so length is vocab_size.
Notes the context window limits the token array length, not the logits length.

questions.prompt: Logits [1, 2, 3] give p(token 3) of about 0.867 at T = 0.5, 0.665 at T = 1.0 and 0.506 at T = 2.0. Describe the trend, state what temperature does to the distribution, and explain why a low temperature cannot make a wrong answer true.

rubric.text: States that p(token 3) falls as T rises (0.867, 0.665, 0.506).
Explains that lower T sharpens and higher T flattens the distribution.
Notes that as T goes to 0 the choice approaches greedy and as T grows it approaches uniform.
States that a positive T never reorders the tokens.
Explains that sampling probability is not truth probability, so concentrating on a wrong top token does not make it correct.

questions.prompt: Describe the steps of scaled dot-product attention, softmax(Q·Kᵀ / √d_k)·V, and explain what the √d_k does. Then explain why the changing vector for "bank" in "river bank" versus "bank account" does not show the model understood either sense.

rubric.text: Scores every query against every key with a dot product.
Divides by √d_k to keep scores in a stable range.
Applies softmax so each row of weights sums to 1.
Outputs a weighted sum of the value vectors.
States that context changing a representation is not evidence of understanding.

questions.prompt: Contrast a programming language with a language model on three points: how input is interpreted, whether output is deterministic, and how errors show up. State the key nuance about where an LLM runs.

rubric.text: Programming language input is a formal grammar interpreted exactly; a language model takes ambiguous natural language.
Programs are deterministic for the same input; language model outputs are sampled and can vary at T > 0.
Program errors are explicit; language model errors are silent and fluent.
States that an LLM is itself a program doing arithmetic on CPUs/GPUs.
Explains that the difference is how the instruction is interpreted: executed exactly vs used as context for prediction.

questions.prompt: Explain the course's design rule "let the model generate, and let functions check." Give two properties of functions that make them good checkers and one concrete example from the course.

rubric.text: States the rule: the model generates and functions check.
Names one property (e.g. deterministic, testable, exact).
Names a second property (e.g. composable, explicit contracts, inspectable failures).
Gives a course example (probabilities(), sample(), JSON contract validator, path policy).
Explains why a model should not check its own output (language model errors are silent).

questions.section: 9. Chapter 1: Division of Labor and The Gate
questions.prompt: Define "the gate" in the course's sense and design one for this case: a model repeatedly gives the same false answer at low temperature. Say what the gate checks, who or what decides, and why repetition and low temperature do not help the answer pass.

rubric.text: Defines the gate as the checkpoint an output must pass before being accepted or acted on.
States the gate must be able to reject an output.
Specifies a concrete check or human decision (not model confidence).
Explains that repeating the answer shows consistency, not correctness.
Explains that lowering temperature only makes the false answer more likely and does not change whether it passes.

questions.section: 9. Chapter 1: Division of Labor and The Gate
questions.prompt: The notes say a model was trained on 300 billion tokens. Using 0.75 words per token and a reading speed of 250 words per minute, estimate how many years of continuous reading that is. Show the steps and say which assumption moves the answer most.

rubric.text: Converts tokens to words: 300B × 0.75 = 225 billion words.
Converts to minutes: 225B ÷ 250 = 900 million minutes.
Converts to years: about 1,700 years (1,711 with continuous reading).
Names the reading rate as an assumption that changes the answer by over a thousand years.
Notes the continuous, no-breaks assumption and that 0.75 words per token is approximate.

questions.section: 10. Chapter 2: The three-response experiment and what the green cannot distinguish
questions.prompt: A response passes a JSON validator. Name the three kinds of validity, say which the validator checks and which it cannot, and give an example of a response that is green yet wrong.

rubric.text: Names JSON validity, schema validity and factual validity.
States the validator covers JSON and schema validity.
States it cannot tell a true claim from a false one.
Gives a concrete green-but-wrong example (valid structure and source ID, false claim).
States a format-pass rate is not an accuracy score.

questions.section: 10. Chapter 2: The three-response experiment and what the green cannot distinguish
questions.prompt: Describe the three-response experiment: what you do, what you record, and what agreement across the three responses does and does not show.

rubric.text: Sends the same evidence-based prompt three times.
Records exact prompt, outputs, model label, date and interface.
Compares factual correctness separately from surface variation.
States agreement shows consistency, not verification.
Notes that three identical answers can all be wrong and temperature is not configurable everywhere.

questions.prompt: Describe the agentic loop step by step, separating the policy from the controller. Explain why stopping is not always success and why a bounded loop still needs permissions.

rubric.text: Lists the loop: state, policy chooses an action, controller executes it, result becomes an observation, state updates, repeat.
Distinguishes the policy (proposes) from the controller (runs the loop, enforces limits).
Names the stopping conditions: goal met or budget exhausted.
Explains that stopping may mean the budget ran out, not success.
Explains that a bounded loop can still take one unauthorized action, so permissions are needed.

questions.prompt: Explain solve-verify asymmetry using one example, then explain how the course uses it to design a generate-then-check workflow and where the advantage breaks down.

rubric.text: States that checking an answer is often cheaper than producing it.
Gives a valid example (Sudoku, factoring and multiplying back).
Describes generating with the model and verifying with an independent check (tests, validators, source lookup).
States that asking the same model "are you sure?" is not independent.
States the advantage disappears when verifying is as hard as solving.

questions.prompt: Explain why fluency is not evidence of correctness, and why "The prompt is better" is not yet a falsifiable claim. Rewrite it so that it is falsifiable.

rubric.text: States fluency means smooth, confident-sounding and a wrong answer can be equally fluent.
States that confident tone is not a calibrated probability of being right.
Explains that a falsifiable claim says what observation would show it wrong.
Explains that "better" is unspecified (at what, measured how, on which cases).
Gives a falsifiable rewrite naming a metric, a case set and a threshold.

questions.source: Opening (before "What you will be able to do")
questions.prompt: You ask Claude the same question twice. The first answer is short; the second has a different example, a different qualification, and perhaps a different conclusion. A colleague says, "The prompt was vague." In a short paragraph, explain what has and has not been established at this point, and what Claude's own fluent explanation of the difference can and cannot contribute.

rubric.text: States that a difference between two outputs has been observed.
States that the cause (the moving part) has not been isolated, and that labels such as "the prompt was vague," "the model was creative," or "the system was unreliable" do not identify it.
Notes that Claude can write a fluent, confident account of why the answers differed, and that the account may even be right.
Notes that Claude cannot check its own account against the machinery, or know which moving part you needed to isolate.
Concludes that the account is a hypothesis for the human to test, not a result.

questions.source: Opening (before "What you will be able to do")
questions.prompt: State the chapter's argument in brief: what Claude is better at than you, what it lacks, and which three jobs stay with you. Explain each job in one phrase.

rubric.text: Says Claude is far better at producing fluent text, working code, and long lists of plausible candidates, at a speed and volume no person matches, so you should not compete with it there.
Says Claude has no stake in whether its output is true and no way to tell you whether it is the thing you needed.
Names the three jobs as conduct, check, and drive.
Explains conduct and check correctly: decide where Claude goes before it runs, and check what comes back.
Explains drive as signing your name to what you keep (owning the decision and the split of work).

questions.source: Opening (before "What you will be able to do")
questions.prompt: The chapter says "a score is not a probability, a probability is not an observed frequency, and an observed frequency is not a correctness judgment." Give one concrete example from the Part 2 experiment for each of the three links in that chain.

rubric.text: Score versus probability: the scores [1, 2, 3] are an ordering (they sum to six), not chances, and must be transformed before they are probabilities.
Probability versus frequency: for example, the assigned probability of about 0.665 for outcome two at temperature one versus the observed 630 of 1,000 (0.63).
Frequency versus correctness: a count such as 849 is a count of an index selected in a constructed experiment and says nothing about whether an answer is correct.
States that one outcome can be made increasingly likely without adding any evidence that it is correct.
States that a run can be made repeatable without making its answer true.

questions.source: Opening (before "What you will be able to do"); Ship It: a report that survives a skeptical reader
questions.prompt: Why does the chapter shrink the machine to three outcomes and three numbers instead of experimenting on Claude directly, and what must you not conclude from the toy?

rubric.text: Says the toy is small enough that every intermediate value can be inspected.
Says there is nowhere for an unexplained operation to hide.
Says the toy will not reproduce Claude, and that this is its advantage.
Says the experiment's numbers come from an offline program (no API key, no direct API credits), not from a fabricated conversation with Claude.
Says the sign-off should not claim that the experiment models a Claude setting.

questions.source: Three jobs that stay yours
questions.prompt: Explain the Conduct job. Say what Claude does well and badly, what the human decides, what a gate is, and what a gate contains.

rubric.text: Says Claude implements well from a complete specification and badly from an incomplete one, and will not tell you which you gave it.
Says the human's job is "not to type less" but "to decide more precisely": design, constraints, and gates.
Defines a gate as a specific, testable condition that must hold before an output moves on.
Says a gate is written before asking Claude for anything.
Lists the gate's contents: what the thing must do, what it must refuse, and the test that would fail a plausible but wrong version.

questions.source: Three jobs that stay yours
questions.prompt: Explain the Check job: why Claude's errors are hard to see, the two habits the chapter prescribes, and why asking Claude to check its own output is not enough.

rubric.text: Says Claude's mistakes arrive fluent, so well-formed prose does the work that verification should have done.
Names habit one: write down what a wrong answer would look like before reading the output.
Says that note must not be revised afterward.
Names habit two: keep the check independent of the thing checked.
Explains that an AI checking an AI is "the first opinion run twice," so although Claude can run tests and propose counterexamples, your name is on the result.

questions.source: Three jobs that stay yours
questions.prompt: The book is about a tool that writes code faster than you do, yet it asks you to build small things by hand. Explain why, using the chapter's account of the Drive job.

rubric.text: Says the purpose is not to out-type Claude.
Says building by hand acquires the baseline that makes conducting possible.
Cites the line that you cannot audit what you do not know (Irreducibly Human).
Describes the split by task: Claude can draft, compute, retrieve, test, and challenge; you choose the question, justify the assumptions, and own the decision.
Gives the chapter's sequence: build the small mechanism, write the gate, conduct Claude against it, check what comes back, sign only what the record supports.

questions.source: Three jobs that stay yours
questions.prompt: The chapter calls the car picture "good and incomplete." Explain where the picture works and where it needs a caveat.

rubric.text: Says nobody races a car, so you should not compete with Claude at pattern and association work.
Says the car does not choose the destination; you do.
Says a car's failures are loud (the engine knocks, the dashboard lights up) while Claude's failures are quiet.
Says confidence and correctness come from different places, so Claude's confident tone is not evidence of correctness.
Says the driver must understand the engine well enough to hear a knock that makes no sound.

questions.source: The unfinished script
questions.prompt: Describe the loop that turns a machine that continues text into a chatbot, and state what the loop does and does not contain.

rubric.text: Describes the loop: feed in the text so far, take a candidate for the next fragment, append it, feed the longer text back, and repeat until the machine proposes an ending.
Says no component answers your question; one component repeatedly answers what plausibly comes next in this text.
Says nothing in the loop reads a document, checks an answer key, or knows whether the growing text is true.
Says retrieval, tools, permissions, and approval gates arrive later as attempts to supply what the loop lacks.
Says every one of those attempts is something you design and then check.

questions.source: One question, asked over and over
questions.prompt: Using the chapter's illustrative table (Unbelievably, Paris, costs, 1,200, euros), explain what a token is and why a request for an exact character count is awkward for the machine.

rubric.text: Says the machine predicts tokens, which are fragments from a fixed vocabulary, not words.
Says a common word may be one token and a rare word several (for example `unbelievable` in three pieces).
Says a space is usually part of the token that follows it, and that numbers and punctuation split too (for example, 1,200 splits into three tokens: the digit 1, a comma, and 200).
Says the five words became eleven tokens and that the split is illustrative, not the output of any particular tokenizer.
Says a character count asks the machine to reason about a unit it does not natively see.

questions.source: One question, asked over and over
questions.prompt: Describe what goes into and what comes out of one prediction step, including what an embedding is and what is (and is not) excluded from the output.

rubric.text: Says each vocabulary entry selects a vector of learned numbers (an embedding), and that operations after that work on vectors.
Says the output is a number for every token in the vocabulary (tens of thousands), not a single token.
Says the numbers are nonnegative and sum to one.
Says every candidate gets a share, including absurd ones; nothing is excluded, things are merely ranked.
Says what is predicted at each step is one token, not a word or a fact (a word spanning three tokens takes three steps).

questions.source: One question, asked over and over
questions.prompt: A model gives `Paris` a high probability after `The capital of France is`. A student says the model "looked it up in an atlas." Explain what the number actually reports and why its agreement with an atlas is not a guarantee for the next case.

rubric.text: Says the distribution ranks continuations of a string.
Says its shape was fixed by fitting parameters to a body of text.
Says the number reports how the phrase tends to continue in the corpus the model was fit to.
Says it is not the output of a lookup against an atlas.
Says the agreement is a fact about the corpus, not a mechanism that guarantees agreement in the next case (the chapter's load-bearing distinction).

questions.source: The transcript is the whole trick
questions.prompt: The chapter shows a chat as `System:`, `User:`, and `Assistant:` lines. Explain how a model that only continues text can hold a conversation, and give the two consequences the chapter draws.

rubric.text: Says the model is handed a single string with role markers that looks like a conversation.
Says the most plausible continuation of a string ending in `Assistant:` is an assistant-sounding reply, and that roles are text, not modes.
Consequence one: a system prompt is a request, not a gate; it competes with every other paragraph in the document.
Says enforcement of a rule that matters belongs in the runtime that wraps the model (permissions in code), not in the preamble.
Consequence two: the model does not remember your last conversation; the whole transcript is resupplied every turn, so long conversations behave differently.

questions.source: The transcript is the whole trick
questions.prompt: Describe the "continue this text" support-call exercise: what you do before you paste the prompt, what the prompt asks Claude to do, and why the order of steps matters.

rubric.text: Says to write down in one sentence what you expect Claude to do, and date it, before pasting.
Says the prompt asks Claude not to answer as an assistant but to continue the string as literal text.
Describes this as getting the mechanism without the costume.
Says to save the result with the exact prompt, the prediction, and the date.
Says the later comparison against a normal request is only worth anything if the prediction was written first.

questions.source: Where the numbers come from
questions.prompt: Describe how pretraining sets the model's parameters, and say what its objective does and does not contain.

rubric.text: Says the parameters (hundreds of billions of values) start random, so the model starts by producing noise, and were never set by hand.
Describes the loop: take a passage, hide the next token, get the model's distribution, and compare it with the token that actually followed.
Says backpropagation nudges every parameter slightly so the true token gets a little more probability and everything else a little less.
Says this is repeated across an enormous corpus.
Says nothing in the loop is told what is true; the target is what the corpus did next, so pretraining yields something that completes internet text rather than behaves like an assistant.

questions.source: Where the numbers come from
questions.prompt: Explain what the second training stage targets and why that is not the same as correctness. Say why this is the first reason the checking stays with you.

rubric.text: Describes the stage: people are shown candidate replies and asked which they prefer, and those judgments shift the parameters.
Says approval and correctness overlap heavily because raters generally prefer accurate answers.
Says they are different targets, and where they diverge the training signal follows approval.
Gives the example: a confident, well-organized, wrong answer is what a rater who does not know the answer can prefer.
Says this follows from the objective (not a scandal about any company's process), and that the machine was shaped to produce what looks right to a reader, who is you.

questions.source: Scale, in units you can check
questions.prompt: A speaker says it would take a person thousands of years to read GPT-3's training text. Using 300 billion tokens and 0.75 words per token, work out the number of words and the reading time in minutes at 250 words per minute, and report the chapter's year figures for 250, 200, and 150 words per minute. Then say what the headline figure hides.

rubric.text: Computes 225 billion words (300 billion x 0.75).
Computes 9 x 10^8 minutes at 250 words per minute (225 billion / 250), about 1,711 years.
Reports about 2,139 years at 200 words per minute and about 2,852 years at 150.
Says the answer moves by more than a thousand years depending on a reading rate nobody stated, so the headline is a division with a hidden parameter, not a measurement.

Says the comparison is still useful as an illustration (more text than a person could read in many lifetimes), and that finding hidden parameters in impressive numbers is a skill the course keeps asking for.

questions.source: Scale, in units you can check
questions.prompt: A speaker says GPT-3's training compute would take "over 100 million years" at one billion operations per second. Using the chapter's figures, evaluate the claim.

rubric.text: States GPT-3's reported total training compute as 3.14 x 10^23 floating-point operations (Brown et al.).
Says at one billion operations per second that takes about 9.95 million years.
Says "over 100 million years" requires roughly 3.2 x 10^24 operations.
Says that is about ten times GPT-3's budget (3.2 x 10^24 / 3.14 x 10^23 is about 10.2), plausible for later systems but a different claim about a different model.
Says both sentences can be true but are not the same sentence, and a reader who cannot tell them apart cannot audit either.

questions.source: Inside one prediction step
questions.prompt: Explain what makes the transformer practical at scale, and distinguish the two jobs that self-attention and the feed-forward network each do.

rubric.text: Says the transformer takes the whole context at once, while earlier models walked through text one position at a time (parallelism).
Says the context job is done by self-attention, which decides for each token which other tokens to read from.
Says the prediction job is done by a feed-forward network, which takes each token's context-informed vector and moves it toward scores for the next token.
Says both are made of parameters fitted together by the single next-token objective.
Says nobody wrote down what attention should look for; those weights came out of the fit like every other parameter.

questions.source: Inside one prediction step
questions.prompt: Figure 1.4a draws attention and the feed-forward network as two learned parts sharing one stream. What caution does the chapter attach to the drawing, and what does it refuse to claim about Claude?

rubric.text: Says that in the paper's design, inside each layer, attention comes first and the feed-forward network second.
Says each sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection, so its output is added to its input.
Says "in parallel" should be read as two learned components sharing one stream, not as simultaneous computation.
Says some later published models (for example PaLM, with "parallel layers") do compute the two side by side.
Says the book makes no claim about which arrangement any deployed model, Claude included, uses.

questions.source: Self-attention: each token chooses what to read from
questions.prompt: Describe how a token gets context in self-attention, naming the three vectors each token produces and the steps from comparison to new vector.

rubric.text: Says every token produces a query, a key, and a value.
Says a token's query is compared with the key of every token it is allowed to see, and a close match scores high.
Says a softmax turns the scores into weights that sum to one.
Says the token's new vector is the weighted mix of the values.
Gives or explains the scaling term: dividing by the square root of the key length keeps the scores from growing so large that the softmax saturates.

questions.source: Self-attention: each token chooses what to read from
questions.prompt: Using the chapter's `bank` table, explain how attention gives the same token different vectors in different sentences, and describe what kind of numbers the table contains and where such weights live in a real model.

rubric.text: Says in "She sat by the river bank" `bank` puts the most weight on `river` (0.60), and in "She paid at the savings bank" on `savings` (0.55).
Says same token, different neighbors, different weights, so the vector leaving attention differs.
Says each row of weights sums to one.
Says the numbers are constructed to show the idea and were not measured from any model.
Says the weights are not stored anywhere; they are recomputed for each new input (what is learned are the projections).

questions.source: Self-attention: each token chooses what to read from
questions.prompt: The chapter adds three precise points about attention and a warning about interpreting it. State them.

rubric.text: Says what is learned is the set of projections that produce queries, keys, and values, not the weights in the table.
Says a token that is generating text reads only itself and the tokens before it (later positions are masked in the decoder), whereas in the paper's encoder every token can read every other.
Says the original runs eight attention functions (heads) in parallel, each with its own learned projections, so a real layer holds many weight tables.

Says every visible token is compared directly with the current one, so the first and hundredth tokens are one comparison apart; distance does not weaken the link, which let the paper do without recurrence and convolution.
Warns that an attention weight shows where one head read, not why the model answered; a heat map is a hypothesis to test, not an explanation.

questions.source: The feed-forward network: an ordinary neural network
questions.prompt: In the chapter's toy feed-forward example (x = [2, -1, 1, 3], a hidden layer of eight numbers), the hidden values before the ReLU are [3, 5, 0, -1, 6, 3, -3, -2]. Give the values after the ReLU, say how many were zeroed, and explain what this layer does and does not do.

rubric.text: Gives [3, 5, 0, 0, 6, 3, 0, 0] as the values after the ReLU.
Says four of the eight hidden values are not positive, so four become zero (ReLU sets negative values to zero).
Says the output is (8, 7, 5, -1): a 4-number vector in, an 8-number hidden layer, and back to 4 numbers.
Says the same weights run on every position separately, so this layer never lets tokens talk to each other; attention already did that.
Says W1 and W2 are what training adjusts (where patterns from the corpus are stored), while the toy's weights were chosen to make arithmetic visible, not fitted.

questions.source: Putting the pieces together
questions.prompt: Walk through the four things that happen in one pass of the model, ending in a distribution over the vocabulary.

rubric.text: Says each token becomes a list of numbers, because the fitting procedure only works on continuous values.
Says attention lets the lists read each other and revise themselves according to context (`bank` after `river` ends up differently from `bank` after `savings`).
Says a feed-forward layer adds patterns stored during training.
Says both operations repeat, layer after layer.
Says the vector at the final position is turned into one score per vocabulary token, and those scores are normalized into a distribution.

questions.source: Putting the pieces together
questions.prompt: Claude is asked, "Why did you give that answer?" and replies fluently with a reason. What status should you give that reply, and why? Use the chapter's account of how model behavior arises.

rubric.text: Says researchers designed the operations, not the behavior.
Says behavior emerges from how the parameters were fitted.
Says nobody, including the builders, can read off why a particular prediction was made.
Says "the model decided X because Y," absent interpretability evidence, is a story about a system rather than a measurement of one.
Says to treat Claude's fluent self-explanation as a hypothesis to test, never as a trace of what happened.

questions.source: Stochastic parrots
questions.prompt: Summarize the stochastic parrot argument and its two halves.

rubric.text: Attributes the argument to Bender, Gebru, McMillan-Major, and Shmitchell and states the claim: a model stitches together linguistic form according to probabilistic information, with no access to meaning.
Says fluency is not comprehension, and that the coherence you perceive is supplied largely by you because humans attribute intent to well-formed text.
Describes the conceptual half (Bender and Koller): meaning is a relation between form and something outside language, which a system trained on form alone cannot reach.
Describes the empirical half: costs of training at scale, the impossibility of auditing web-scale corpora, and the harms of deploying systems whose fluency invites unearned trust.
Says conflating the two halves is the usual mistake.

questions.source: Stochastic parrots
questions.prompt: A classmate dismisses Claude with "it's just autocomplete" and says that settles the stochastic parrot debate. Respond using the chapter's account of the dispute.

rubric.text: Gives the critics' view: the conceptual half settles by stipulation what ought to be investigated, and probing work suggests internal representations track non-linguistic structure.
Gives the defenders' reply: internal structure is not grounded reference, and the empirical half stands however the philosophy resolves.
Says the book does not settle the dispute.
Says "it's just autocomplete" is weaker than the paper's claim.
Says systems that merely replayed observed sequences would not generalize to strings absent from training, as these demonstrably do.

questions.source: Stochastic parrots
questions.prompt: State the version of the skeptical claim that this chapter stands behind, and explain why you do not need a position on machine understanding to accept it.

rubric.text: States that the mechanism ranks continuations, and ranking a continuation highly is not evidence that it is true.
Says to look at what the transformation receives as input and notice that an answer key is not among its arguments.
Says no position on machine understanding is needed.
Says you need not believe Claude is hollow to check its work, nor that it understands to use it.
Says what you need is a gate before it runs and a check after.

questions.source: What Part 1 gives you, and what it leaves with you
questions.prompt: Part 1 ends by noting that if you ask the same question twice and the answers differ, "something else moved." What did not move, and what does the Part 2 toy show can differ even when the distribution is fixed?

rubric.text: Says the parameters did not change between runs.
Says the architecture did not change between runs.
Says Part 1 cannot yet say what the variation implies.
Says in the toy, selection from a fixed distribution produces different observed counts; the seed changes the selected sequence under otherwise fixed conditions.
Distinguishes this from temperature, which changes the weights, and from count, which changes how many observations are collected.

questions.source: The gate: write the experiment before you run it
questions.prompt: Write the contract for the Part 2 probability-and-sampling function as the chapter states it.

rubric.text: Probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one.
A larger score never gets a smaller probability at positive temperature.
Equal scores get equal probabilities.
The function refuses an empty list, a nonfinite score, and a temperature that is zero, negative, or nonfinite.
Sampling with the same seed repeats.

questions.source: The gate: write the experiment before you run it
questions.prompt: The chapter's gate asks for a sentence about what a failure would look like and a statement of what the experiment may claim. Explain both, and say what role Claude may play in writing the gate.

rubric.text: Says to write one sentence about what you would see if the program were wrong, and to date it.
Says that if written after reading the output, it describes the output rather than testing your understanding.
Says the experiment may claim only a distribution over three indices and counts of draws.
Says it cannot say that any outcome is correct.

Says Claude can sharpen the gate but cannot write it for you without defeating its purpose, because the gate is where your understanding goes on the record and what you test Claude's implementation against.

questions.source: Three scores are not yet three chances
questions.prompt: A student proposes turning [1, 2, 3] into probabilities by dividing each score by 6. Compute that result and say why the chapter does not use this rule.

rubric.text: Computes the result as about [0.167, 0.333, 0.500], noting that the scores sum to six and the result sums to one.
Says it is a different transformation from the one implemented in the lesson.
Says it would fail on negative scores.
Says the chapter is explaining a particular mechanism, not inventing any normalization that happens to work on one positive list.
Describes the actual mechanism: exponentiate score differences, then divide by the total weight, because an exponential turns any finite real input into a positive weight.

questions.source: Three scores are not yet three chances
questions.prompt: Explain why, for positive temperature, the ordering of the scores survives the transformation, and how that prediction can serve as a debugging instrument.

rubric.text: Says dividing by a positive T preserves score order.
Says the exponential preserves the order again.
Says every weight is divided by the same positive total.
Says changing a positive temperature can change how strongly the largest score dominates but cannot make a smaller score the largest probability.
Says that if an implementation gives the smallest score the largest probability, you have reason to suspect an error such as negated differences or wrongly paired labels.

questions.source: The subtraction that changes nothing important
questions.prompt: For scores [1, 2, 3] at temperature 1, compute by hand the shifted scores, the three weights (to three decimals), the total weight, and the three probabilities (to three decimals).

rubric.text: Shifted scores are [-2, -1, 0] (subtract the maximum, 3).
Weights are about 0.135, 0.368, and 1.000.
Total weight is about 1.503.
Probabilities are about 0.090, 0.245, and 0.665.
Notes that the probabilities sum to one and that outcome two (score three) is the favorite.

questions.source: The subtraction that changes nothing important
questions.prompt: Show algebraically why subtracting the maximum score before exponentiating leaves the distribution unchanged, and say what the choice buys the computer.

rubric.text: Writes the shifted numerator as exp(z_i/T) times exp(-m/T), where m is the maximum score.
Writes the shifted denominator as exp(-m/T) times the sum of exp(z_j/T).
Says the common factor cancels, so the intended distribution is unchanged and only the intermediate weights change.
Says that after subtracting, the largest exponent is zero (its exponential is one) and the others are no larger than one, so large intermediate exponentials are not needed.
Uses the [1000, 1000] test (shifted to [0, 0], then [1, 1], then [0.5, 0.5]) and says it is evidence for this concrete case, not a proof for every numeric input.

questions.source: The subtraction that changes nothing important
questions.prompt: The reference function raises an error for an empty list, a nonfinite logit, and a zero, negative, or nonfinite temperature. Give the chapter's reason for each refusal and explain why the refusals are where a human's decisions live.

rubric.text: Empty list: it offers no outcome to normalize.
Zero temperature: it makes the division invalid.
Negative temperature: it would reverse the ordering the chapter just relied on.
Nonfinite logits are refused because the logits must be finite.
Says Claude writes the happy path unprompted and the boundary only if your gate demands it, so the refusals are where the human's decisions live.

questions.source: The subtraction that changes nothing important
questions.prompt: Your test checks that the returned probabilities sum to approximately one, and it passes. What does this test show and not show? Why does the check use approximate equality?

rubric.text: Says the check uses approximate equality because floating-point arithmetic has limits.
Says a sum close to one shows one property only.
Says it does not show the ordering is right.
Says it does not show equal scores get equal probabilities or that an invalid temperature is rejected.
Says it does not show that sampling consumes the probabilities correctly, so the claim should be narrower than the slogan "numerically stable."

questions.source: Temperature is a concentration control, not a fact checker
questions.prompt: Using the ratio p_i / p_k = exp((z_i - z_k) / T), compute the ratio of outcome two (score 3) to outcome one (score 2) at T = 0.5, 1, and 2, and explain what the trend says about temperature.

rubric.text: At T = 1 the ratio is exp(1), about 2.718.
At T = 0.5 the ratio is exp(2), about 7.389.
At T = 2 the ratio is exp(0.5), about 1.649.
Says a smaller positive T makes the exponent larger and the ratio larger, while a larger T brings the ratio closer to one.
Says normalization cancels out of the ratio, so temperature changes relative concentration, which explains the effect without a slogan about creativity.

questions.source: Temperature is a concentration control, not a fact checker
questions.prompt: For scores [1, 2, 3], which temperature, 0.5 or 2, gives more probability to outcome two, and which gives more to outcome zero? Answer using the chapter's table, and say what stays fixed across the table.

rubric.text: Says T = 0.5 gives outcome two more (about 0.867 versus about 0.506).
Says T = 2 gives outcome zero more (about 0.186 versus about 0.016).
Says the largest score remains the favorite throughout, with its share moving from about 87 percent to about 51 percent.
Says the ordering is fixed, and that predicting only the winner misses most of the experiment.
Says scores, ordering, and transformation stay fixed while temperature changes, so nothing in the operation supplies evidence about the meaning of any selected answer.

questions.source: Temperature is a concentration control, not a fact checker
questions.prompt: The chapter constructs a hypothetical in which the three labels are proposed answers and the independently checked answer is label zero. Explain what happens when temperature is lowered, and what this does and does not show.

rubric.text: Identifies the hypothetical as explicitly constructed, with the answer key stipulated as label zero.
Says lowering temperature concentrates selection on label two, which is wrong under that key.
Says the transformation works as designed; the failure is treating its preference as a truth guarantee.
Says this must not be reported as an observed Claude error.
Says no change in concentration can supply information the program never receives.

questions.source: Temperature is a concentration control, not a fact checker
questions.prompt: A classmate says, "Low temperature means the model picks the highest-scored answer." Respond using the chapter's interface and counts.

rubric.text: Says low temperature is not the same as choosing the largest score directly.
Says this interface rejects zero temperature rather than switching to a deterministic mode.
Cites the T = 0.5 counts: the top outcome was selected 849 of 1,000 times, with 133 and 18 for the others, so it is concentrated but not exclusive.
Says the point is not a promise about any Claude setting.
Says even if the top score were always selected, that would be concentration, not correctness.

questions.source: A distribution is not the sample you happened to see
questions.prompt: At T = 1 the chapter assigns about 0.66524 to outcome two, and the seed-7 run recorded 630 of 1,000. Compute the expected count and the observed share, and explain why the gap is not automatically a bug.

rubric.text: Computes the expected count as about 665.24.
Says an expected count of 665.24 cannot be an observed count because counts are integers.

Gives the observed share as 0.63 against an assigned probability of about 0.66524, and says both belong in the report because they answer different questions (what chance was assigned, what fraction appeared).
Says one gap does not make the sampler broken; you need an acceptance criterion appropriate to the experiment.
Notes that the existing reproducibility test checks that the same call returns the same counts, not agreement with every theoretical proportion.

questions.source: A distribution is not the sample you happened to see
questions.prompt: The chapter's counts table is: T = 0.5: 18, 133, 849; T = 1: 102, 268, 630; T = 2: 202, 329, 469. Say what the table shows about temperature and what it does not show.

rubric.text: Notes that each row totals 1,000.
Says outcome zero's count rises (18, 102, 202) and outcome two's falls (849, 630, 469) as temperature rises, as the distribution flattens.
Says the outcome with the highest score had the highest count at every temperature.
Says counts are evidence of the recorded executions, not exact expressions of the theoretical probabilities (for example 102 observed against about 90 expected for outcome zero at T = 1).
Says a count of an index selected in a constructed experiment does not show that any answer is correct.

questions.source: A distribution is not the sample you happened to see
questions.prompt: A small sample returns a dictionary with no key for outcome zero. What does that mean, how should a report handle it, and what should you not conclude?

rubric.text: Says the dictionary has no key for an outcome never selected.
Says a missing key means no recorded selections.
Says missing counts should be retrieved or reported as zero.
Says it does not mean removal from the probability model; "not observed in this run" differs from "not a possible outcome."
Gives an illustration, such as outcome zero having a positive assigned probability (about 0.016 at T = 0.5) even if it is never drawn.

questions.source: A distribution is not the sample you happened to see
questions.prompt: A teammate says, "Our fixed-seed run is reliable because it reproduces every time." Respond using the chapter's account of the seed.

rubric.text: Says a seed lets you return to a particular experiment while debugging.
Says the seed gives the sample no factual status.
Says that if a fixed sequence repeatedly selects the hypothetically wrong label, repeatability preserves the mistake.
Says a result you can reproduce on demand is still only as true as what produced it (the fluent wrong answer in miniature).
Says the reproducibility test shows repeatability, not agreement with correctness or with every theoretical proportion.

questions.source: First prompts: the same experiment, one floor up
questions.prompt: Prompt 1 asks Claude the same one-sentence question in four conversations. Explain why four separate new conversations are required and what you record.

rubric.text: Says sending it four times in one conversation is wrong because the transcript grows, which changes the input.
Says to open four separate new conversations and send the prompt once in each.
Says to record all four and note what is stable (the claim, roughly) and what moves (examples, hedges, clause order).
Says this is the counts table, one level up.
Says to write your prediction first and save the actual responses with the date and displayed model label, never a remembered summary.

questions.source: First prompts: the same experiment, one floor up
questions.prompt: Prompt 2 asks "What is the capital of Australia?" with the instruction to answer with one word, no punctuation and no explanation. Predict what happens to the spread of answers compared with prompt 1, explain why, and say what the result does not show.

rubric.text: Says it uses the same procedure: four fresh conversations.
Says the spread of answers should shrink compared with prompt 1.
Says a constrained format leaves fewer high-probability continuations to choose among, so the answers converge.
Says this is the closest thing to lowering temperature without a temperature control.
Says it made the answer more repeatable and no more true.

questions.source: First prompts: the same experiment, one floor up
questions.prompt: Prompt 3 asks Claude for a specific quantitative finding from a peer-reviewed paper on spaced repetition and for its confidence that the citation is real. Explain what you do next and what the exercise teaches.

rubric.text: Says the prompt asks for authors, year, and the exact number, then a separate confidence rating that the citation is real.
Says you must check the citation yourself.
Says the response was fluent and well-formed whatever you find.
Says the ranking machinery produced a confident-looking string and confidence was never one of its inputs.
Says Claude cannot be the independent check on its own citation, because the process that made it would be vouching for it.

questions.source: First prompts: the same experiment, one floor up
questions.prompt: Describe prompt 4 (Claude as a reviewer of your reasoning): when to use it, what it asks, and why it withholds a verdict.

rubric.text: Says to use it only after you have written your own prediction and reasoning.
Says the prompt tells Claude not to say whether you are right.
Says it asks Claude to name the single assumption your reasoning depends on most.
Says it asks Claude to describe an input that would make it fail.
Says withholding the verdict is deliberate because you want the boundary case, not the grade; Claude challenges and you decide.

questions.source: Build It: the baseline that lets you audit
questions.prompt: Describe the Build It step: what you write before opening the reference, what you explain, how you test it, and what you compare afterward.

rubric.text: Says to write your implementation in the learner workspace before opening the reference solution.
Says to start with the probability transformation on a short list whose ordering you can inspect by eye.
Says to explain each intermediate quantity (shifted score, weight, total, probability) and what would count as an impossible value for it.
Lists the lesson's six boundary checks: sum near one, equal large scores, temperature comparison, repeatable sampling, rejection of zero temperature, and rejection of an infinite score.
Says your own version is the baseline, and that you compare it with the reference and name a difference in behavior, not in line count or style.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.prompt: Describe the Use It step, in which you conduct Claude Code against your gate: what you hand over, what you do with the result, and the three things the chapter asks you to do afterward.

rubric.text: Says to give Claude the gate (the contract and the test list), not your implementation.
Says you run your tests on what it returns, yourself.
Says to note which tests failed, since a failing test is often a gap in your gate that Claude cannot see.
Says to compare its implementation with your baseline and name one behavioral difference (a boundary it handled that you missed, or one it silently ignored).
Says to ask Claude for a deliberately wrong version that still passes your tests and check by hand whether it does; if it does, your test list was too weak.

questions.source: Ship It: a report that survives a skeptical reader
questions.prompt: A reviewer sees an outcome-two count of 849 in your report and asks whether that proves the answer is correct. Write the reply the report should make easy, and state a claim the report may make.

rubric.text: Says 849 is a count of an index selected in a constructed experiment.
Says correctness would need an answer key or a source check tied to a meaningful claim.
Offers a bounded claim such as: in the recorded local run, decreasing temperature from two to one-half concentrated the assigned probability on the largest score.
Says the sample counts are recorded separately from that claim.
Says the report begins with the prediction written before running, preserved even if wrong, because replacing it with the correct answer destroys the comparison.

questions.source: Ship It: a report that survives a skeptical reader
questions.prompt: Describe the sign-off template and explain why it should be written from your own record rather than drafted by Claude.

rubric.text: Names the template's lines: Checked, How, Not checked, Not claiming, and Signed or withheld.
Says Claude can draft its words in seconds and the draft will be fluent, so you write it from your record.
Says the "Not checked" line does the work, and an AI-written sign-off never includes it because the system has no record of what you did not do.
Gives examples of what belongs in "Not checked" or "Not claiming," such as inputs outside your tests, other Python versions, correctness of any outcome, or that this models a Claude setting.
Says that if your evidence does not support signing, withholding is an honest result.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.prompt: Using the driver's-seat table, explain who does what for the tasks "Explaining a surprising output" and "Saying what the result supports," and how the sampling report should show the split.

rubric.text: For explaining a surprising output: Claude proposes hypotheses.
For explaining a surprising output: you test each against the code and the input, because an explanation from the system under test is a story, not a trace.
For saying what the result supports: Claude flags an overclaim.
For saying what the result supports: you choose the verb and sign, because your name is on the claim.
Says the report should record one delegated task and one retained judgment, each pointing to a transcript line or an edit; otherwise the split happened in your head and not in the record.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.prompt: Describe how the chapter wants you to verify and reflect on your work, including the difference between "recorded," "computed," and "established correctness."

rubric.text: Says verification begins with a claim small enough to test, such as shifted and direct formulations agreeing on moderate inputs, rejection of an invalid temperature, or repetition of a seeded call.
Says to name which claim each check addresses.
Says the worked-example script and its JSON do not substitute for your own prediction and implementation.
Says "recorded" describes an observation, "computed" a calculation, and "established correctness" requires a criterion the sampler never receives.

Says the reflection is which distinction you originally collapsed (scores and probabilities, probabilities and frequencies, or repeatability and truth) and the input or calculation that separated them again.

questions.source: Assessments - ungraded practice
questions.prompt: The chapter's last Assessment asks what would transfer from the three-outcome experiment to a real Claude interaction. Which conclusions does the toy support, which questions about Claude need other evidence, and what kinds of evidence does the chapter name?

rubric.text: Says the toy supports conclusions about a distribution over three indices and counts of draws.
Says it cannot say that any outcome is correct.
Says questions about a real Claude interaction need documented interface details.
Says they also need actual transcripts and independently checked sources.
Says the evidence plan should be designed without running paid requests, and should not claim the toy models a Claude setting.

questions.source: The next boundary
questions.prompt: Suppose a response is stable, repeatable, and neatly formatted, yet claims the source says red when the source says blue. Explain why the sampler cannot catch this, what Chapter 2 builds in response, and the mistake it warns against.

rubric.text: Says the response may still be unacceptable despite being stable, repeatable, and neatly formatted.
Says the sampler cannot reject the mismatch because it never receives the source's meaning as a condition to check.
Says Chapter 2 builds a contract around an answer: required fields, types, source identifiers, and an evaluation set.
Says structure earns its place by rejecting specific failures, and the mistake is asking it to reject failures it was never written to recognize.
States the question Chapter 2 adds: when the program says an answer passed, exactly which obligation did it pass?

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.prompt: Apply the Computational Skepticism note to one sentence of your sampling report that contains a probability. What do you do, and what does the note claim and not claim?

rubric.text: Says the probabilities in this chapter concern selection among constructed indices, not the chance that an answer is true.
Says to state the event to which the sentence's probability refers (for example, "the sampler selects outcome two").
Says not to quietly replace that event with "outcome two is correct."
Says the companion book's diagnostic is to keep confidence claims separate from observed correctness.
Says the note contributes an auditing question and does not claim that a calibration study was run.

questions.source: Irreducibly Human
questions.prompt: Using the chapter's Irreducibly Human note, state what AI should and what the human should do in this chapter's work, and what to do if you cannot explain unaided why a repeatable sample can select a wrong answer.

rubric.text: Says AI should help diagnose errors after your first attempt.
Says AI should suggest boundary cases, run authorized checks, and organize actual results.
Says AI should label hypothetical examples, distinguish proposed explanations from observations, and not invent your initial prediction.
Says the human should make the prediction, build the initial mechanism, explain the transformation and one rejection case, and decide what the evidence supports.
Says that if you cannot explain it unaided, you should take another pass through the three numbers rather than write a more elaborate prompt that conceals the gap.

questions.source: Opening section (untitled introduction)
questions.prompt: The chapter opens with a source whose only sentence is "The color is blue." (identifier s1) and a response that says the fixture says red while citing s1. Explain why this response passes the validator, and what the chapter says the failure actually is.

rubric.text: States that the source sentence for s1 says blue while the response claims red.
Says the response is valid in form: well-shaped, nonblank answer, and a known identifier, so every implemented rule is satisfied.
Says the validator's pass does not involve any comparison between the answer and the source's content.
Notes that nothing crashed and the program returned exactly the result its rules required.
Locates the failure in the distance between what the validator checks and what a reader might assume a green result means, not in an exotic model behavior.

questions.source: Opening section (untitled introduction)
questions.prompt: The chapter reports a format-pass rate of one-third for its three constructed responses. Name the three responses, say which one is accepted, and explain why calling the result an accuracy score would misname it.

rubric.text: Identifies the three responses: a string that is not JSON, a response citing an unknown identifier, and a properly shaped response citing a known identifier.
States that only the third is accepted, so the rate is one accepted out of three, 1/3.
Notes that the accepted response contradicts the supplied sentence, so it is accepted without being correct.
Explains that the rate measures acceptance by the format and identifier rules.
Concludes that calling it an accuracy score would misname the measurement.

questions.source: Opening section (untitled introduction)
questions.prompt: The chapter calls its example "an executed, constructed counterexample, not a transcript of Claude making a mistake." Explain what that means and what the chapter says about keeping constructed strings and real model responses apart.

rubric.text: States that the three responses were constructed by hand and no model was called.
States that the example was executed, so the validator's acceptance results are real results.
States that a locally constructed string is useful test data.
States that it becomes misleading only when presented as an observed model response.
Says that when you later compare actual prompts with Claude Code, the real responses are saved separately from these fixtures.

questions.source: Opening section (untitled introduction)
questions.prompt: Chapter 1 gave three jobs: conduct, check, and drive. Explain what each becomes in this chapter and what Claude is and is not good at in this setting.

rubric.text: Conduct: the gate becomes a contract plus an evaluation set, written for the consuming program before any prompt is tried.
Check: becomes the discipline of naming what a pass covers and what it leaves out.
Drive: becomes deciding what "acceptable" means for this consumer and this claim, which no schema holds.
Says Claude is strong on the near side: given a complete contract it can write the validator, enumerate malformed inputs, draft prompt variants, and tabulate pass rates.
Says whether an answer follows from the sentence it cites is a verification question that belongs on the far side.

questions.source: Opening section (untitled introduction)
questions.prompt: A colleague proposes asking Claude whether its own answer follows from the sentence it cited, and treating a "yes" as verification. Using the chapter's argument, explain why this does not give an independent check and what kind of check the chapter wants.

rubric.text: Says producing an answer and verifying it are different operations.
Says asking the generator to vouch for itself is more of the first operation, not a second opinion.
Says a check run by the system that produced the answer is not independent of it.
States the part of the argument the chapter keeps: a trustworthy check fails differently from the thing it checks.
Says choosing that check is a human decision, and that the book states its strongest version of the claim as a wager, not a proven fact.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.prompt: Explain why the chapter says the contract must be written before the prompt. What goes wrong if you tune the prompt until the output looks right, and what role does Claude's handling of incomplete specifications play?

rubric.text: Says the consumer's need is the only criterion that exists before an output does.
Says that tuning first makes the contract become whatever the output happened to look like.
Says that every later pass rate then measures agreement with your own habituation.
Says Claude implements well against a complete specification but may quietly fill an incomplete one with something plausible instead of flagging the gap.
Concludes that completeness is the human's job and the prompt is derived from the contract, not the other way around.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.prompt: The teaching contract accepts exactly two keys. A response contains answer, sources, and confidence, and all three values look reasonable. Predict the validator's result and discuss the trade-off, naming one consumer who finds the rule protective and one who finds it an obstacle.

rubric.text: Predicts that the validator rejects the response because of the extra key.
Explains that a consumer assuming a fixed shape finds the rule protective, because unexpected additions become visible instead of silently ignored.
Explains that an exploratory analysis wanting extensible metadata finds the same rule an obstacle.
States the trade-off as strict predictability versus accepting some useful objects, and that it cannot be called good or bad without naming the downstream job.
Says this is a choice a schema cannot make for you, so you choose the contract for your consumer.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.prompt: A teammate says "I added 'always obey the schema' to the prompt, so we do not need to validate the output." Respond using the chapter's distinction between a request and a check.

rubric.text: Says the prompt requests behavior from the producer.
Says the validator checks the returned object against executable conditions.
Says a request can be ignored or misunderstood.
Says the local check has a definite acceptance rule.
Connects this to Chapter 1's point about the system prompt, one level up: a request is a hope and a check is a gate.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.prompt: The chapter gives a baseline request that asks for a JSON object with exactly two keys and a nonempty list of supplied source identifiers. Which parts of the request's intention does the validator enforce, which does it not, and why does the chapter want this asymmetry made visible now?

rubric.text: Says the executable function enforces the output contract: exactly the two keys, a nonblank string answer, and a nonempty sources list of known identifiers.
Says it knows which identifiers are allowed.
Says it does not understand whether the answer follows from the contents of those sources.
Says the asymmetry should be made visible before a passing response encourages you to forget it.
Describes the baseline request as a proposal for an experiment, not a proven improvement.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.prompt: Consider the constructed response {"answer":"The sources do not say.","sources":["s1"]}. What does the reference validator do with it, why, and why do the obvious fixes (a status field, "be accurate" in the prompt) not work? What should you do if you redesign the contract?

rubric.text: States that the validator accepts it.
Explains it is accepted for the same reason the false claim was: it cannot tell an honest refusal from an assertion.
Notes that the reference has no field for insufficient evidence.
Explains that adding a status field fails because the validator rejects the extra key, and that "be accurate" in the prompt does not supply a refusal state.
Says that whether a refusal is an acceptable answer, and how the consumer should see it, is a decision about the interface.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.prompt: The chapter says "none of this makes the design waterfall." Explain what it means by that, using the refusal finding, and say what you must record when a finding reopens an earlier decision.

rubric.text: Says a finding such as the missing refusal state can reopen an earlier decision.
Says reopening a decision does not make the process waterfall.
Says the change must be recorded.
Names a new contract version and new tests as part of the record.
Says any case that guided the redesign counts as development evidence from then on.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.prompt: Describe the "Consumer" and "Contract" lines of the gate for the teaching example. What must each say, who decided them, and how does the contract treat text outside the JSON object?

rubric.text: The Consumer line is one sentence naming the program that reads the answer and what it does with it.
For each line, you note who decided it: you, or a fixed requirement of the consumer.
The contract allows exactly the keys answer and sources.
The answer is a nonblank string, and sources is a nonempty list of strings, every one in the supplied identifier set.
Text outside the JSON object is a rejection, not something to repair silently, and the validator returns a decision, not a diagnosis.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.prompt: Describe the evaluation set the gate calls for and the rules governing the held-out list. Why must both lists be dated?

rubric.text: States five development questions and five held-out questions.
States that both are listed and dated before any response is inspected.
States that the held-out list is sealed: not shown to Claude.
States that it is not used to revise the prompt until the revision is frozen.
Says these decisions are written down before running anything.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.prompt: Describe the evidence criterion the gate requires: its content, the outcomes it records, and when it must be written.

rubric.text: States that for each question there is one sentence saying what "supported" means for it.
Names supported and contradicted as recorded outcomes.
Names "cannot be reviewed" as a third recorded outcome.
Connects it to Computational Skepticism for AI: record pass, fail, or unknown against a criterion fixed before you read the output.
Says it must be written before you know which prompt wins.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.prompt: The gate lists wrong versions your tests must catch and one wrong response they cannot. Name each of them and say where the uncatchable one is caught instead.

rubric.text: Names a validator that checks only that the keys exist.
Names a validator that accepts a source list when any entry is known, where the contract says every entry.
Names a validator that skips the nonblank check.
Names the well-formed and wrong response, the color fixture, as the one no validator test will catch.
Says your evidence column must catch the color fixture.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.prompt: For each held-out question the gate asks for a "what a failure looks like" sentence. What must the sentence describe, when must it be written, and what does it mean if you cannot write it?

rubric.text: Says it describes an answer that would pass the validator and fail the evidence criterion.
Says it is written and dated before you see a response.
Says that if you write it afterward you have described the output, not tested your understanding.
Says that if you cannot write the sentence, you do not yet know what you are checking for.
Says one such sentence is needed for every held-out question as part of the pass condition.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.prompt: State the gate's pass condition and say what the experiment may and may not claim once it is run.

rubric.text: Says every line of the contract must have a named test that fails if the line is deleted.
Says both question lists must be dated.
Says each held-out question must have its failure sentence.
Says the experiment may claim acceptance by a stated validator of recorded responses plus a separate support judgment on the claims reviewed.
Says it cannot claim that any answer is correct beyond those reviewed claims.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.prompt: How can Claude help sharpen the gate, and why can it not write the gate for you?

rubric.text: Says you can ask Claude for a malformed input your list lacks.
Says you can ask Claude for a contract line your tests do not defend.
Says Claude cannot write the gate without defeating its purpose.
Says the gate is the criterion fixed before the output exists.
Says a criterion drafted after the outputs arrive is a description of the outputs.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.prompt: Trace the strings "not json" and {"answer":"x","sources":["missing"]} through validate() with allowed identifiers {"s1"}. For each, name the first boundary it fails and the rules that never ran.

rubric.text: For "not json": json.loads raises and the exception path returns False.
For "not json": none of the dictionary or field checks runs.
For the second string: parsing and the shape checks succeed.
For the second string: it fails source membership because missing is not in the supplied identifier set.
Notes that validate() returns only False in both cases, so the reviewer must name the reason by stopping at the first relevant boundary.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.prompt: List the obligations validate() imposes on the answer and sources fields, and for each give an input that violates it.

rubric.text: The answer must be a string, so the integer 1 fails because the function does not coerce.
The answer must be nonblank after strip(), so a whitespace-only answer fails.
The sources field must be a list.
The list must not be empty.
Every entry must be a string in source_ids, and one valid identifier cannot compensate for another invalid entry.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.prompt: The reference validator collapses every rejection into a Boolean False. Evaluate this design choice using the chapter's reasoning.

rubric.text: Calls it an intentional simplification worth judging.
Gives the benefit: a Boolean is convenient for a pass rate and easy to test.
Gives the cost: it tells a reviewer nothing about how to repair a response.
Says a richer result naming the parse failure, key mismatch, wrong type, or unknown source is a reasonable extension to your own version, not a behavior of the reference.
Says the absence of a message is not the absence of a reason, so for each failing fixture you stop at the first relevant boundary and name it, instead of saying the output was bad.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.prompt: Describe the scratch-copy experiment the chapter proposes on the reference validator and what it shows about "the tests pass."

rubric.text: Says to predict the result first, then check.
Says changing all to any in a scratch copy leaves all six tests passing.
Says deleting the nonblank check leaves all six tests passing, as does deleting the nonempty-source check.
Concludes that the contract promises three behaviors the lesson's tests never defend.
Concludes that "the tests pass" means they pass for the behaviors they exercise, and that additional tests should target such a gap chosen by reason, not repeat the happy path.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.prompt: Someone tells you that validate() "verifies source support." How do you respond using the chapter's argument?

rubric.text: Says to ask them to point to the comparison between source content and answer content.
Says they cannot, because source_ids supplies identifiers, not passages.
Says the validator receives only the allowed identifier set, not the source sentence.
Says membership in a registry and support for a proposition are different relations.
Says the validator can reject an invented address such as missing but cannot decide whether the words attached to s1 support the answer.

questions.source: A source identifier is an address, not an argument
questions.prompt: The chapter says the review asks two distinct questions. State them, explain how they relate, and illustrate with the color fixture.

rubric.text: States the first question: does the referenced source exist in the supplied collection?
States the second question: does that source support this particular claim?
Says passing the first makes the second possible but does not answer it.
Says an address can point to a real document while the accompanying summary misstates it, as when s1 is cited for red.
Says the address remains useful because it gives the reviewer somewhere to look.

questions.source: A source identifier is an address, not an argument
questions.prompt: Why does the chapter say the color counterexample is stronger than a vague warning about hallucination, and does it show that the validator is broken?

rubric.text: Says we know which check is absent.
Says we can trace why the response passes without speculating about model internals.
Says the third response satisfies every implemented condition.
Says the validator is not broken because it succeeds at enforcing its stated structural and identifier contract.
Says the validator fails only if someone misrepresents that contract as a complete evidence check.

questions.source: A source identifier is an address, not an argument
questions.prompt: Who should answer the support question for a claim and its cited source? Discuss Claude's role, its limits, and what you should and should not ask for in an explanation.

rubric.text: Says Claude can be asked to set the two sentences side by side, and in a case this small you can verify the comparison at a glance.
Says that if the generator is the only reviewer of its support, you have the first opinion run twice.
Says a brief explanation with cited evidence makes the answer easier to inspect but is still output to evaluate.
Says not to request hidden chain-of-thought or treat an articulate rationale as access to an authenticated internal process.
Says what you need is a reviewable claim, the referenced material, and a short justification that can be checked against the material.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.prompt: Before running the three-response experiment you are told to write predictions. Give the predictions the chapter's analysis supports for the validator and for a reviewer holding the source sentence, and say how the third validator prediction should be reached.

rubric.text: Says predictions are written before reading the results, using the identifier set {"s1"}.
Says the validator decision and the reviewer's judgment are predicted separately.
Says the third validator prediction should be based on the function, not on whether the answer is true.
Gives the validator sequence false, false, true.
Gives the review sequence: cannot be reviewed, cannot be reviewed, contradicted by s1.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.prompt: Explain how pass_rate computes its result for the three-response fixture and what the denominator and the sample do and do not tell you.

rubric.text: Says each accepted response contributes one and each rejected response contributes zero.
Computes one acceptance among three, so 1/3, saved as 0.3333333333333333.
Says the denominator is the number of supplied responses and the function does not know how they were selected.
Says the three cases were constructed to expose three boundaries, are not a random sample, and no model was called to generate them.
Concludes that one-third describes acceptance of this fixture set by this validator and estimates nothing about how often a real service will make these mistakes.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.prompt: Why does pass_rate raise an error on an empty list of responses instead of returning 0 or 1?

rubric.text: States that with no responses the function raises an error (ValueError).
Explains that zero could be mistaken for a tested system that failed every case.
Explains that one could be mistaken for perfect performance.
Explains that an empty experiment has no denominator.
Concludes that this makes absence of evidence harder to disguise as a performance number.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.prompt: Reproduce the chapter's table for the three responses: for each, give the validate() result, the obligation failed or passed, and the support review. Then say how the report should treat the third row.

rubric.text: For "not json": False, failed at parsing with no later rule run, and cannot be reviewed because there is no claim to compare.
For the missing-identifier response: False, parsed and shaped correctly but failed source membership, and cannot be reviewed because the cited address resolves to nothing.
For the red response: True, passed every implemented condition, and contradicted by s1, "The color is blue."
Says "format accepted and evidence contradicted" is the expected report for the third row, not an inconsistent one.
Says not to invent one numeric evidence score to make the table symmetrical; decide how unsupported, contradicted, and cannot-be-reviewed results are represented first.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.prompt: Explain the fluency trap and how it applies to a True from validate(), including the cost asymmetry between the validator and the support review.

rubric.text: Defines the trap: the more fluently an output presents, the more confident you become in it and then in your own evaluation of it.
Says form and content are independent.
Says a True is a verdict in the shape of a settled question.
