rubric.text: Says requiring source identifiers is useful for traceability.
Says "has a source identifier" is a different obligation from "is supported by that source".
Says a structural pass names only the obligation it passed.
Says that when the selected context is insufficient, the correct result may be an abstention or a request for another source.
Says not to fill the gap with a plausible answer and cite the nearest passage, and that the task packet should specify how insufficiency is represented.

questions.source: Relevance and entailment are separate checks; Anthropics
questions.prompt: A teammate says: "Just give Claude the whole corpus; more text is always safer." Respond using the chapter, including how the Anthropic context-engineering article is meant to be used.

rubric.text: Says more text can include the missing evidence.
Says more text can also contain contradictions, irrelevant material, and more content than a bounded task should expose.
Says context selection is an engineering and data-governance decision.
States the goal as sufficient, authorized evidence with an inspectable selection path.

Says the article treats context as a designed collection of instructions, tools, data, and history, and is used to compare selection strategies, not to claim count vectors implement Claude's context mechanisms.

questions.source: The gate: write the source list and the evidence rules first
questions.prompt: Summarize half one of the gate: the design decisions, the contract, and what the retriever may claim.

rubric.text: States the design: count vectors over lowercase `\b\w+\b` tokens, cosine as the score, zero scores dropped before the cutoff, ties broken by document key, default k of two.
Says the design is written down so the decisions are on your record and not inherited defaults.
States the contract: cosine is never negative, identical direction scores one, and an empty side scores 0.0 as a convention.
States that `retrieve` returns only positive scores, best first, equal scores in key order, at most k rows, and refuses a k that is not a positive integer.
States that the retriever may claim only a ranking of overlap under one representation, not relevance in a reader's sense, support, or completeness.

questions.source: The gate: write the source list and the evidence rules first
questions.prompt: The gate lists wrong versions of the retriever that your tests must catch. Name five of them and explain how to confirm that your tests really catch them.

rubric.text: Names sorting worst-first.
Names breaking ties by insertion order.
Names checking k with isinstance so that True slips through.
Names two more from: ignoring k beyond a fixed size, dropping the normalization, dropping the zero filter.
Says to confirm by mutating a copy of the reference, and that a wrong version that survives means the gate is not finished.

questions.source: The gate: write the source list and the evidence rules first
questions.prompt: The gate says to read the lesson's six tests against your list of wrong versions before trusting them. Describe the gaps the chapter finds and why each lets a wrong version through.

rubric.text: Says the relevance test has a single positive-scoring document.
Explains that best-first and worst-first sorts return the same thing for a single document.
Says no test has two equal scores, so insertion-order ties go unnoticed.
Says the invalid-k test uses zero, which an isinstance check also rejects, so the Boolean slip-through goes unnoticed.
Says no test makes k smaller than the number of positive matches, so ignoring k goes unnoticed.

questions.source: The gate: write the source list and the evidence rules first
questions.prompt: Describe the expected-source list in half two of the gate: what it contains, when it is written, and why you should not ask Claude to write it first.

rubric.text: Lists the contents: title or identifier, owner, version or date, why each source is authorized, and the number of items expected.
Says it is written before you ingest anything.
Says it is dated.
Says Claude's answer would be built from the task description you gave it, the same material you are trying to check.
Says the book warns that a fluent AI-generated frame contains no information, because the AI started from the same documentation you did.

questions.source: The gate: write the source list and the evidence rules first
questions.prompt: Explain how to write the claims list and the evidence rules in the gate, including the four row labels and who may mark a row supported.

rubric.text: Says the claims list has one sentence per question the report must answer.
Says each claim must be small enough for a single passage to support or not, and a sentence with an "and" is split.
Defines supported as a quoted passage stating the claim, within its scope, date, and population.
Names the other labels: contradicted, insufficient (on topic but unresolved, with the missing piece named), and not reviewed.
Says the person who read the original authorized source may mark a row supported, and that when the sources do not say, the report must say so.

questions.source: The gate: write the source list and the evidence rules first
questions.prompt: The abstention rule "refuse when no document scores above zero" is proposed. Explain what it does well, where it fails in both directions, and what the gate asks you to write.

rubric.text: Says it avoids answering from an empty selection in the synonym fixture.
Says positive overlap can still be insufficient, so the rule establishes no support.
Says raising the threshold excludes some useful short passages.
Says the gate asks for the positive-scoring case the rule wrongly lets through and the case a stricter threshold wrongly refuses.
Says the gate also asks what review remains.

questions.source: The gate: write the source list and the evidence rules first
questions.prompt: The chapter says "design first is not design frozen". Explain what you do if ingestion turns up a source you did not list, or a listed source is absent, and what the packet may claim at the end.

rubric.text: Says the finding reopens the gate.
Says you keep the original list, dated.
Says you add the revision with its reason.
Says the gap between what you expected and what you found is the most informative thing the exercise produces.

Gives the allowed claim form, "under this corpus and these rules, these claims were supported by these passages", and says not to call the packet comprehensive unless the inventory justifies the word.

questions.source: Build It: preserve the scoring path
questions.prompt: Describe the Build It sequence and say why you write your own version before opening the reference.

rubric.text: Says your own version is your baseline: the record of what you understood before Claude touched anything.
Says you implement `vector`, verify the count for repeated mixed-case text, and calculate the office-hours cosine by hand before running it.
Says you preserve the tokens, counts, dot product, norms, and final score rather than a lone decimal.
Says you implement retrieval with positive-score filtering and deterministic sorting, and add a tie test, the synonym miss, and the tests the lesson's six leave open.
Says you should not describe the total as complete retrieval coverage, and any synonym map stays in your learner version with its provenance.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code, then build a bounded Cowork task packet
questions.prompt: Describe how you conduct Claude Code against your gate, including what you give it, what you do with the result, and what you preserve.

rubric.text: Says you give it the contract, the test list, and the audit-view specification, not your implementation.
Says you run your tests on what it returns, yourself.
Says a failing test is often a gap in your gate, which Claude cannot see because it has only what you wrote.
Says you preserve the transcript: prompt, plan, diff, commands, outputs, date, and displayed model label.
Says that if a session failed or did not run, you record that rather than substituting a fixture.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code, then build a bounded Cowork task packet
questions.prompt: After Claude Code returns an implementation, the chapter asks for a comparison with your baseline and a deliberately wrong version. Explain how to read each outcome.

rubric.text: Says a boundary Claude handled that you missed is a revision to your gate.
Says a boundary Claude silently ignored is a defect your tests failed to catch.
Says you ask Claude to propose a deliberately wrong version that still passes your tests.
Says you check by hand whether it does, and that if it does, your list was too weak and you found out cheaply.
Says you verify every suggestion Claude makes about your representation against the displayed mechanism.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code, then build a bounded Cowork task packet
questions.prompt: Explain what the task packet must contain and how the corpus should be built, including the limit on what you may upload.

rubric.text: Says the task packet names the goal, permitted sources, output format, exclusions, and acceptance checks.
Says it states how the selected passages were obtained.
Says the corpus is built from material you are authorized to use, recording source identity, version or date, and inclusion criteria.
Says not to upload restricted material merely because the interface can accept it.
Says that, under the Chapter 5 data boundary, who may read what is a decision people make, not one the interface makes.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code, then build a bounded Cowork task packet
questions.prompt: You run retrieval and discover that a required answer claim has no sufficient evidence in the selected context. Describe what the chapter tells you to do, and what it tells you not to do.

rubric.text: Says to inspect both selected and omitted candidates using the audit view.
Says to compare the inventory with the expected-source list dated before ingestion.
Says to identify, for each required claim, whether sufficient evidence appears in the selected context.
Says to revise the query, representation, corpus, or task scope.
Says not to revise the final prose alone and assume the evidence problem disappeared.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code, then build a bounded Cowork task packet
questions.prompt: You may run your task packet through Claude Cowork. Explain what you must preserve, what you may not claim, and what to do if the interface is unavailable.

rubric.text: Says to preserve actual interface details and output.
Says the chapter cannot claim which internal retrieval steps the product used.
Says to compare your explicit packet and evidence table with the interface task as an observed workflow, not as proof of internal equivalence.
Says that if the interface is unavailable, you ship the offline corpus, retrieval results, and proposed packet.
Says to mark the generation portion not run, with no fabricated results or direct API spending.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (Debug the pipeline in the order information moves)
questions.prompt: A report contains a claim that the evidence does not support. Using the chapter's debugging table, describe the order in which you investigate, the first stage where rewriting the answer helps, and when debugging ends.

rubric.text: Says to start upstream rather than rewriting the answer repeatedly, beginning at the top with eligibility.
Gives the order of the remaining stages: ingestion, representation, scoring and cutoff, selection into context, use, claim.
Says to preserve the score of a document that fell below k rather than pretending it was never considered.
Identifies use as the first stage where rewriting the answer helps, and says support is still a separate review.
Says debugging ends when the stated conclusion matches the actual evidence, not when every stage has produced a green marker.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (Debug the pipeline in the order information moves)
questions.prompt: For the first five stages of the debugging table (eligibility, ingestion, representation, scoring and cutoff, selection into context), say what a failure looks like and whose repair it is. Which of the five does the reference implementation never demonstrate?

rubric.text: Says an eligibility failure is a source excluded by a permission or scope decision, which retrieval cannot legally repair, and the claim may need narrowing.
Says an ingestion failure is a skipped format or the wrong folder read, and that the reference starts from a constructed dictionary and never demonstrates ingestion.
Says a representation failure is the synonym case where the vectors share no coordinate, and no prompt after retrieval repairs it.
Says a scoring and cutoff failure is a positive-overlap document ranked below the cutoff, and that a larger k adds review burden to record.
Says a selection-into-context failure is another filter or manual choice narrowing what Claude saw, which you record by naming each narrowing.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (Debug the pipeline in the order information moves)
questions.prompt: The chapter says its seven-stage decomposition is "not a claim that production systems implement these modules". Explain what the decomposition is, and what you can still record when an interface's internals are unavailable.

rubric.text: Says it is a decomposition of the artifact you can inspect.
Says it does not claim production systems implement these modules.
Says a real interface may combine operations.
Says a real interface may keep internals unavailable.
Says you can still record the source boundary, visible inputs, selected context when exposed, output, and your independent evidence review.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (Chunk boundaries create another representation)
questions.prompt: The reference treats each dictionary value as a complete document. Explain what changes if you add chunking, covering the risks at chunk boundaries, the effect of chunk size and overlap on ranking, and the identifiers you need.

rubric.text: Says adding chunks introduces a selection decision before cosine ranking, and it is yours.
Says a claim and its qualification can fall in adjacent chunks, so retrieving only the claim-shaped fragment can make a passage look stronger than its source.
Says a large chunk can dilute lexical overlap with unrelated terms and lower its normalized score.
Says chunk overlap can reduce some boundary misses but duplicates tokens and candidates and influences ranking and context volume, so the choice is recorded.
Says chunk identifiers must preserve source identity and location, because a citation to chunk-7 is hard to audit otherwise.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (Chunk boundaries create another representation)
questions.prompt: Describe a harmless chunking experiment the chapter suggests, and say what conclusion the chapter wants you to draw from it and what conclusion it does not.

rubric.text: Describes a corpus example with two adjacent sentences, one stating a policy and the next naming an exception.
Says to compare retrieval when the two sentences stay together and when they are split.
Says to state whether the answer still needs the omitted qualification.
Says the reviewer needs enough surrounding text to see whether a qualification was cut away.
Says these are hypotheses to test on declared text, not reasons to assert that one chunk size is correct.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (Build an evidence table that can say no)
questions.prompt: Design the claim-to-source evidence table the chapter describes. State its columns, how it must treat rows that lack support, and why.

rubric.text: Says it needs more than claim and citation columns.
Lists the added columns: the exact supporting passage or stable location, a reviewer judgment, and a note about scope or missing qualification.
Says the judgment distinguishes supported, contradicted, insufficient, and not reviewed, as defined in the gate.
Says an insufficient row is actionable evidence: narrow the sentence, retrieve more material, or abstain.
Says that if the table cannot represent a gap, it pressures the reviewer to hide one, so rows are not forced into supported.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (Build an evidence table that can say no)
questions.prompt: Using the office-hours hypothetical, show how atomic claims and row provenance work in the evidence table.

rubric.text: Labels "appointments are mentioned" as supported by the supplied sentence.
Labels "appointments occur Tuesday at two" as insufficient because the time is absent.
Explains that a paragraph-level judgment could conceal that one part is grounded while another is invented.
Says a string entered by the learner is a constructed fixture.
Says a passage copied from a real policy needs an authorized source, a version or retrieval date where relevant, and enough location information to revisit it, and the roles are not merged unlabeled.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (Build an evidence table that can say no)
questions.prompt: Explain the two disciplines that keep the packet honest about what produced a selection: preserving the query, and distinguishing the source collection from the context finally shown to Claude.

rubric.text: Says to preserve the query that actually produced the selection.
Says a revised query may retrieve better evidence but its success cannot be attributed to the original run.
Says to keep both queries, label the revision, and record any synonym a human supplied after seeing the failure.
Gives the collection-versus-context example: the corpus may hold twenty items, the retriever may return two, and the interface may receive one.
Says a complete selection record names each narrowing, and without it a reviewer may blame the generator for information the workflow never supplied.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (The packet, assembled)
questions.prompt: The chapter says the result is "accountable context", not maximal context. Define it, explain how the packet's parts relate, and say what case the packet must include.

rubric.text: Defines accountable context as enough authorized material to support the bounded answer, an explicit record of what was left out, and a route for saying the evidence is insufficient.
Says the corpus inventory shows what was eligible and the retrieval record shows what the algorithm selected.
Says the task packet shows what Claude was permitted and asked to use, and the evidence table connects claims to exact passages and records gaps.
Says the dated expected-source list sits in front of all of them.
Says the packet must include at least one omitted or insufficient case, explaining whether the source was absent from the corpus, scored zero, or fell below k.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (The packet, assembled)
questions.prompt: Write the sign-off the chapter describes in prose: what each verb may and may not claim, what the "Not checked" line is for, and when you withhold.

rubric.text: Says "retrieved" describes what the selection rule returned and "quoted" describes what you copied.
Says "supported" describes a claim and a passage you actually compared.
Says "verified" and "comprehensive" need more than this packet offers unless you did the work behind them.
Says the "Not checked" line does the work, and that an AI-written sign-off leaves it out because the system has no record of the sources you never opened or the file that failed to load.
Says you write the sign-off from your record, and if your evidence does not support signing, you withhold.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (The driver's seat)
questions.prompt: Choose two rows from the driver's-seat table and, for each, say what Claude should do, what you should do, and why it stays with you.

rubric.text: Correctly describes Claude's role in the first chosen row, such as doing the ranking fast and showing every score, or implementing the retriever from the contract.
Correctly describes your role in that row, such as reading the full audit view rather than only the winners, or building your own baseline first and running your tests on its version.
Gives the chapter's reason for that row, such as omissions being invisible in a list of winners, or that you cannot audit a ranking you never computed.

Correctly describes Claude's and your roles in the second chosen row, such as Claude proposing a synonym map, chunk size, or larger k with cases that might break it while you decide and record where each came from, or Claude proposing a label while you label first from the original.

Gives the chapter's reason for the second row, such as that interchangeability is a fact about the policy and population and not the words, or that what the source means in the world, its scope, date, and who it governs, is your reading.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (The driver's seat)
questions.prompt: The chapter asks you to record one task you delegated and one judgment you retained. What evidence counts, and what does it mean if you cannot produce it?

rubric.text: Says the packet records one delegated task and one retained judgment.
Names the Claude Code transcript showing what you gave it as evidence.
Names the dated expected-source list and its comparison with the inventory as evidence.
Names the rows where your label differed from Claude's proposal, or where you changed your mind, as evidence.
Says that if you cannot point to the transcript line or the edit that shows each, the split happened in your head and not in the record.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.prompt: Describe the Verify and reflect tasks: the expected-source gap, the claim audit, and the vocabulary check.

rubric.text: Says you recalculate one cosine score independently and preserve the interpreter and input corpus rather than reporting a score without its representation.
Says you compare the expected-source list with the inventory and write the gap in one sentence (a source expected and not found, one found and not expected, or neither).
Says you do not rewrite the list to match, because the gap is the learning.
Says you audit one claim against the original source, not only the selected chunk, because chunk boundaries can omit qualifications, and revise or remove the claim if it exceeds the passage.

Says "relevant" should refer to a scoring or human topical judgment you can describe, and "supported" to a claim-evidence relationship you actually inspected, and they are not swapped because both sound favorable.

questions.source: Assessments - ungraded practice
questions.prompt: The query is "office hours". Document d1 is "office hours appointment" and d2 is "office hours". Predict and compute what happens to both scores and to the ranking when "appointment" is added to the query, and explain how the dot product and norm each change.

rubric.text: Gives the scores before the change: d2 is 1.0 and d1 is about 0.8165.
Gives d1 after the change as 1.0 (dot product 3, both lengths sqrt(3)).
Gives d2 after the change as about 0.8165 (dot product 2, lengths sqrt(3) and sqrt(2)).
States that the ranking reverses so d1 ranks above d2.
Explains that the query's length changes for both documents, while the dot product changes only for d1 (from 2 to 3) and stays 2 for d2.

questions.source: What you can now trace
questions.prompt: The closing section describes what you can now trace and what the three jobs look like in this chapter. Explain why a zero-overlap document can be relevant and a high-overlap document insufficient, and how the packet shows you did conduct, check, and drive.

rubric.text: Says a zero-overlap document may be semantically related, and a high-overlap document may still be insufficient.
Says this is not a contradiction, because the score and the support review have different jobs.
Says conducting means you wrote the retriever's contract, the tests that must fail the wrong versions, and a dated list of expected sources before Claude implemented or ranked anything.
Says checking means you refused to let a high score stand in for support and traced what was excluded before treating a selected passage as sufficient.

Says driving means you handed Claude the scoring, implementation, and quoting while keeping the list of what should exist, the label on each claim, and the choice to narrow or abstain, and you signed or withheld.

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.prompt: Explain the access-boundary assumption from the companion Computational Skepticism chapter and how the chapter tells you to apply it to a passage in your corpus.

rubric.text: States that a dataset's effective reach is its schema plus whatever its contents reference.
Says the claim is sharpest for reference-rich material such as email.
Says it is weak for a self-contained table of sensor readings.
Says to check whether a passage quotes, links, or defers to a document that is not on your source list.
Says that if it does, the passage cannot be read as complete without that document, and the dependency belongs in the packet as an unresolved item.

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.prompt: Explain the row-trace step and what the chapter says to do when the original source is unreachable.

rubric.text: Says to follow one answer passage back to its original source.
Says that where the original is unreachable, you document the opacity.
Says the chapter counts documented opacity as a finding and not a failure of the procedure.
Says to record which of "not retrieved", "not in the corpus", and "not true" you could establish and which you could not.
Says these are two questions for the packet and not a measurement of this retriever or corpus.

questions.source: Chapter 8 - MCP from scratch (opening)
questions.prompt: Two servers advertise a tool called `lookup`. Both return valid JSON-RPC messages and copy request identifiers correctly; one reads a declared public fixture and the other writes files as a side effect. Explain why protocol syntax cannot separate them and which question a clean handshake leaves unanswered.

rubric.text: States that protocol syntax cannot tell the two servers apart, so it cannot show that they deserve different permissions.
Defines interoperability as whether components can exchange messages they understand.
Defines authorization as whether a particular capability should run in this task.
Says a clean handshake settles the first question and is silent on the second.
Notes that both servers copy request identifiers correctly, so identifier handling does not distinguish them.

questions.source: Chapter 8 - MCP from scratch (opening)
questions.prompt: Claude is handed only the tool listing for the two servers in the opening scenario. What does Claude lack, what does it not lack, and who decides whether to connect?

rubric.text: Says the listing gives Claude two descriptions to compare, and a description is a sentence the server wrote about itself.
Says that what Claude lacks is not skill with JSON.
Says Claude lacks any standpoint on whether this server belongs in this task.
Names at least two facts Claude lacks: whose data sits behind the server, what a stray file write would cost, who maintains it.
States that the decision to connect is the human's, with Claude's role being to read the transcript and list every discrepancy.

questions.source: Chapter 8 - MCP from scratch (opening)
questions.prompt: The chapter says it applies the book's three jobs at the scale of one connection. Name the three jobs and say what each means for an MCP connection.

rubric.text: Names Conduct, Check, and Drive as the three jobs.
Conduct: fix the order of events and the scope of use before anything is connected.
Check: ask what a transcript entitles you to believe and what it never tested.
Drive: let Claude read the transcript and list every discrepancy.
Says the decision to connect stays with the human under Drive.

questions.source: Chapter 8 - MCP from scratch (opening)
questions.prompt: The research run recorded four observations of the local Python server. List them, and explain what claim they do and do not support.

rubric.text: Listing tools before initialization returns an error.
An initialize request returns protocol version `2025-11-25`.
A valid initialized notification returns no response.
Looking up an unknown record produces a tool result with `isError: true`.
States that these are executed observations of this server, not claims about MCP generally.

questions.source: Chapter 8 - MCP from scratch (opening)
questions.prompt: A classmate writes: 'The teaching server always answers 2025-11-25, so it violates the MCP lifecycle specification.' Evaluate the claim using the chapter's discussion of the version result.

rubric.text: Says the server returns its one supported version without inspecting the client's requested version.
Says that under the versioned lifecycle specification a server may return another supported version when the requested one is unsupported.
Says the client is then left to decide whether it can continue.
Concludes that a fixed fallback is not, by itself, a violation.
Notes the server remains a teaching subset whose omissions the later sections spell out.

questions.source: Chapter 8 - MCP from scratch (opening)
questions.prompt: The chapter warns that protocol education 'decays into a cargo cult of field names'. Explain what that means and what reading the lifecycle 'as behavior' asks you to track.

rubric.text: Describes the cargo cult as copying field names or visible keys without understanding the behavior behind them.
Says a message can copy every visible key of the example and still miss the state machine around it.
Names tracking which message may come next.
Names tracking what state changes and which response belongs to which request.
Names tracking what the host may infer from a result.

questions.source: Chapter 8 - MCP from scratch (opening)
questions.prompt: A student says: 'I ran the default demo, so my server is integrated with Claude.' Using the chapter's opening, say what the demo is and what must happen before anyone may claim a live Claude integration.

rubric.text: Says the server runs offline and needs no direct API credits.
Says the default demo terminates without waiting on standard input.
Says a client may be connected only later, in an explicitly controlled exercise.
Says a live Claude integration must not be claimed unless you actually configured, ran, and recorded it.
Notes that Claude Code remains the assumed course assistant, which is separate from the offline server.

questions.source: What you will be able to do
questions.prompt: Name the four questions the chapter wants you to keep apart for any connection, and give one scenario in which a connection passes one question but fails another.

rubric.text: Names whether the exchange is well formed.
Names whether the code does what the listing says.
Names whether this task may use the connection.
Names whether the returned content supports the claim built on it.
Gives a valid scenario in which one question is passed and another failed (for example, a well-formed exchange with an undeclared write).

questions.source: Four parties and one decision
questions.prompt: Name the four parties in an MCP connection and state what each does. Then say what MCP itself does and does not do.

rubric.text: The server implements capabilities and describes them.
The host constructs requests, interprets responses, exposes selected tools to Claude, and decides what content enters context.
Claude, or a workflow around it, proposes using a tool.
People and policies define authority.
MCP supplies a communication structure; it did not choose the tool and does not vouch for what comes back.

questions.source: Four parties and one decision
questions.prompt: Three of the four parties are software, and none can answer the fourth party's question. State that question and explain, party by party, why each of the three cannot answer it.

rubric.text: States the question: whether this server, this data, and this action are appropriate for this task.
Server: its description is its own testimony.
Host: it can enforce a policy but cannot write one.
Claude: it can weigh a description against a request but has only what the session supplied, which does not include who owns the data, what the task is for, or what a wrong answer costs.
Says the protocol carries the capability declaration while the authority is written somewhere else, by someone, before the call.

questions.source: Initialization is a state transition
questions.prompt: Describe the two state variables in the reference server and trace both through the legal sequence of initialize, the initialized notification, and a tool request.

rubric.text: Both flags start false.
A valid initialize request sets `initialized` to true and returns server information and capabilities.
A `notifications/initialized` message arriving while `initialized` is true sets `ready` to true.
Tool operations are rejected until the server is ready.
Says the two flags are related but not interchangeable.

questions.source: Initialization is a state transition
questions.prompt: Why does the protocol use two steps, an initialize request and response followed by an initialized notification, instead of treating the server as ready once initialize succeeds? Include the cost of the design.

rubric.text: The request and response let client and server exchange protocol information.
The notification lets the client say it has finished that phase.
Readiness becomes a statement by the client and a precondition for the server.
It is not inferred from the fact that a process exists or that a tool list could be built.
The cost is state, a place where two parties can disagree about history; a stateless server would be shorter but impossible to hold to an order.

questions.source: Initialization is a state transition
questions.prompt: A client sends `notifications/initialized` before it has sent `initialize` and receives nothing back. What did the server do, why is the silence correct, and what can the client not infer from it?

rubric.text: A message with no `id` is treated as a notification.
Before initialize, nothing changes: `ready` stays false.
The handler returns `None`, because no response is expected on this route.
The silence is not a lost message to be patched with an invented acknowledgement.
Silence looks the same as a notification that took effect, so the client cannot infer readiness and must keep its own record of the lifecycle.

questions.source: The initialize exchange
questions.prompt: The recorded run sends an initialize request whose requested version is `unsupported-fixture`. What happened, and what can and cannot be concluded?

rubric.text: The server answered `2025-11-25` anyway.
The server does not inspect a `params` object on initialize.
On this branch it cannot distinguish a supported request from a malformed one.
Capability negotiation is narrow: a tools capability with an empty object, with nothing checked about the client, which suffices for the tool list that follows.
It does not certify any lifecycle clause.

questions.source: The initialize exchange
questions.prompt: Compare the claim 'The fixed version violates MCP' with the claim 'The teaching server does not evaluate the requested version or validate the required initialization fields, so it is not a conformance implementation.' Which is better, and what test does the better one suggest?

rubric.text: The first claim overstates the case, since a server may return another supported version.
The second names the mechanisms actually missing.
The second says the teaching server is not a conformance implementation, rather than saying it violates the protocol.
Proposes a concrete next test, such as sending initialize with an unsupported requested version or without the required initialization fields and checking whether the server evaluates it.
Says a criticism too broad to test is one more fluent claim.

questions.source: Discovery reveals a declared capability
questions.prompt: After readiness, `tools/list` returns one tool. Describe the declaration (name, description, input schema) and say who uses it and for what.

rubric.text: The name is `lookup`.
The description is 'Read a public course fixture'.
The input schema requires exactly one property, `key`, which must be a string, and allows no additional properties.
A host uses the declaration to build a request.
In some integration designs a model or a user uses it to decide whether the tool is worth calling, and it is server-supplied text about the server.

questions.source: Discovery reveals a declared capability
questions.prompt: The tool description says 'Read a public course fixture'. In what sense is it accurate, what word in it does the server have no standing to assert, and where does that word belong?

rubric.text: It is accurate in the author's sense, because the code consults one mapping.
'Public' is a classification of data.
Nothing in the code classifies anything, so the server cannot tell you the fixture is public.
The word belongs in the permission ledger, filled in by whoever owns the data.
A description can be technically accurate and still carry a word the server had no standing to assert.

questions.source: Discovery reveals a declared capability
questions.prompt: A candidate server's description says it only reads a public course fixture. Explain why you should not accept that on faith, and how a tool description can influence a model.

rubric.text: A defective or malicious server could advertise a harmless purpose and do something else.
Evaluating a candidate takes source inspection, sandboxing, provenance, or other evidence appropriate to the deployment.
Recalls the Chapter 1 point that a system prompt is a request, not a gate.
A tool description placed in Claude's context is more text competing for influence there.
A misleading description can steer which tool gets chosen before any runtime check runs.

questions.source: Discovery reveals a declared capability
questions.prompt: 'Discovery is not consent to call.' Explain this with a contrast between a read-only server and a write-capable server whose listings are equally well formed.

rubric.text: A host can learn which tools exist and still deny them under its permission policy.
A read-only tool may suit public course fixtures and not restricted material.
A write-capable server needs a different action boundary.
This holds even when its listing is equally well formed.
Concludes that a well-formed listing is evidence about capability, not permission to call.

questions.source: Requests, identifiers, and tool results
questions.prompt: A `tools/call` can go wrong at three layers. Name them, give the lookup example of each, and say what a host learns by reading the reply this way.

rubric.text: Lifecycle: the call came too early.
Request: the tool or its arguments are wrong, such as an unknown tool or a bad `key`, reported as `-32602`.
Task: the lookup ran and found nothing, reported as a result with `isError` true.
The reply tells you which layer failed, if you read it that way.
Request-validation failures mean the tool never produced a content result.

questions.source: Requests, identifiers, and tool results
questions.prompt: Why is a missing record a tool result with `isError: true` and not a JSON-RPC error? What does that let a host do, and what mistake does the chapter name?

rubric.text: The request was well formed, the method existed, and the tool ran its lookup.
The failure belongs to the task result, whose text is `Record not found`.
Keeping the layer distinct lets a host decide whether to revise the arguments, report an absence, or stop.
It avoids treating every negative as a broken protocol.
A host that ignores `isError` and presents `Record not found` as an ordinary fact misuses a well-formed result.

questions.source: Requests, identifiers, and tool results
questions.prompt: Explain two limits that apply to every reply: what a matching identifier does not prove, and why returned content stays untrusted.

rubric.text: A matching id shows which response belongs with which request.
It says nothing about whether the tool used the intended data.
It says nothing about whether the result is safe to pass on.
The content stays untrusted data: a successful response containing text does not make the text correct.
In this fixture the mapping is declared in source so you can compare directly, while a different server's result needs provenance appropriate to where it came from.

questions.source: History is part of the protocol
questions.prompt: Using the transition table, explain what a list of isolated JSON examples hides. Use two pairs of rows.

rubric.text: `tools/list` fails in row 2 and succeeds in row 7.
The only difference between those rows is history.
Rows 3 and 6 receive the same response, which is none.
In row 3 nothing changes, while in row 6 readiness begins.
Concludes that a message must be read together with the prior state, not alone.

questions.source: History is part of the protocol
questions.prompt: A fresh server receives, in order: (1) `tools/list` with id 1, (2) `initialize` with id 2, (3) `tools/list` with id 3, (4) `notifications/initialized`, (5) `tools/list` with id 5. Predict the response and the (initialized, ready) state after each message.

rubric.text: Message 1: error `-32000`, state stays F, F.
Message 2: a result with version `2025-11-25`, state T, F.
Message 3: error `-32000` again, state stays T, F.
Message 4: no response, state T, T.
Message 5: a result listing one tool, `lookup`, state stays T, T.

questions.source: History is part of the protocol
questions.prompt: Explain why a method named `bad` can receive different error codes, and what an error code does and does not tell you. Include the two parse-level cases in stdio mode.

rubric.text: Sent to a ready server, `bad` receives `-32601`.
Sent in row 2's state it would have received `-32000`.
An error code reports the branch the server reached, not every defect the message had.
The text `{` fails before the handler: the main loop catches a parsing `ValueError` and emits `-32700` with a null id.
The text `{}` parses and receives `-32600`, so the raw text should be preserved to tell the two apart.

questions.source: History is part of the protocol
questions.prompt: The chapter names two behaviors 'never chosen by anyone'. Identify them, and explain why the chapter does not call them bugs or specification violations.

rubric.text: A second `initialize` sent to a ready server leaves `ready` true.
A `tools/call` sent without an id is dropped without a response, even when the server is ready.
Neither behavior is pinned by the lesson's tests.
The chapter does not claim to know what the specification requires for either.
They are what the code does because nothing said otherwise, which is the cost of leaving a handshake rule implicit.

questions.source: History is part of the protocol
questions.prompt: Describe what the default demo and the `--stdio` mode do, and why you should not infer production transport guarantees from the stdio loop.

rubric.text: The default demo constructs a server, initializes it, sends the notification, lists tools, prints the response, and exits.
The `--stdio` flag opts into reading newline-delimited messages until input ends.
The loop reads one line at a time.
It prints one JSON response per non-notification result and flushes.
It has no framing, cancellation, timeout, concurrency, or security feature beyond that.

questions.source: Compatibility is not authorized: Four ledgers for one connection decision
questions.prompt: Name the four ledgers. For each, state its question, what fills it, and what reopens it. Then say whether one ledger can stand in for another.

rubric.text: Protocol: is the exchange well formed and in order; filled by the transcript; reopened by a protocol-version change.
Capability: does the code do what the listing says; filled by source inspection, disposable fixtures, and who maintains it; reopened by a new advertised tool or a new release.
Permission: does this task allow that capability; filled by the task brief, the data owner, and your policy; reopened by a changed task or broader data scope.
Evidence: does the returned content support the claim built on it; filled by comparison with the declared source; reopened by a changed corpus.
States that no ledger can stand in for another, and that the ledgers are a teaching device rather than a standard.

questions.source: Compatibility is not authorized: Four ledgers for one connection decision
questions.prompt: Apply the four ledgers to the teaching lookup. What can each ledger record?

rubric.text: Protocol ledger: a legal initialization and call.
Capability ledger: the code reads one in-memory mapping and performs no file write.
Permission ledger: whether the public fixture is allowed for the classroom task.
Evidence ledger: a comparison of `505A Dana Hall` with the declared fixture source.
States that none of these records can stand in for another.

questions.source: Compatibility is not authorized: Four ledgers for one connection decision
questions.prompt: Consider two cases: (a) the protocol ledger is perfect but the capability ledger reveals an undeclared write; (b) the capability is properly read-only but the returned fixture is stale. For each, say what succeeds and what fails, and what the word 'passed' must always include.

rubric.text: Case (a): the connection succeeds and the behavior exceeds the task boundary.
Case (a): the failure appears in the capability ledger, not the protocol ledger.
Case (b): permission is satisfied.
Case (b): the evidence claim fails.
'Passed' must always name which review passed.

questions.source: Compatibility is not authorized: Four ledgers for one connection decision
questions.prompt: How should you record what you did not inspect, and why does the last column of the ledger table turn a verdict into a bounded decision?

rubric.text: Write 'uninspected', not 'none'.
The absence of observed harm in a test you did not perform is not evidence that the capability is absent.
For a closed-source server, advertised behavior may be the only evidence available, and the decision should say so.
The 'what reopens it' column bounds the decision by naming the changes that trigger review.
Trust becomes a decision over identifiable inputs that reopens when one changes, not a permanent property of a server's name.

questions.source: Compatibility is not authorized: The host is part of the mechanism
questions.prompt: Where does the server's responsibility end, and what do the host and client decide? Why can the teaching server not demonstrate the client's side, and what would a complete interoperability test need?

rubric.text: The server's responsibility ends at its reply, and the host decides what enters context.
The client must decide whether it supports the server-selected version, and the specification's fallback route depends on that decision.
The teaching server implements only the server object, so it cannot demonstrate the client's behavior.
A complete interoperability test needs both sides, or an explicit harness that represents the client's obligations.

Names at least three host defenses (approval before consequential tools, independent argument validation, restricted data access, call caps, result verification) and notes the chapter does not claim any particular host implements all of them.

questions.source: Compatibility is not authorized: The host is part of the mechanism
questions.prompt: You are recording an actual host integration. What host configuration belongs in the record, what stays out, and why?

rubric.text: Include the command and the working directory.
Include the environment boundary and the enabled tools.
A transcript without configuration leaves the source of the server ambiguous.
Leave out secrets.
Do not commit credentials or private paths to make the record complete.

questions.source: Compatibility is not authorized: Laundering: valid transport, borrowed authority
questions.prompt: Explain 'laundering' as the chapter uses it, including what each hop in the lookup chain adds and what none of them checked.

rubric.text: A valid text result is inserted into Claude's context and restated fluently, until a string a server produced reads as an established fact.
The JSON-RPC envelope gives the text the shape of a protocol-valid reply, and the matching id gives it the look of an answer to your question.
`isError: false` gives it the look of success.
Claude's sentence gives it fluency.
None of those hops checked the content: polish is not provenance.

questions.source: Compatibility is not authorized: Laundering: valid transport, borrowed authority
questions.prompt: Fill in the chapter's handoff table for the course lookup: for each of the three handoffs, say what passes, what it is trusted to be, and how that trust is earned. Then say what an unverified handoff allows.

rubric.text: States the defense: treat each handoff as a decision and write down what is passed, what it is trusted to be, and how that trust was earned.
Server to host: the reply carrying `505A Dana Hall`, trusted to be the fixture's value for key `office` from this server version, earned by comparison with the mapping in the inspected source.

Host to Claude's context: that text as data to cite with its role, not an instruction and not a current fact, earned by the recorded host configuration and your instruction about how the text may be used.
Claude to answer: a sentence such as 'The course fixture lists the office as 505A Dana Hall', earned by keeping the fixture role and tracing the value to the source comparison.
A handoff with no verification lets an unverified output travel onward wearing the authority of every clean step it passed through.

questions.source: Compatibility is not authorized: Laundering: valid transport, borrowed authority
questions.prompt: From the first row of the handoff table, what may the host infer and what may it not? What is the right continuation when the tool returns a missing record, and why can the model's own loop not be relied on to stop a guess?

rubric.text: The host may infer that this server returned the displayed fixture text for a particular request under the recorded implementation.
It may not infer that an external fact is current or universally correct without another source check.
The phrasing is narrower because the evidence is narrower.
For a missing record, the right continuation is the absence itself plus a decision about whether to ask another authorized source.
Nothing in the loop that produces Claude's next token stops a fluent guess; the stop must be a rule written into the host or instruction and a check run on the answer afterward.

questions.source: The gate: write the connection decision before you connect
questions.prompt: State the contract for the state machine that the gate asks you to write.

rubric.text: Tool operations are refused until initialize and then the initialized notification have both arrived, in that order.
A notification never produces a response.
Every response carries the id of the request it answers.
A tool-level negative is a result with `isError`, while a protocol-level problem is an error with a code.
The subset does not claim version negotiation.

questions.source: The gate: write the connection decision before you connect
questions.prompt: For the task of finding the office for key `office` from the declared course fixture, write the connection contract: what each of the permission, capability, and evidence ledgers must contain, and what each entry needs.

rubric.text: Permission ledger: names the sources the task may read, the effects it may have (none beyond returning text), and where results may go.
Capability ledger: lists the claims to check in source: one mapping, no write, no network.
Evidence ledger: requires that every value Claude may cite be compared with the declared source first.
Every entry is given an evidence type.
Names at least four of the five evidence types: advertised, source-inspected, executed on a fixture, independently sourced, uninspected.

questions.source: The gate: write the connection decision before you connect
questions.prompt: Describe the three constructed wrong versions your checks must catch, and which ledger or test catches each.

rubric.text: A server that sets `ready` inside the initialize branch skips the notification, and applied to a copy of the reference it leaves all six of the lesson's tests passing.
The case that fails it, `tools/list` after initialize and before the notification, is not among the lesson's tests.
A `lookup` with a flawless lifecycle that appends to a log file on every call passes the protocol ledger and fails the capability ledger.
A read-only `lookup` whose fixture value disagrees with the declared source passes three ledgers and fails the evidence ledger.
If your checks cannot tell these from the right server, the gate is not finished.

questions.source: The gate: write the connection decision before you connect
questions.prompt: Explain the failure sentence, the pass condition, and the role of a qualified reviewer in the gate.

rubric.text: The failure sentence is written and dated before you read any transcript, saying what you would see if your table were wrong.
If it is written after reading the output, you have described the output.
The pass condition is that a stranger holding your transcript, the source, and the task brief can mark every line of the four ledgers with an evidence type.
The stranger finds no empty cell, no word like safe or trusted without a named evidence type, and a re-review trigger beside the decision.
Whether the fixture is public needs a qualified reviewer, its owner, and you should record who that is.

questions.source: Build It: implement the state machine before connection
questions.prompt: Why does the chapter ask you to build the state machine by hand before consulting the reference, and what are the build steps?

rubric.text: Your own version is the record of what you understood before Claude touched anything.
It is also the instrument you will measure Claude's version against.
Create the two flags and the base message validation, implement initialize and then the initialized notification, and test both orders.
Add `tools/list` behind the readiness check, then the lookup tool, separating malformed arguments, unknown tool, known record, and missing record.
Once you can explain your version, compare it with the reference and name a difference in behavior, not in line count or style.

questions.source: Build It: implement the state machine before connection
questions.prompt: Describe how to use the six existing tests, and which lifecycle case you should add and why.

rubric.text: Read the six existing tests before the reference and predict each error code or state.
Add one malformed-argument case and one lifecycle case the suite lacks.
The best candidate is initialize, then `tools/list` without the notification, which must still return `-32000`.
That case catches the ready-on-initialize change, which leaves all six existing tests passing.
State what remains outside the subset.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code, then ask it for discrepancies, not a verdict
questions.prompt: Describe how to conduct Claude Code against your gate and what to do with what it returns, including what you preserve.

rubric.text: Give Claude the gate (transition table, contract, test list), not your implementation.
Ask for a server that satisfies the contract and passes your tests, then run your tests on what it returns yourself.
Note which tests failed, since a failing test is often a gap in your gate that Claude could not see.
Compare its server with your baseline and name one difference in behavior.
Preserve the actual transcript (prompt, plan, diff, commands, outputs, date, displayed model label), and if a session failed or did not run, record that rather than substituting a fixture.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code, then ask it for discrepancies, not a verdict
questions.prompt: Explain how to test whether your own tests are strong enough, using a deliberately wrong server and a control. What do you do when a case slips through?

rubric.text: Ask Claude for a deliberately wrong server that still passes your tests, and run your tests against it.
As a control, make the ready-on-initialize change to a copy of your own server and run the same tests.
If the tests do not catch it, your list was too weak, and you found out cheaply.
A case your gate missed reopens the gate: revise it, date the revision, and keep the original.
Designing first is not freezing the design.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code, then ask it for discrepancies, not a verdict
questions.prompt: Describe the discrepancy prompt: what you give Claude, what you ask for, what you withhold, and what you do with the answer.

rubric.text: You provide a transcript, the server source, and the advertised description.
You ask for every place where they disagree, or where one claims more than another supports, with the line relied on quoted.
You withhold the verdict: no advice on whether to connect, and no calling any behavior safe.
You check every item against the source yourself, since some will be wrong and an item's absence is not evidence that no discrepancy exists.
The decision is yours: allow, deny, or pending, in your own words.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code, then ask it for discrepancies, not a verdict
questions.prompt: Explain the trap in using a server's import list as evidence that it cannot write files, and say what evidence does establish it. Then say how to treat an external candidate whose inspection is incomplete.

rubric.text: The reference imports only `argparse`, `json`, and `sys`.
That proves nothing about files, because `open` is a builtin and needs no import.
What establishes that the lookup writes nothing is the call branch itself, where the only data consulted is a literal mapping.
For an external candidate, use only source and documentation you have actually inspected, and record the decision as pending or deny if inspection is incomplete.
Do not invent a server's behavior from its tool description, and note that the exercise certifies no external package.

questions.source: Ship It: an MCP evaluation packet
questions.prompt: A student's evaluation packet contains only the `tools/list` output and the sentence 'looks safe'. List what is missing.

rubric.text: A chronological transcript preserving requests, notifications, responses, identifiers, state transitions, and errors.
One successful and one failing call with matching ids, and an explanation of why the missing record is a tool error and not a protocol error.
For each capability: what the server says, what source inspection shows, which disposable tests ran, and what remains unknown.
An allow, deny, or pending decision for the bounded task, with a reason.
Says a valid tool listing belongs in the evidence but is not the decision, and that 'safe' needs a named evidence type.

questions.source: Ship It: an MCP evaluation packet
questions.prompt: In your packet, a fixture value is deliberately wrong. Where should it be caught, which ledger catches it, and what must you not conclude?

rubric.text: The packet includes a handoff analysis: the three-row table filled in for your own run.
The source comparison that catches the wrong value must be shown, and it must happen before generation.
The evidence ledger is the one that fails.
You must not call the protocol exchange failed when the factual check is what rejects the value.
Notes the wrong value still passes the protocol, capability, and permission ledgers.

questions.source: Ship It: an MCP evaluation packet
questions.prompt: Describe the sign-off template line by line: what goes on each line, and what the 'Not checked' and 'Not claiming' lines are for.

rubric.text: Checked: which ledger lines, and the evidence type for each.
How: by hand, by a test written before reading the reference, by source comparison, or with Claude's help, saying which parts.
Not checked: examples such as network behavior, other versions of the server, client-side version handling, and whether the fixture is true in the world.
Not claiming: that the server is secure, conformant to MCP, or endorsed beyond this task and version.
Decision (allow, deny, or pending, for a named task and server version), a re-review trigger, and a signed or withheld line with name and date.

questions.source: Ship It: an MCP evaluation packet
questions.prompt: Distinguish the decision from the sign-off, and say which verbs the evidence earns.

rubric.text: The decision is about the server, while the sign-off is about your evidence for the decision.
You can sign a deny, and you can withhold your signature from an allow that your evidence does not support.
The 'Not checked' line is the one an AI-written sign-off leaves empty, because the system has no record of what you did not do.
Earned verbs: recorded for a transcript, inspected for source you read, executed for a fixture you ran, compared for a source check.
Secure, trusted, and verified need a criterion this exercise never supplies.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.prompt: Using the driver's seat table, divide the work on out-of-order and malformed messages and on implementing the state machine, and give the reason each part stays with you.

rubric.text: Claude can generate many out-of-order and malformed messages quickly and run them.
You decide the expected response for each message.
The expected response is the contract, and the code cannot supply it.
Claude can implement the state machine from your gate and write tests, but you build your own baseline first and run your tests, including against a wrong server.
You cannot audit a lifecycle you have not built.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.prompt: Using the driver's seat table, divide the work on the lifecycle page, on classifying the data, and on allow, deny, or pending, and give the reason each part stays with you.

rubric.text: Claude can quote and summarize the lifecycle page, but you check the clauses and keep the version claim narrow.
A recollection of a protocol is not the protocol.
Claude can draft the capability inventory, but you decide what the data is and what the task may touch.
Classification and scope are facts about your world that a transcript does not contain.
Claude can draft the packet, but you decide, set the re-review trigger, and sign or withhold, since the decision carries your name and the cost of a wrong one lands on whoever owns the data.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.prompt: Does the chapter claim that Claude cannot reason about trust decisions? Explain what it does claim.

rubric.text: The trust decision rests on facts about the world around the transcript.
Names those facts: who owns the data, what the task needs, what a wrong answer costs, and who maintains the server.
The transcript contains none of them.
The claim is not that Claude is incapable of reasoning about such facts; in this task they are not among its inputs unless you supply them.
Accountability for a wrong decision lands on a person.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.prompt: Explain what it means to read the transcript 'in both directions', and what a tool list or tool result in isolation leaves out.

rubric.text: Reading as the server: given this state and message, which branch runs, what response it produces, and what state changes.
Reading as a reviewer: given this response, which request and prior transition must be present before the interpretation is justified.
The two passes catch different omissions.
A tool list in isolation omits the initialize request, the notification, the process configuration, and the source version; a tool result in isolation loses the arguments and identifier.
Every error code you report should be attached to the raw constructed message and server state it came from, because 'MCP failed' erases the mechanism.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.prompt: Describe the correspondence review between transcript and source, and the 'what did not happen' row you should add. Why must you not call the subset conformant?

rubric.text: The review checks that the advertised tool name matches the dispatch branch.
It checks that the schema matches the argument validation and that `isError` appears for the recorded missing key.
It is stronger than the listing or code inspection alone, and it is still evidence about the tested implementation and version.
The default demo did not connect to Claude, expose a network port, write a file, authenticate a user, or validate a production deployment.
A narrow server can be complete as a teaching artifact and incomplete as a product, and a happy path that resembles the specification does not make it conformant.

questions.source: Assessments - ungraded practice
questions.prompt: Describe the 'Too early' Assessment, including what you must explain and what test you must write.

rubric.text: Send `tools/list` before readiness and preserve the code.
Complete initialization and retry.
Explain the changed state rather than calling the first message malformed.
Write the test that stops the ready-on-initialize change.
Show that test failing against that change.

questions.source: What you can now trace
questions.prompt: A student says: 'I had Claude Code build the server and tell me it was safe, then I signed the sign-off.' Using the chapter's three jobs, say what the student skipped.

rubric.text: Conduct was skipped: no lifecycle table, four-ledger contract, or wrong servers were written before Claude saw any code.
Check was skipped: no record of what a wrong server would show, and no separate evidence types for each ledger.
'Safe' without a named evidence type fails the pass condition, since secure, trusted, and verified need a criterion the exercise never supplies.
Drive was misapplied: the student handed Claude the question of whether to connect, which the chapter keeps with the human.
The sign-off should be written from the student's own record, since an AI-written sign-off leaves the 'Not checked' line empty.

questions.source: Connecting a tool is not training a model
questions.prompt: Why does the chapter end by saying that connecting a tool is not training a model, and what does it set up for Chapter 9?

rubric.text: An MCP server can add information and actions to a host without changing model parameters.
That distinction is the bridge to Chapter 9.
Chapter 9 implements a tiny logistic predictor whose weight and bias genuinely update under a loss function.
It compares that mechanism with changes to prompts, context, tools, and settings.
The gate question comes with us: before you change anything, state what should change and what would show that it did.

questions.source: Anthropics
questions.prompt: What does the 'Anthropics' section ask you to do with Anthropic's MCP builder materials and evaluation guide, and what does it say not to do?

rubric.text: Compare your server with Anthropic's MCP builder materials and evaluation guide, which were checked through the course research on 2026-09-06.
Identify one answerable task and an independently verifiable result for the read-only fixture.
Keep the versioned specification as the protocol authority.
Do not treat upstream examples as permission to connect an unreviewed server.
Do not install an external skill merely because the links exist.

questions.source: Conducting AI
questions.prompt: Apply the Conducting AI test to the check 'ask Claude whether `505A Dana Hall` looks right'. Why is it weak, what is a stronger check, and what exercise does the chapter propose for each check in your packet?

rubric.text: An audit reduces error only to the degree that the checker fails differently from the thing it checks.
Asking Claude whether the value looks right, with no source in hand, judges plausibility.
Plausibility is the ground the original answer stood on.
Comparing the value with the mapping in the inspected source fails in an unrelated way: it errors loudly and cannot be persuaded.
For each check, write one sentence on how it can fail and one on how the thing it checks can fail; if the two match, you have a repeat, not a check.

questions.source: Conducting AI
questions.prompt: What does a successful MCP exchange establish, what does it not establish, and how does the chapter divide the final responsibilities between Claude and the human?

rubric.text: A successful exchange establishes transport behavior.
It does not make the returned value true.
It does not authorize the next action.
Claude can organize and inspect the transcript and propose which source to compare against.
The human decides whether the server, data, and action scope are appropriate for the task.

questions.source: Chapter 9 - Training and configuration (opening)
questions.prompt: A teammate writes up an improved answer as "we trained Claude on our policies" after uploading documents and revising a system prompt. In a paragraph, say what actually changed, what the verb "trained" claims, and why that claim matters for what you maintain, audit, and pay for.

rubric.text: States that what changed is the input available during that interaction (the uploaded documents and the revised prompt).
States that training changes parameters through an objective and an update rule.
Says a prompt change lives in a text file you can diff and copy, while a retrieval change lives in a corpus and a selection step and disappears when the corpus does.
States that prompting and retrieval change the information supplied to an already configured model for inference, not its parameters.
Explains that the verb decides what happens next: one word hides three different things to maintain, audit, and pay for.

questions.source: Chapter 9 - Training and configuration (opening)
questions.prompt: A report says: "Average loss fell from 0.6931471806 to 0.0215209850 and the four held-out points were all right, so the model learned and it generalizes." Which half of the conclusion does the evidence support, and which half does it not? Justify both.

rubric.text: Accepts that "learned" is supported, because the parameters changed by a rule you can print.
Rejects "generalizes" as unsupported by this evidence.
Explains that the loss is the number the optimizer was told to lower, on the data it was shown.
Notes that the four held-out points were chosen by one person around the same sign boundary as the training data.
Concludes that neither number says what the sentence says it does, and that no line of code is at fault.

questions.source: Chapter 9 - Training and configuration (opening)
questions.prompt: Name Chapter 1's three jobs and say how each applies to a change request in this chapter. For each, say what you do and what the chapter calls the moment or place where it happens.

rubric.text: Conduct: states what should change, and how you will tell, before you change it.
Identifies that Conduct moment as the gate.
Check: claims only what the record supports, and signs or withholds.
Identifies that Check moment as the sign-off.
Drive: decides what kind of question is being answered, because the causal question and its justification are yours (the driver's seat).

questions.source: Chapter 9 - Training and configuration (opening)
questions.prompt: Describe the classifier built in this chapter in two or three sentences, then state three things the chapter says the exercise does not do or is not.

rubric.text: Describes a one-feature binary logistic classifier with two learned parameters, a weight and a bias.
Mentions the four constructed training examples, the sigmoid, the binary logistic loss, and gradient descent.
States that nothing in the exercise modifies Claude's weights.
States that nothing in the exercise exposes Claude's logits, optimizer, or training data.
States that it is not a miniature language model in every relevant sense and not a fine-tune of anything, but a transparent case of one row in a table of five.

questions.source: Chapter 9 - Training and configuration (opening)
questions.prompt: The chapter asks you to write and date two predictions before reading the reference. State the two predictions, with the correct answer for this toy, and explain why the timing matters.

rubric.text: The initial probability for every point when both parameters are zero is one-half.
The weight should move in the positive direction on the first update, reasoned from the labels and the signs of the features.
Adds that you also write what a wrong answer would look like.
Explains that a prediction written after you have seen the output describes the output.
Says a model that returns plausible decimals is no substitute for knowing which direction should reduce the loss.

questions.source: Name the mutable object before you change it
questions.prompt: Name the five objects a system change can modify. For each, say what you edit and where the change lives.

rubric.text: Weights: parameters edited through an objective and an update rule, living in the saved parameter values.
Prompt: instruction text and examples, living in a file or message you can diff.
Context: which documents, passages, or records are supplied this turn, living in the corpus or store and the selection step.
Tools: which actions and information sources the host exposes and which are permitted, living in server code, configuration, and permission rules.
Settings: how outputs are drawn at run time (temperature is the example), living in run-time configuration.

questions.source: Name the mutable object before you change it
questions.prompt: Which of the five rows involves an optimizer, and what can someone outside the people who train Claude observe about it? Given that limit, why does the chapter build a toy classifier?

rubric.text: States that only the weights row involves an optimizer.
States that for Claude nobody outside the people who train it can watch that row change.
Notes that the course does not claim otherwise.
Explains that the toy lets you watch the weights row change once, completely.
Explains that this lets you recognize the other four rows by contrast, without leaning on metaphor.

questions.source: Name the mutable object before you change it
questions.prompt: A colleague rewrites a system prompt and Claude's behavior changes dramatically. Another colleague changes one few-shot example and the answer changes. For each, say what the evidence supports and what it does not.

rubric.text: Identifies the system prompt as text in the input of an interaction.
States that behavior can change dramatically while the stored parameters stay untouched.
Identifies few-shot examples as input that demonstrates a pattern inside the current context.
Says the few-shot result supports prompt-context sensitivity under the recorded interaction.
Says neither result supports a claim that Claude was retrained.

questions.source: Name the mutable object before you change it
questions.prompt: Explain what retrieval, an MCP server, and a permission rule each change, and say why calling a permission change "learning" is a problem.

rubric.text: Retrieval decides which source passages enter the context; adding a document changes what inference can see and nothing about the model.
An MCP server changes the actions and information the host exposes.
A permission rule changes which proposed operations the runtime allows.
Both change capability and governance: a system can become more capable through tooling while the model stays exactly as it was.
Calling a permission change "learning" turns a human governance decision into something that sounds like a property of the machine.

questions.source: Name the mutable object before you change it
questions.prompt: Does the chapter rank the five objects? If not, say what ordering it calls useful, and give two statements it makes about when training is or is not the right tool.

rubric.text: States that the chapter does not rank the rows.
States that prompting and retrieval are often the right tool for task-specific behavior.
States that training can be expensive, unnecessary, or out of reach.
Names the useful ordering as reversibility and inspectability.
Places text you can diff and revert in a second at one end and parameters you can only refit at the other.

questions.source: Name the mutable object before you change it
questions.prompt: A single configuration file contains a temperature value and a permission rule for a tool. What does "trace the object, not the filename" mean here, and where should details about Claude's interface and configuration come from?

rubric.text: States that a configuration file can hold several kinds of setting at once.
Classifies the temperature value as a setting (run-time configuration of how outputs are drawn).
Classifies the permission rule as belonging to the tools row (what is permitted).
Concludes that the filename does not tell you which object changed, so you trace the object.
Says Claude interface and configuration details come from current official documentation, and that you claim no access to proprietary weights or private training procedures.

questions.source: Persistence is not proof of training
questions.prompt: A saved system prompt, a retrieved document, a permission rule, and a memory record all persist after the interaction that made them. Why can't "it stuck" be the test for learning, and what does identify training?

rubric.text: Names at least three of the four persistent non-training changes.
Says "it stuck" cannot be the test, because several non-training changes persist.
States that training is identified by its mechanism, not by later influence.
Gives the toy as direct implementation evidence: train returns w and b after using labels and a loss-derived gradient.
Explains that a saved prompt influences later requests by being included again as input, so both have durable effects through different routes in the software.

questions.source: Persistence is not proof of training
questions.prompt: A product remembers a user's preferences from one session to the next. How should you describe this behavior, and what would you need before saying the model "learned the user"?

rubric.text: Says the system may retrieve stored preferences or prepend them to the context.
Says that without evidence of parameter updates you describe the memory or context behavior you observed.
Says "learned the user" in the technical sense used here requires evidence of parameter updates.
Identifies personalization as the same case as saved prompts and retrieved documents: persistence is not proof of training.
Proposes a test: remove the stored preferences, hold the rest fixed, rerun the same input, and see whether the behavior goes with them.

questions.source: Persistence is not proof of training
