questions.prompt: Design the test that shows whether a saved piece of text, rather than anything else, is responsible for a Claude behavior. Say what you change, what you hold fixed, how many runs you use and why, and how this differs from asking what correlates with the improvement.

rubric.text: Changes one object (removes the saved text) and holds the rest fixed.
Runs the same input again.
States that if the behavior goes with the text, the text was holding it.
Explains that with sampling in play one run per condition shows little, so repeated runs (Chapter 1) apply.
Explains this is an intervention (doing something to the system and watching what follows), not a question about what correlates with the improvement.

questions.source: What a production record can and cannot show
questions.prompt: For each change you make, you keep a before and an after. Say what to keep for training, a prompt, retrieval, and tools, and explain why an observed output difference alone does not identify the mechanism.

rubric.text: Training: the parameter values and the data, objective, rate, and budget that produced them.
Prompt: both texts.
Retrieval: the corpus and the selected passages; tools: the configuration diff and the authorized decision.
Says an output difference usually does not uniquely identify the mechanism, since it could come from prompt text, retrieved context, tool output, model version, or sampling conditions.
Says the surrounding record is what lets you attribute the change cautiously.

questions.source: What a production record can and cannot show
questions.prompt: A teammate reruns a task after adding a few-shot example and also after the service quietly moves to a newer model version. The answers improve and the teammate writes that the new example fixed the problem. Using the chapter, explain what the record cannot show and how to repair the comparison.

rubric.text: Notes that model version is one of the things that could produce a different answer, alongside prompt text, retrieved context, tool output, and sampling conditions.
States that an output difference usually does not uniquely identify the mechanism.
Says the comparison should change one object and hold the rest fixed.
Says repeated runs per condition are needed because sampling is in play.
Says the supportable claim concerns inputs under the recorded interaction, not a change to Claude's weights, and that the surrounding record lets you attribute cautiously.

questions.source: What a production record can and cannot show
questions.prompt: A hosted service shows you only a current model label and a response. What may you say about its before state, and what kinds of reproducibility could you offer for a result?

rubric.text: States that you do not invent a before state you cannot see.
Says which internal details remain unknown.
Notes that the toy is useful because its state is completely visible, and that this should teach restraint where it is not.
Names kinds of reproducibility: rerun the Python training from supplied data, replay a prompt under recorded but aging service conditions, or inspect a configuration diff.
Says each kind has different dependencies and that identical output is not the only acceptable repeat.

questions.source: The model: two numbers and a squashing function
questions.prompt: For the one-feature classifier, write the score and the sigmoid. Compute the score, the probability, and the loss for the training points when w = 0 and b = 0, and say what the result shows about what the model has encoded.

rubric.text: Writes the score as a = wx + b and the sigmoid as 1 / (1 + e^(-a)).
Shows that at w = 0 and b = 0 every score is zero regardless of x.
Shows that since e^0 = 1 the sigmoid is one-half, so the initial prediction is one-half for all four training points.
States that the loss for either label is negative log one-half, about 0.6931471806, so the average is the same value.
Concludes that the model has not yet encoded any relationship between feature sign and label.

questions.source: The model: two numbers and a squashing function
questions.prompt: The reference sigmoid uses two branches, one for x >= 0 and one for x < 0. Explain what the negative branch does and why, and say exactly what the lesson test of sigmoid(-1000) does and does not show.

rubric.text: States that the negative branch computes e / (1 + e) with e = exp(x).
States that it rewrites the same mathematical quantity.
Explains that it avoids evaluating an unnecessarily large positive exponential when x is very negative.
States that the test checks that sigmoid of negative one thousand is approximately zero without overflow.
Says this is evidence for the demonstrated numeric behavior, not a promise about arbitrary types or all floating-point edge cases.

questions.source: The model: two numbers and a squashing function
questions.prompt: After training, the learned weight is positive. Say what a positive weight does to positive and to negative inputs, and what it does not mean. Then say which parts of the chapter's evidence come from a cited source and which from local execution.

rubric.text: A positive weight makes positive x values produce positive scores and probabilities above one-half.
Negative x values produce probabilities below one-half when the bias stays near zero.
This geometry matches the constructed labels.
The parameter does not learn a word meaning or a causal relationship; it fits the relationship represented in the supplied pairs.
The cited logistic-regression chapter draft supports the weighted-input and sigmoid mechanism, while the numerical results come from the local implementation and an independent calculation.

questions.source: The gate: say what should change before you change it
questions.prompt: Write the Change and Objective lines of the gate for the toy, and explain why the chapter says the objective is a choice.

rubric.text: Change: weights only, the two numbers w and b, starting from zero.
States that the prompt, context, tools, settings, and Claude's own weights are not in play.
Objective: the average binary logistic loss on the four training pairs, and nothing else.
States that "better" means lower on this objective on these pairs, which is the only thing the run may be called.
Explains that the optimizer lowers whatever you give it, so the objective is a choice made in the gate.

questions.source: The gate: say what should change before you change it
questions.prompt: Write the Held-out and Stop rule lines of the gate. What one claim can the held-out set support, and what do you do if the budget must change?

rubric.text: Fixes four held-out pairs now, never passed to train, and lists them or says they are fixed in advance.
Says they share the training data's sign pattern, so they can support one claim: these four fixtures are classified correctly at threshold one-half.
Stop rule: exactly 200 updates at rate 0.2, from a zero start.
No stopping early because the loss looks flat, and no extra steps because the held-out result looks bad.
If the budget must change, reopen the gate and write down why, treating any evaluation points already seen as development data.

questions.source: The gate: say what should change before you change it
questions.prompt: After 200 steps, a teammate sees that the held-out result looks bad, adds 100 more steps, and reports the new held-out result as the result. Evaluate this against the gate in the chapter.

rubric.text: Says the gate forbids extra steps because the held-out result looks bad.
Says that if the budget must change, the gate is reopened and the reason written down; reopening is a logged act.
Says the held-out points have now guided a choice, so they have become development data.
Says the new held-out result is no longer an independent use of those points.
Says an independent evaluation should be built if the claim requires one, and the change of role recorded.

questions.source: The gate: say what should change before you change it
questions.prompt: The gate promises tests that catch three wrong versions of the program. Name them, say what each does, and say what it means if your tests cannot tell them from the right program.

rubric.text: Summing the gradient instead of averaging makes the first step four times too large (0.6 instead of 0.15) while the loss still falls.
Copying the x factor into the bias update makes b move on the first step although the symmetric data say it should not.
Letting a held-out point into the training list makes the "held-out" result stop meaning anything.
States that if the tests cannot tell these from the right program, the gate is not finished.
Notes that because the summed version's loss still falls, watching the loss alone would not catch it.

questions.source: The gate: say what should change before you change it
questions.prompt: Write a dated failure sentence for the first update and say why it must be written before the run. Then state what this experiment may claim, what it may not, and the pass condition.

rubric.text: Failure sentence: if the first update is right, w moves positive and b stays at zero; if w moves negative, or b moves, a sign or an x factor is wrong.
Says it is written and dated before the run, because written after reading the output it only describes the output.
May claim: the parameters were updated by this rule, training loss on four pairs fell, and four constructed points were classified correctly.
May not claim: generalization, calibration, a change to Claude, or any cause.
Pass condition: every test written from the gate passes on the code, and every sentence in the report fits inside the "may claim" line.

questions.source: The gate: say what should change before you change it
questions.prompt: Claude can write the loop in seconds. Explain which parts of the gate it cannot choose for you, why, and what it can do for the gate instead.

rubric.text: Identifies the objective, the held-out set, and the stop rule as human decisions.
Explains that none can be derived from the data, because the data have no opinion about what "better" should mean.
Says that for the toy these are the author's choices (no model produced them) and for a real change request they are yours.
Says Claude can sharpen the gate by proposing the wrong version and the test that catches it.
Explains that if Claude chose the objective, your report would be a statement about someone else's objective.

questions.source: Loss makes the objective explicit
questions.prompt: Give the ordinary binary cross-entropy for predicted probability p and the stable expression the reference evaluates from the score a. Say how the reference uses it and why the stable form is used.

rubric.text: Gives -y log(p) - (1 - y) log(1 - p).
Gives max(a, 0) - y*a + log(1 + e^(-|a|)).
States that the reference averages this value across the data.
Explains that the stable form avoids computing logarithms of probabilities rounded too close to zero or one for large scores.
States that it is a numerically safer route to the same logistic objective for the accepted finite inputs.

questions.source: Loss makes the objective explicit
questions.prompt: A student describes the training function's history as the learning curve and says the loss function is safe on any input. Correct both statements using the chapter.

rubric.text: States that history appends only the initial and the final loss.
States that two values are not a learning curve.
Says that if you add full history, you must state that your version changed the implementation.
States that the loss function assumes nonempty data because training validates that before calling it.
States that invoked directly on an empty list it would divide by zero, so describe guarantees at the call boundary that actually exists.

questions.source: Derive the first update
questions.prompt: Using the training data [(-2, 0), (-1, 0), (1, 1), (2, 1)] at w = 0, b = 0 and rate 0.2, compute by hand the four errors, the four weight-gradient contributions, the average weight and bias gradients, and the new w and b.

rubric.text: Errors (prediction minus label) are 0.5, 0.5, -0.5, -0.5.
Weight contributions (p - y)x are -1.0, -0.5, -0.5, -1.0.
They sum to -3, so the average weight gradient is -0.75.
The errors sum to zero, so the average bias gradient is zero.
New w = 0 - 0.2(-0.75) = 0.15, and b stays at zero.

questions.source: Derive the first update
questions.prompt: State the derivative of the logistic loss with respect to the score for one example, show how it gives the weight and bias gradient contributions, and explain in words why the first weight update should be positive.

rubric.text: The derivative with respect to the score is prediction minus label, the error e.
Because the score is wx + b, the weight contribution is e times x and the bias contribution is e.
Gradient descent subtracts the learning rate times the gradient.
Since the average weight gradient at the start is negative, subtracting it moves w up.
Increasing a positive weight pushes positive examples toward label one and negative examples toward label zero.

questions.source: Derive the first update
questions.prompt: Describe the central finite-difference check of the weight gradient at zero, give the value it should approximate, and say what agreement does and does not establish.

rubric.text: Evaluates the loss at a small positive and a small negative perturbation and divides the difference by twice the perturbation.
Gives approximately -0.74999999999, agreeing with the analytic -0.75.
Says agreement within the tolerance checks the analytic expression at this point and fails differently from the derivation, because it never uses the derivative formula.
Says it is an independent calculation, not an independent dataset, reviewer, or causal source.
Says that if logistic loss is the wrong objective the derivative and finite difference still agree, because whether it is the objective you meant is the gate's question.

questions.source: The loop, its rate, and its stop rule
questions.prompt: Describe what the training function validates and what each step does, name three things it does not do, and state what the existing tests do and do not show about the result after 200 steps.

rubric.text: Validates that labels are zero or one, features are finite, steps is a positive integer, and the rate is positive and finite.
Initializes both parameters to zero and records the initial loss; each step builds errors from the current parameters, averages the gradient contributions, and updates weight and bias.
Does not shuffle, use minibatches, or adapt the rate: it is batch gradient descent on the complete declared dataset.
After 200 steps the weight is about 3.1669517461, the bias is effectively zero, and the training loss is 0.0215209850.
The existing tests check that the loss fell and the weight is positive; passing them does not show the optimizer behaves under every dataset or rate.

questions.source: The loop, its rate, and its stop rule
questions.prompt: A classmate says the 0.15 first step is what the data demand. Respond using the chapter. Then compute the first step at rate 0.1 and at rate 0.4, and say what the chapter does and does not establish about choosing a rate.

rubric.text: Explains that 0.15 is the average gradient -0.75 scaled by the rate 0.2 you chose, so it does not arise from the data alone.
Computes the first step as 0.075 at rate 0.1 and 0.3 at rate 0.4.
States that the rate is supplied to train and never updated: it is a setting of the experiment, not a learned parameter.
States that a very large rate can overshoot or become unstable on some data, and a very small one makes limited-step progress slow.
States that the research establishes no safe universal range, so you test chosen values on declared fixtures and do not write an optimization theorem from one decreasing-loss run.

questions.source: The loop, its rate, and its stop rule
questions.prompt: The demo runs exactly 200 steps. What does that number mean, what does the function lack, and how should you run a fair comparison of rates or step counts?

rubric.text: States that 200 is the demo setting, not a discovered natural stopping point.
States that the function runs exactly that many updates, with no convergence test, validation-based early stopping, or best-checkpoint selection.
States that a lower final training loss shows what happened after the configured loop, not that the budget was right.
Says to hold the data and initial parameters fixed and keep every result, including runs that behave badly.
Says to choose evaluation criteria before looking for the most attractive run, otherwise the comparison becomes a search whose selection is hidden.

questions.source: The loop, its rate, and its stop rule
questions.prompt: Reverse all four training labels and keep the features. Compute the first-step average weight gradient and the new weight at rate 0.2, and say what the chapter predicts about the preferred weight direction. Then explain what happens to the separation between fit and evaluation if the held-out points are duplicated into the training data.

rubric.text: Computes the weight contributions with reversed labels as +1.0, +0.5, +0.5, +1.0, which average to +0.75.
Computes the new weight as 0 - 0.2(0.75) = -0.15.
States that the preferred weight direction should reverse (negative rather than positive).
States that duplicating the evaluation points into the training data contaminates the separation between fit and held-out assessment.
States that apparent improvement on those points becomes hard to interpret, because the optimizer has already used them.

questions.source: Held-out means separately specified, not magically representative
questions.prompt: With the trained parameters, the held-out predicted probabilities for x = -3, -0.5, 0.5, and 3 are about 0.00007478, 0.17030378, 0.82969622, and 0.99992522. Apply the threshold, state the result, state the strongest claim the chapter allows from it, and say what a broader claim would need.

rubric.text: Applies the threshold at one-half and predicts labels 0, 0, 1, 1.
States that all four held-out labels are correct.
Says "held out" means only that the points were not passed into the training function, a statement about how they were handled.

States the allowed claim: the trained parameters classified four separately specified sign-pattern fixtures correctly; "the model generalized" is too broad because the points were designed around the same sign boundary and are not representative of a natural population.
Says a broader performance claim needs a justified sampling process, a task definition, and a larger evaluation.

questions.source: Held-out means separately specified, not magically representative
questions.prompt: You use the held-out result to decide whether to change the number of steps. What has happened to the held-out set, what should you record, and how many roles for data do you now need?

rubric.text: Says that once the held-out set guides a choice (a rate, a step count, or a decision to keep going) it has become development data.
Says its next use is no longer independent.
Says to record the change of role when it happens.
Says to build an independent evaluation if the claim requires one.
Says that once you tune anything you need three roles: training, a development set to tune against, and a held-out set you touch once.

questions.source: What a lower loss claims
questions.prompt: Suppose label one means "escalate this message to a person," and a missed escalation is far worse than a false alarm. Training loss falls. What does that establish, what does it not, and what should the gate have named?

rubric.text: States that lower training loss shows the update rule reduced the objective on the pairs it was shown.
States that it does not establish fit to pairs it was not shown, which is what the held-out set is for.
States that it does not establish that the objective was the right one, which no dataset can establish.
Explains that logistic loss penalizes errors by how confident the model was in the wrong direction, not by what each error costs, so a lower loss can sit beside the wrong behavior.
Says the gate should have named the costs of the two errors, and the report should say "training loss decreased" rather than "better."

questions.source: Score, probability, and decision are three layers
questions.prompt: Distinguish score, probability, and decision in the toy classifier. Say what produces each, and what happens when you move the threshold.

rubric.text: The score wx + b comes from the parameters.
The probability comes from the sigmoid.
The decision comes from a threshold, here one-half.
The threshold is a choice you made and training never saw; moving it moves the decisions with identical parameters.
You record all three layers and know which one a claim is about.

questions.source: Score, probability, and decision are three layers
questions.prompt: The learned bias is extremely close to zero. Explain why, why it would be a mistake to conclude that bias is unnecessary, and where the decision boundary sits.

rubric.text: Notes that the data are symmetric: each negative feature with label zero has a positive partner with label one.
Notes that at the origin the errors sum to zero, so the first bias update is zero.
States that across training the symmetry keeps the learned bias extremely close to zero in the recorded run.
Says bias shifts the decision boundary whenever the relationship is not centered at zero, and that removing one point or changing one label can break the symmetry.
States that the boundary sits where wx + b = 0, because sigmoid zero is one-half, so with positive w and nearly zero b it lies near x zero.

questions.source: Score, probability, and decision are three layers
questions.prompt: The held-out probabilities are more extreme farther from zero (0.99992522 at x = 3 versus 0.82969622 at x = 0.5). A teammate says this shows the model's confidence is well calibrated. Respond using the chapter.

rubric.text: States that more extreme probabilities farther from zero are an observed property of this fitted curve under the learned positive weight, on selected points.
States that this is not evidence that the confidence is calibrated.
Notes that a model's probability is tied to its mechanism and objective.
Explains that calibration means matching observed frequencies, which takes a calibration study on suitable labeled data.
States that four sign fixtures cannot support a calibration claim.

questions.source: Decide what kind of question you are asking
questions.prompt: x counts the reminder emails a student opened in the first month, y records whether they passed, and the fitted weight is positive. Contrast "what label will the model assign to a student who opened four emails?" with "if we require every student to open the emails, will more of them pass?" and say what evaluating the function at a larger x does and does not tell you.

rubric.text: Says the first question is about the model, and evaluating the fitted function answers it.
Says the second question is about the world, and the function answers a different question.
Says evaluating at a larger x gives the model's response to a changed input, not the course's response to a changed behavior.

Names at least three other sources of the association: opening helps, students already on track open more (reverse arrow), a third factor such as motivation or free time, or a sample of only students who stayed enrolled.
Says a positive weight cannot tell you which source you have, because each is consistent with it.

questions.source: Decide what kind of question you are asking
questions.prompt: Explain how acting on a prediction can undermine it, and why a causal sentence about the chapter's four training pairs would be a story rather than a finding.

rubric.text: States that acting on a prediction can change the process that generated the data.
States that a model fit to a period in which nobody acted on its flags can say little about what happens once people do.
States that the four constructed pairs were chosen to make the gradient visible.
States that they contain no information about any process in the world.
Concludes that a causal sentence about them is a story attached to a fixture.

questions.source: Decide what kind of question you are asking
questions.prompt: Name the three rungs of Pearl's ladder as the chapter gives them, state the one-line version of what the ladder implies for prediction, and say what the limit does and does not claim.

rubric.text: Names association (what goes with what), intervention (what happens if I do this), and counterfactual (what would have happened to this case had we done otherwise).

States that prediction is not identification: interventional and counterfactual answers generally cannot be recovered from purely observational data without structural assumptions that did not come from the data.
Says the limit is about information, about what observational data can yield, and is not a proof that no machine architecture could ever reason causally.
Says someone must supply and defend the causal assumptions, and that more data, confident intuition, or a fluent explanation does not supply them.
Says observational data can support a causal claim under assumptions you state and defend.

questions.source: What is Claude's here, and what is yours
questions.prompt: In the causal part of the chapter, what can Claude do, what does it lack, and what judgment stays with you?

rubric.text: Claude can write causal diagram notation, list the confounders it can think of, work out what follows from a stated structure, and run the code.
Its fluent paragraphs about confounding exist because such text is abundant in what such systems learn from, and fluency about causation is not identification of it.
It lacks your study design, how the data were collected, and the domain facts about your students.
It has nothing riding on the decision.
The identification judgment (choosing the variables and asserting the structure you are prepared to defend) stays with the person who will act.

questions.source: What is Claude's here, and what is yours
questions.prompt: State the working rule the chapter gives for deciding, before you hand Claude the algebra, what kind of question a stakeholder is asking, and say how the chapter's report is meant to show you drew that line.

rubric.text: Write one sentence saying whether the question is "what will the model say" or "what happens if we act."
Also write who decided.
Notes the book's observation that deciding whether the question is causal is itself a causal judgment.
States that the report ends with one predictive claim the fixture supports and one intervention claim it does not establish.
States that the pair is the evidence that you drew the line.

questions.source: Build It: the baseline that lets you audit
questions.prompt: Describe the order of work in Build It, and say what you do if your first-step weight does not equal 0.15.

rubric.text: Implements sigmoid and tests zero, a large negative input, and a symmetry you can justify; implements the stable loss and calculates the origin by hand.
Implements one gradient step before writing the full loop.
Reads the six lesson tests before the reference and predicts the direction and rejection cases.
If the value differs from 0.15, inspects averaging, signs, and use of the current parameters.
Does not adjust the expected result until the discrepancy is explained, because it came from the hand derivation, the independent route.

questions.source: Build It: the baseline that lets you audit
questions.prompt: In Build It you change the update to sum the gradient instead of averaging. Compute the first step at rate 0.2 for the toy data, say what three predictions you write before running it, and explain why a lower final loss would not show the code is right.

rubric.text: Computes the summed first-step gradient as -3, so the step is 0.2 x 3 = 0.6, four times the reference 0.15.
Names the three predictions: which of the six lesson tests will fail, how far the first step lands from 0.15, and whether the final loss after 200 steps is higher or lower than 0.0215209850.
Notes that tests 03 and 04 check only that the loss fell and that the weight is positive, so they cannot tell the summed version from the averaged one.
Notes that the loss still falls in the summed version.
Says that whatever number appears at step 200, a lower number does not show the update rule is right.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.prompt: You hand Claude Code your gate. Say what you give it, what you do with what it returns, and how the three follow-up checks work.

rubric.text: Gives it the gate (change, objective, held-out list, stop rule, and test list) but not your implementation.
Runs your own tests on what it returns, yourself.
Notes which tests failed, since a failure is often a gap in the gate (for example, early stopping you never asked for means your stop rule had a hole).
Compares its implementation with your baseline and names one difference in behavior, such as keeping held-out points out of training, how the average is computed, or recording more than two losses.
Asks Claude to propose a deliberately wrong version that still passes your tests and checks by hand whether it does; if it does, the test list was too weak.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.prompt: What must you preserve from a Claude Code session, what do you do if the session failed or did not run, and why can't Claude judge whether your tests are enough?

rubric.text: Preserves the prompt, the plan, the diff, the commands, and the outputs.
Records the date and displayed model label.
If a session failed or did not run, records that.
Does not substitute a fixture for the missing session.
States that whether your tests are enough cannot be judged by the system they are testing.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.prompt: Design the chapter's second task, which touches Claude's behavior: what conditions do you prepare, what rule governs them, what do you write first, what do you record, and what do you say about what is being changed?

rubric.text: Prepares a baseline prompt, a few-shot prompt, and a retrieved-context condition on the same bounded task.
Changes only one object between conditions.
Writes a prediction for each condition first.
If run, records the actual responses, interface, date, and displayed model label; if not run, labels the design proposed.
States that these conditions change inputs, not Claude's weights.

questions.source: Ship It: the comparison report and its sign-off
questions.prompt: List what the Ship It report must contain, including how it separates mathematical success from decision authority.

rubric.text: Includes loss history, before and after parameters, held-out results, and a comparison of parameter learning, prompt changes, and context changes.
Preserves the training data and evaluation points, and records the interpreter, step count, rate, initial values, final values, and threshold.
Says which results came from the lesson and which from your extension.
Includes a table with mutable object, mechanism, persistence, evidence, and remaining limits, keeping permissions and tools separate from model parameters.
Ends with one predictive claim supported by the actual toy evaluation and one intervention claim it does not establish.

questions.source: Ship It: the comparison report and its sign-off
questions.prompt: Fill in the "Not checked" and "Not claiming" lines of the sign-off for this chapter's work, and explain why the "Not checked" line matters when Claude drafts the sign-off.

rubric.text: Not checked includes data beyond the four training and four held-out fixtures, and other rates, step counts, or starts.
Not checked also includes calibration of the probabilities, any change to Claude itself, and any real-world effect of changing x.
Not claiming includes that the model generalizes, that lower training loss means better, and that any input causes any outcome.
Says the "Not checked" line is the one an AI-written sign-off omits, because the system that wrote it has no record of what you did not do.
Says you write the sign-off from your own record, and that withholding is an honest result if the evidence does not support signing.

questions.source: Ship It: the comparison report and its sign-off
questions.prompt: Choose the right verb for each claim and justify it: "lowered the objective on four pairs," "learned," "generalizes," and "causes." What is the rule for choosing?

rubric.text: "Lowered the objective on four pairs" describes what the optimizer did.
"Learned" describes a parameter change, which is accurate here.
"Generalizes" needs a criterion you have not run.
"Causes" needs assumptions the fixture cannot supply.
The rule: choose verbs to match the evidence, since a pass names the obligation it passed and no more.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.prompt: Using the driver's seat table, say for (a) deciding whether the question is prediction or intervention and (b) deciding what the result supports: what Claude should do, what you should do, and why it stays with you. Then say what the report must record about the split.

rubric.text: (a) Claude can draft a diagram, list confounders, and compute under a stated model.
(a) You decide which kind of question it is, justify the assumptions, and get domain evidence, because the assumptions are not in the data and you are the one who acts.
(b) Claude can flag an overclaim.
(b) You choose the verb and sign, because your name is on the claim.
The report records one task delegated and one judgment retained, with a transcript line or edit showing each; otherwise the split happened in your head and not in the record.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.prompt: Classify these four proposed changes by the object each modifies and say how you would observe each: a rewritten system prompt, a new document in a workspace, a newly enabled tool, and a lowered temperature. What may you not conclude if the only evidence is a different output?

rubric.text: Rewritten system prompt: the prompt, observed by comparing both texts.
New document in a workspace: the context, observed through the passages that actually entered the input.
Newly enabled tool: the tools, observed through the configuration diff and the decision that authorized it.
Lowered temperature: a setting, observed through the recorded setting for each run.
States that if the only evidence is a different output, you should not jump to a claim about changed weights.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.prompt: List the checks the chapter asks you to run when you verify your work, including what to do with the words "history" and "generalization" and with your strongest causal verb.

rubric.text: Runs the demo, the lesson tests, your gradient check, and the held-out calculation.
Recomputes the first update independently and preserves exact outputs rather than reconstructing them after reading the expected values.
Checks every use of "history": two loss values are initial and final, not a full curve.
Checks every use of "generalization": four designed points are separate fixtures, not evidence of population performance.
Inspects the strongest causal verb (association or intervention?) and narrows the claim if the data and design cannot support it.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.prompt: The chapter says the most useful reflection is local. Name the four distinctions it suggests you may have collapsed, say what you do about them, and state what it says about mechanism labels.

rubric.text: Names the four distinctions: training and context; lower loss and better; held-out and representative; prediction and intervention.
Says to name the calculation or the one-object test that separated them again.
Says mechanism labels should make evidence easier to inspect, and that when they hide the mutable object they have become branding.
Says to ask of any change which component changed, who changed it, and what evidence records the transformation.
Says that if those questions stay unanswered, you use a narrower description until the mechanism is known.

questions.source: What you can now explain
questions.prompt: Describe what Conduct, Check, and Drive looked like at this chapter's scale, in terms of what you did.

rubric.text: Conducted: wrote the change, the objective, the held-out list, and the stop rule before the loop ran.
Conducted: tested Claude's version against those items.
Checked: wrote "training loss decreased" when that was all that was measured.
Checked: let neither persistence nor a good-looking prompt stand in for training.
Drove: handed Claude the algebra and the loop, kept the question of whether this was prediction or intervention, and signed or withheld.

questions.source: Irreducibly Human
questions.prompt: State the "AI should" and "Human should" responsibilities the chapter gives for the prediction-versus-intervention question, and say what the chapter does and does not take from the companion passage.

rubric.text: AI should inspect calculations, run bounded experiments, tabulate predictions, and challenge assumptions.

AI can compute consequences under an explicitly stated model and propose candidate confounders, and should label assumptions as assumptions instead of presenting a plausible story as established causation.
Human should decide whether the task asks for prediction or intervention, and justify the outcome and causal assumptions.
Human should obtain relevant domain evidence and own the decision to act; human intuition is not sufficient causal proof either.
The chapter uses the passage's information boundary, not a claim that a particular machine architecture can never represent causal reasoning.

questions.source: Irreducibly Human
questions.prompt: Write the form the chapter gives for an intervention claim, and explain what it means if you can or cannot fill in its provisos. Then explain why changing x in the fitted Python function does not measure a real-world effect, and what in the record shows who wrote the assumptions.

rubric.text: Gives the form: "if I change x by doing D, the outcome changes by about this much, provided P, Q, and R."
If you can fill in P, Q, and R, you have found the assumptions to defend and the evidence to go and get.
If you cannot, you have a prediction.
Changing x in the fitted function measures the model's response, not necessarily the effect of changing a real-world variable.
Points to the transcript line or the edit showing that you, not Claude, wrote the sentence that names the assumptions.

questions.source: Chapter 10: Planning before acting (opening)
questions.prompt: A plan has all eight fields set to the single string x. Predict what missing_fields returns for it, say what that result does and does not show about the plan, and say what the check is for.

rubric.text: States that missing_fields returns an empty list because every field is bound to a nonempty (truthy) string.
Says the empty list is the correct result for the rule the function implements, not a bug.
Says the result does not show that the objective matters, the scope is safe, a risk is plausible, the verification tests the claim, or the stop condition is observable.
Says the check's job is to catch absence and false-valued entries under a declared list, that is, structural omissions.
Says this does not make field checks pointless; trouble begins when a clean form is presented as a trustworthy plan.

questions.source: Chapter 10: Planning before acting (opening)
questions.prompt: The chapter says Claude implements well against a complete specification and badly against an incomplete one. Explain what Claude will and will not tell you about this, which decisions determine whether a build goes well, and what a plan is in the chapter's terms. Why is reviewing the plan the gate?

rubric.text: States that Claude will not tell you which kind of specification, complete or incomplete, you gave it.
Names at least four of the decisions made before the build: which problem, which boundary, which order, which evidence between steps, which point to stop.
Defines a plan as those decisions written down where another person can challenge them.
States that reviewing the plan is the gate.
Explains that because these decisions are made before the build, the written plan is the place where another person can still say no.

questions.source: Chapter 10: Planning before acting (opening)
questions.prompt: Chapter 1 named three jobs that stay with you. State what Conduct, Check, and Drive look like in this chapter's planning work.

rubric.text: Conduct: the plan is the design that precedes implementation, and the reviewed plan is the gate, so nothing changes until a condition you can state is met.
Check: a plan predicts action and a result records it, so a complete form is not a plan and an acyclic graph is not an executable one.
Check: you review the plan with counterexamples before anything runs.
Drive: the choice of problem, and the values inside that choice, are yours.
Drive: Claude can suggest framings and attack your selection, and you defend it.

questions.source: Chapter 10: Planning before acting (opening)
questions.prompt: The chapter's Python build is offline, yet it also uses Claude Code. Explain what part Claude Code plays, what status its returned plan has, and what you must do if the interface is unavailable.

rubric.text: States that the Python build runs offline and needs no direct API credits.
Says Claude Code can propose or critique a plan through the assumed course account.
Says the returned plan remains a proposal.
Says that if the interface is unavailable you preserve that fact and complete the offline construction.
Says you must not invent a Claude-authored plan or a human approval to make the artifact look finished.

questions.source: The plan is the design, and the review is the gate
questions.prompt: A classmate says a plan should reproduce Claude's reasoning in full. Using the chapter, explain what a plan is, what it should expose, and why it is worth the most before anything has run.

rubric.text: Says the plan is not hidden reasoning and need not reproduce private deliberation.
Describes the plan as a public action contract another person can critique.
Says it exposes the destination, allowed inputs and scope, intended steps, tools, risks, evidence, and stopping rule.
Says it is worth the most before anything has run because a revision costs a paragraph there and a rollback later.
Says a plan nobody reviewed is a draft however complete its form, so the review is the gate.

questions.source: The plan is the design, and the review is the gate
questions.prompt: Define a phase gate as Conducting AI uses the term, and explain how design by contract expresses the same idea. In this chapter's sense, what is a plan?

rubric.text: Defines a phase gate as the explicit point where Claude's work stops and a person's begins.
Says the gate is stated as a specification of what each side handles.
Says it also includes a testable condition that must hold before the output moves downstream.
Explains that in design by contract you write the contract and the agent writes the implementation.
Says assertions or tests derived from your contract check the implementation, and that a plan is that contract for a whole piece of work.

questions.source: The plan is the design, and the review is the gate
questions.prompt: Describe the Boondoggle Score at the level the chapter does, how much weight the chapter places on its sorting questions, and how the eight fields relate to it.

rubric.text: Says the Score lays out the prompts for Claude in dependency order.
Says it lists the human's actions in the same order.
Says it places a testable handoff condition between each Claude task and each human task.
Notes that it is the author's own instrument and that the five sorting questions have no external validation that the author knows of.
Says to treat the Score as a heuristic, not a diagnostic, and that the eight fields are a smaller instrument, this course's own review tool.

questions.source: The plan is the design, and the review is the gate
questions.prompt: A teammate says "design first" means freezing the plan before work starts. Respond using the chapter's reasoning about how problem and solution develop, what you do when a result contradicts the plan, and the chapter's narrower claim.

rubric.text: Cites the design research that problem and solution develop together, so a move in the solution space can surprise you and force a reframing of the problem.
Says a plan is a controlled state with versions.
Says that when a result contradicts an assumption, you revise the plan and record the reason rather than pushing forward on a stale one.
Uses the discount-rule example: auditing the diff shows rounding was never specified, which reopens the requirement, and the instruction is to log it and go back.
States the narrower claim: the first version of the plan should exist and be reviewed before Claude changes anything, so that when evidence reopens a decision you can see which decision it was.

questions.source: Formulate before you plan
questions.prompt: Explain the error of the third kind and why its cost is highest when Claude executes a plan fluently. Say why choosing the problem comes before filling in the eight fields.

rubric.text: Defines the error of the third kind as a right answer to the wrong problem.
Attributes the phrase, as Conducting AI uses it, to Allyn Kimball in 1957.
Says a perfectly ordered plan can optimize the wrong objective.
Says a polished, internally checked answer to the wrong question carries authority the question never earned.
Says the first decision in a plan, which problem it is for, is not in any of the eight fields.

questions.source: Formulate before you plan
questions.prompt: Why not simply ask Claude to frame the problem first? Use the idea of a primary generator and explain what goes wrong with auditing afterward.

rubric.text: Says the book argues that a system trained to continue text tends toward the common and likely, so its framing is the modal one, and that this is an argument about tendencies, not a theorem.
Defines the primary generator (Jane Darke) as a first, usually tacit idea of what this is really about that decides which solutions you can see.
Says you cannot start without one.
Says that if you have not named yours before Claude supplies its own, its anchor becomes yours by default, dressed as neutral analysis.
Says the audit then comes too late because you would be checking the output against the framing it already assumes.

questions.source: Formulate before you plan
questions.prompt: State the distinctness test. Then apply it: in the plus-one regression, a patch returns the constant 3 and is applied without diagnosing the cause. Score it against formulation A (the input-two test goes green), B (the declared plus-one behavior restored without changing anything outside the learner module and its test), and C (the learner can explain the bug).

rubric.text: States the test: would the two formulations require different solutions even to test; if one solution satisfies both, they are one formulation in two outfits.
Says the constant-3 patch passes A because input two gives 3.
Says it fails B because input five gives 3, not 6.
Says it fails C because the cause was never diagnosed, so the learner cannot explain it.
Concludes that this result separates A from B, and that formulations that disagree about whether a result succeeded are separate problems.

questions.source: Formulate before you plan
questions.prompt: A correct x + 1 patch that Claude wrote is accepted by you without reading it. Score it against formulations A, B, and C of the plus-one regression, say which pair of formulations it separates, and say what the result implies about the interest formulation B leaves out.

rubric.text: Says it passes A because the input-two test goes green.
Says it passes B because the declared plus-one behavior is restored within scope.
Says it fails C because the learner cannot explain the bug.
Says this result separates B from C.
Notes that B centers maintainers and callers and decenters the learner's understanding, so the plan should say so, for example by assigning a separate step to the learner's understanding.

questions.source: Formulate before you plan
questions.prompt: Why must the constraint set for choosing among formulations be written before you score anything, and why is feasibility alone not enough? Name the two criteria the book adds.

rubric.text: Says the constraint set is written before you score anything.
Says that if every criterion is about cost, time, and buildability, you have built a machine that selects the most tractable framing.
Says the most tractable framing is the one Claude would have picked unasked.
Names salience as an added criterion: if this is solved, does it address what matters here?
Names whose interests the framing centers and decenters as the other added criterion.

questions.source: Formulate before you plan
questions.prompt: In the plus-one regression, say whose interests each of the three formulations centers. Then write one sentence that defends a selection and explain why silence about what was left out is a different thing.

rubric.text: Says formulation A centers whoever reads the test report.
Says formulation B centers the maintainers and callers of the function.
Says formulation C centers the learner.
Says none centers everyone, so choosing one is choosing whom the plan does not serve, and the plan should say so.

Gives a defended selection such as "I chose B; it decenters the learner's understanding, which a separate step addresses" and calls silence about what was left out a laundered selection; the values decision sits inside the formulation, not after it.

questions.source: Formulate before you plan
questions.prompt: Divide the formulation work between you and Claude. What can Claude do, what can it not do, and why does the practice not depend on settling the philosophical question about models?

rubric.text: Says Claude can add candidates you missed.
Says Claude can find a result that passes one formulation and fails another.
Says Claude can attack your selection.

Says Conducting AI argues that a model cannot certify distinctness in your domain or make the values selection because both need situated judgment and a name on the decision, and that the chapter reads this as an argument, not a measurement.

Says the practice is to write your candidates first, let Claude extend and criticize them, and defend the one you pick, including what it leaves out; someone answers for the choice and Claude has no name to put there.

questions.source: Formulate before you plan
questions.prompt: Explain what it means for a plan to have drifted from its purpose, and how carrying the selected formulation into the plan prevents it. Use formulation B of the plus-one regression as the example.

rubric.text: Says the selection should be carried into the objective, scope, verification, and stop fields.
Says drift is when the selection lives only in introductory prose while the checks measure something else.

Applies it to B: the objective names the restored plus-one behavior within the learner module and its test, the scope excludes other files, and the verification tests the behavior beyond the single input-two case.
Says a defended selection also names what the chosen formulation leaves out.
Says the values decision sits inside the formulation and so must be reflected in the fields, not left after it.

questions.source: The eight fields are eight questions
questions.prompt: List the eight required plan fields in the order the reference declares them. Explain what the code can see versus what a reviewer asks, and give the question for at least three fields.

rubric.text: Lists objective, inputs, scope, steps, tools, risks, verification, and stop, in that order.
Says the code can only see whether a name is bound to a value.
Says a reviewer asks the question each name stands for.

Gives a correct question for at least three fields, for example objective: what outcome, stated so someone can tell whether it happened; scope: what may change and what must stay untouched; verification: what observation will support the completion claim.
Says each field is a place where a decision was made or was not.

questions.source: The eight fields are eight questions
questions.prompt: For each of these entries, name the field it fills, explain why it passes missing_fields but fails review, and rewrite one of them so that a reviewer can challenge it: "Be careful", "Research", "Claude Code", "There may be risks".

rubric.text: Maps the entries to fields correctly: "Be careful" to scope, "Research" to steps, "Claude Code" to tools, "There may be risks" to risks.
Says all four pass missing_fields because they are nonempty, truthy values.

Says they fail review because nobody can challenge them or tell whether they were done (no paths or exclusions, no output or finished test, no operations or approval boundary, no mitigation, owner, or stop trigger).

Rewrites at least one as a challengeable entry, for example scope as file paths, permitted operations, excluded systems, and output destinations, or tools as the tool, the reason, and the operations it may and may not perform.
States that this is the difference between a field that is present and a field that has a job.

questions.source: What missing_fields actually checks
questions.prompt: Predict what missing_fields returns for a plan built with keys in this order: stop is False, verification is "run the learner tests", risks is 0, tools is None, steps is ["inspect", "fix"], scope is "learner test file only", inputs is [], and objective is "Fix the plus-one bug". Explain your reasoning and say what the result does not tell you.

rubric.text: Gives the result ['inputs', 'tools', 'risks', 'stop'].
Explains the truth-value rule: absent and false-valued entries are missing, so an empty list, None, zero, and False all fail.
Says the list follows the order of the FIELDS tuple, not the order of the keys in the dictionary.
Identifies objective, scope, steps, and verification as passing because they hold nonempty truthy values.
Says the result does not show that the passing entries are meaningful, since the single string x would pass equally.

questions.source: What missing_fields actually checks
questions.prompt: Argue that a check blind to meaning is still worth running, and say how to use it. Include the pattern from earlier chapters that the all-x plan repeats.

rubric.text: Says the check is deterministic and cheap.
Says it fails differently from a reviewer: it never gets tired and never notices meaning.
Says to use it to clear the easy failures so that human attention goes to the hard ones.

Names at least two of the earlier-chapter examples: a strict format validator can pass false content, a permission flag can be true without authenticating a person, a plan-presence checker can pass empty language.
Says to keep the signal narrow instead of expecting one empty list to certify the artifact.

questions.source: Dependencies are directed obligations
questions.prompt: Explain why the chapter says steps are a graph and not a list. Use "verify has after: [build]" to explain what an arrow means, and say who decides which arrows exist and what the ordering function can and cannot do.

rubric.text: Says steps are a graph and each arrow is an obligation.
Says that if verify has after: [build], then build must appear before verify.
Says verify may not be called ready until build has produced what verify needs.
Says you decide which arrows exist.
Says the function can only order the arrows you declared.

questions.source: Dependencies are directed obligations
questions.prompt: For each of duplicate, unknown-prerequisite, and cycle, give a minimal plan that triggers it, the error order raises, and why the cases need different remedies. Why is a missing prerequisite not a cycle?

rubric.text: Duplicate: two steps with the same id; rejected with Duplicate step because one key cannot unambiguously represent two steps.
Unknown prerequisite: for example verify depends on test but test is absent; rejected with Unknown prerequisite because the plan references nonexistent work.
Cycle: two present steps depend on each other, or one depends on itself; neither can become ready, so Dependency cycle is raised.
Says a missing prerequisite is not a cycle and the remedies differ.
Says duplicates and unknown prerequisites are checked before the ordering loop begins, while the cycle is detected inside it when the graph is nonempty but has no ready step.

questions.source: Dependencies are directed obligations
questions.prompt: Trace order on these steps: z has no prerequisites, b comes after z, a comes after z, and final comes after both a and b. Give the output and describe what each pass of the loop does.

rubric.text: Gives the output z, a, b, final.
First pass: z is the only ready step; it is appended and removed from the graph and from the remaining prerequisite sets.
Second pass: a and b are both ready; they are sorted and appended as a, then b.
Third pass: final is ready and is appended, and the graph is empty so the loop ends.
Notes that alphabetical order within a batch is a convention and not evidence that alphabetical execution is best; it says only that a and b do not depend on one another.

questions.source: Acyclic does not mean executable
questions.prompt: Consider three steps with ids a, b, and c and no dependencies. What does order return, and what does that not tell you? Give two ways an acyclic graph can still describe work that cannot be done.

rubric.text: Says order returns a, b, c in sorted order.
Says the function has no knowledge of what each step requires in the world.
Says an omitted dependency can make the graph acyclic while the work remains impossible in that order.
Says a step can depend on a predecessor whose output is too vague to use; "review after build" is coherent but the reviewer needs a diff, test results, and acceptance criteria.
Says an arrow says one step comes after another but does not define the handoff object.

questions.source: Acyclic does not mean executable
questions.prompt: A plan orders inspect, delete, verify without a cycle. Explain why it is a valid ordering yet should not be executed automatically, and say which checks in this chapter cannot catch the problem.

rubric.text: Says it is a valid ordering because the graph has no cycle.
Says the graph has no operation allowlist and no approval model.
Says semantic review must compare each action with scope, authority, and consequence.

Says planning before acting does not mean automatically executing any valid graph; the plan creates a review surface that should expose the action early enough for a person or runtime boundary to reject it.
Says the structural checks (missing_fields and order) are not responsible for catching it, since neither compares an action with scope or authority.

questions.source: Acyclic does not mean executable
questions.prompt: Implementation needs review, and review needs a completed implementation. Diagnose this cycle, give the resolved sequence, and explain why you should not just remove an edge.

rubric.text: Diagnoses that one overloaded word, review, is doing two jobs.
Distinguishes plan review, which approves a proposed method, from result review, which evaluates actual output.
Gives the resolved sequence plan review, then implementation, then result review.
Says not to resolve every cycle by removing an edge because a cycle can reveal that two steps were poorly defined.
Says to ask what each step actually needs as input before touching an arrow.

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.prompt: A handoff condition reads "the code was reviewed and looks reasonable." Explain why it fails the chapter's test, give the procedure for repairing it, and give a replacement that passes.

rubric.text: States the test: someone who did not build the pipeline can read the condition, observe the system, and decide whether it holds.
Says "reviewed" and "reasonable" fail because five reviewers will do five different things and all call it reviewing.
Gives the procedure: write the condition, circle every interpretive word, and replace each with a criterion.
Says to hand it to someone who did not write it and ask them to apply it to a sample case, going again if they cannot decide.
Offers a replacement naming observable items, such as exact commands, exit statuses, output, and a current diff hash or version description, rather than "looks good".

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.prompt: For the symlink plan (one denial test for the Chapter 5 learner permission function, with steps inspect, fixture, test, run, review), write the handoff conditions for the run to review edge and the fixture to test edge.

rubric.text: For run to review, requires the exact commands.
For run to review, requires exit statuses and output.
For run to review, requires a current diff hash or version description, so the reviewer can determine whether the checks correspond to the proposal.
For fixture to test, requires resolved paths proving that both locations are disposable.
For fixture to test, requires that the destination lies outside the approved subdirectory while remaining inside the temporary parent, so another student can predict what the test exercises.

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.prompt: On the run to review edge, why is Claude's sentence about the test not the evidence? Say who produces the evidence, what an edge needs, and what failure behavior an edge should define.

rubric.text: Says the exit status and output come from the test runner.
Says an AI describing its own check is the first opinion run twice.
Says an edge needs something that fails differently from the thing it certifies, which Chapter 11 builds out.
Says that if the targeted test fails, you do not proceed as though review means approval; you return to implementation or stop pending diagnosis.
Says that if source authorization is missing, you do not improvise a replacement input.

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.prompt: Name the five Boondoggle sorting questions and use them to decide which edges of the symlink plan need the most evidence. Contrast adding a new test with a command that writes outside the fixture.

rubric.text: Names the five questions: how cheap the output is to verify, what being wrong costs, whether this is an ordinary input or a tail case, whether the action can be undone, and whether the step will leave a trail you can review.
Says reversibility and the trail do most of the work here.
Says a new test in a version-controlled workspace can be reverted from the diff, so its edge needs evidence but not a human gate.
Says a command that writes outside the fixture, or deletes, cannot be reverted from a diff, so it gets a hard human approval or falls outside the scope.
Says evidence is attached to state-changing edges first, and that a fluent sequence diagram cannot make an unsafe transition acceptable.

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.prompt: In the delegation chapter's two-team scenario, one team documented each handoff and the other wrote "the loan officer reviews." Say what happened to each team and what the scenario does and does not show.

rubric.text: Says the team whose documentation specified each handoff could be reviewed on substance.
Says the team that wrote "the loan officer reviews" was tabled because nobody could say what its pipeline did.
Says a clear map can be reviewed.
Says a clear map does not show that the decisions inside it are good.
Connects the scenario to the source's claim that delegation is a contract, not a partition of labor, whose handoff condition must be testable.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.prompt: Replace the stop entry "Stop when done" for a bounded task such as revising a document with required sections and source checks. Give the three exits, an example condition for each, and who owns each.

rubric.text: Completion names an observable outcome, for a document such as required sections, source checks, and a named decision.
Halt names conditions under which action stops before completion, such as out-of-scope files, missing authorization, restricted inputs, a failed independent check, or an unresolved dependency.
Defer is what a resource budget such as a time or turn limit produces, and yields an incomplete status.
Gives each exit an owner: an automated test can halt on a failing assertion, and a person decides whether a newly discovered risk changes scope.
Says "Stop when done" and "when it looks good" are not exits, since the stop field asks who decides, on what evidence, that the work is over or must not continue.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.prompt: An agent reaches its turn limit after finishing three of five steps and reports "Done." Evaluate this using the chapter's account of the defer exit.

rubric.text: Says a time or turn limit bounds effort without proving success.
Says reaching one yields an incomplete status, never a fabricated final result, so "Done" is wrong.
Says the report should preserve the partial artifacts.
Says the plan should name who decides whether to resume.
Distinguishes defer, which a resource budget produces, from halt, which names conditions such as out-of-scope files or missing authorization.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.prompt: A teammate lets Claude decide whether a newly discovered risk widens the scope, because Claude summarized the evidence well. Respond using the chapter.

rubric.text: Says each exit needs an owner.
Says a person must decide whether a newly discovered risk changes scope.
Says a summary is not a decision with a name on it.
Says Claude can help search approved sources or propose a smaller task but cannot grant permission the user or the institution has not given.
Says not every uncertainty is a block, since missing information obtainable within scope differs from a decision that needs new authority.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.prompt: Why add refusal paths to a plan? Give three examples from the symlink plan and say what a refusal must report.

rubric.text: Says a plan written only for success pressures every observation into forward motion.
Defines refusal as the workflow preserving its state and reporting what blocks the next transition.
Gives the hard stop: a resolved target outside the disposable parent.
Gives the scope stop (a required edit to the course reference instead of the learner copy) and the diagnosis route (a failed existing test goes back to diagnosis, not approval).
Says a refusal must report why the step stopped, what evidence was available, and what decision would allow safe resumption, since an unexplained halt looks like a crashed workflow.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.prompt: Besides turns and time, the chapter names further resources that bound a plan. Name them, say what the plan should do about each, and say what a deadline can and cannot justify.

rubric.text: Names the optional live API call and says it is labeled separately and requires explicit authorization.
Says this chapter's offline work needs no live API call.
Names human attention as a resource and says a plan that produces hundreds of review items without prioritization is structurally complete and practically unauditable.
Says the plan should state what needs human judgment.
Says a deadline can justify a reduced objective but does not make skipped verification acceptable without disclosure.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.prompt: Explain "a plan predicts, a result records." Say what each of steps, verification, and stop predicts, what habit the chapter asks for, and what goes wrong if the plan is edited after the run.

rubric.text: Says steps predict what will be done, verification predicts what you will observe if it worked, and stop predicts which events end the work.
Says a result is a record of what happened and the two are different documents to keep apart.
Says to write the prediction first and date it.
Says to write what a wrong outcome would look like before reading the result and not to revise that note afterward.
Says that editing the plan after the run to match it turns it into a description of the result and loses the review that justified acting; the gap between plan and record is what you learn.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.prompt: Describe two cross-field reviews: objective against verification, and steps against inputs, tools, and scope. Give an example of each failing.

rubric.text: Says objective against verification asks whether the check measures the outcome the objective names.
Gives an example such as a test confirming a file exists not establishing that its contents implement the behavior, and says that if the check is a proxy you name what it can and cannot reject.
Says every step needs information it is authorized to use.
Says that if no step writes, a write-capable tool is unnecessary, and that a step needing a capability the tools field lacks makes the plan infeasible.
Says an available tool can still be forbidden for this task, because capability does not create authority.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.prompt: Describe the remaining cross-field reviews: risks against mitigations, owners, and stops; edges against handoff objects; and final scope against revisions.

rubric.text: Says risks should state which are accepted, which trigger a mitigation, and which trigger deferral.
Says not to assign ownership to a fictitious human or use Claude as the signer of a human decision.
Says that for edges you ask what exactly a step such as run produces for review, since a bare id relation gives order without correspondence.
Says a late change to the objective can invalidate earlier risk and verification analysis.
Says to preserve versions and rerun the relevant review rather than keeping stale supporting fields, because reopening the plan is a normal event with a recorded reason.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.prompt: Describe four kinds of realistic counterexample and the practice of writing one before approval. Give two examples of constructing a counterexample.

rubric.text: Says an objective can be specific but wrong for the stakeholder.
Says verification can be executable but test a proxy.
Says scope can be precise but authorize too much, and risks can be detailed but disconnected from action.
Says a stop condition can be observable but trigger only after harm has occurred.
Says to write one counterexample before approval and ask whether the plan rejects it, for example a valid citation that does not support the claim, or an in-scope path with an unapproved operation.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.prompt: Divide the counterexample work between Claude and you, and explain why to keep the rejected counterexamples. What does a pre-mortem of this kind not prove?

rubric.text: Says Claude generates counterexamples quickly and in volume, and that work is worth handing over because it has no stake in the outcome.
Says which counterexamples are plausible here, and which risks deserve load-bearing checks, is your call.
Says you preserve rejected counterexamples when their dismissal reveals an assumption.
Says to keep the original counterexample beside the revised plan, or the final version will look inevitable and hide the failure it was built to stop.
Says the pre-mortem does not prove the plan cannot fail; it shows that identified failure modes shaped the design before the system acted.

questions.source: The gate: a reviewed plan, before Claude implements
questions.prompt: For the symlink plan's gate, state the objective, what may and may not change, the steps in order, the tools, and two of its risks with their mitigations.

rubric.text: States the objective: demonstrate rejection of an outside-pointing symlink in a disposable fixture, without accessing unrelated data.

States the scope: may change the learner test file, and the learner implementation only if evidence requires it; may not touch the course reference, real personal files, institutional settings, or publication.
Gives the steps in order: inspect, fixture, test, run, review, and the tools: Python, Claude Code for review assistance, the local test runner, and no direct API call.
Names at least two risks: targeting a real file, reporting a stable fixture as race resistance, or editing the reference.
Names the mitigations: a temporary directory, explicit path inspection, and diff review.

questions.source: The gate: a reviewed plan, before Claude implements
questions.prompt: State the symlink plan's stop field (all three exits) and its dated "predicts" line, and say what result would show the plan was wrong.

rubric.text: Completion: the fixture demonstrates the rejection, existing tests pass, the diff stays within scope, and the report limits its claim to the stable preflight case.
Halt: any command targets material outside the disposable arrangement, or scope must expand without review.
Defer, keeping partial artifacts, if a needed source is unavailable.
The predicts line is dated before the run: the new test passes, existing tests still pass, and the diff lists only allowed files.
A failing existing test or an out-of-scope file in the diff means the plan was wrong and it reopens.

questions.source: The gate: a reviewed plan, before Claude implements
questions.prompt: When the symlink plan is encoded and run through missing_fields and order, what comes back, how does that compare with the all-x plan, and what separates the two plans?

rubric.text: Says missing_fields returns an empty list, the same as for the all-x plan.
Says order returns inspect, fixture, test, run, review.
Says the output is the same for different plans and only the review described in the chapter separates them.
Says the plan can still be wrong, since the learner code may differ from the reference or the documentation may have changed.
Says the improvement over all-x is not longer prose but that another person can predict the actions and challenge the evidence.

questions.source: The gate: a reviewed plan, before Claude implements
questions.prompt: State the first three conditions that must hold before a plan goes downstream, and explain why missing_fields alone is not enough.

rubric.text: States that the objective was chosen from at least three candidates that pass the distinctness test pairwise.
States that the plan names one interest the choice leaves out.
States that missing_fields returns an empty list and the cross-field review found no field contradicting another, and that neither alone is enough.
States that order returns an order.
States that every state-changing edge carries an evidence condition a stranger can apply and a failure route.

questions.source: The gate: a reviewed plan, before Claude implements
questions.prompt: State the last three conditions for clearing a plan, explain why the sixth cannot be filled by Claude, and say whether passing the gate freezes the plan.

rubric.text: Condition four: the stop field has completion, halt, and defer exits, each with an owner.
Condition five: you wrote one counterexample before approval and the plan rejects it, or you revised the plan until it did.
Condition six: a named person has approved it, with a date; if nobody has, the status is pending and nothing consequential runs.
Says approval is a person's act and a sentence from Claude saying "approved" records nothing.
Says the gate does not freeze the plan: it fixes the version Claude implements against, and a result that contradicts the plan reopens it so the revised version goes through the gate again.

questions.source: Build It: the baseline that lets you audit the plan
questions.prompt: Why does the chapter have you implement missing_fields and order before opening the reference? Describe what you do with the six tests and what your version is for.

rubric.text: Says you cannot audit an ordering you have never computed.
Says you implement both functions in your learner workspace before opening the reference.
Says you read the six tests first and predict the results, naming at least four of the cases (empty order, dependency order, self-cycle, unknown prerequisite, duplicate id, empty plan).
Says your version is the baseline, the record of what you understood before Claude touched anything.
Says it is the instrument you measure Claude's version against.

questions.source: Build It: the baseline that lets you audit the plan
questions.prompt: The chapter asks you to hand the all-x plan's steps value to order and predict the result before running it. Make the prediction from the code and explain what it shows about the two checks.

rubric.text: Says the all-x plan's steps value is the single string x, not a list of step dictionaries.
Says order iterates over it and reads an id from each item, so it cannot read the value and fails with an error (a TypeError in Python) instead of returning an order.
Says the presence check passed the plan while the ordering function may not be able to read it.
Says the two checks are each correct under their own rule and neither is responsible for the other's assumptions.
Says you predict before you run, and that a structural pass from one check does not mean the plan is ready for the next.

questions.source: Build It: the baseline that lets you audit the plan
questions.prompt: In a plan with steps inspect, build, and verify, the step verify is given after "build" as a bare string instead of the list ["build"]. Predict what order raises, say whether its message points at the real cause, and give the fix.

rubric.text: Says set("build") produces a set of single characters, not a set containing the id build.
Says none of those characters is a step id, so order raises Unknown prerequisite.
Says the message misleads: it suggests a step is missing from the plan although build exists.
Says the real cause is that after has the wrong type, a string instead of a list, which order does not check.
Gives the fix: pass after as a list, ["build"], and trace the error to unknown dependency rather than saying ordering failed generically.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against the plan
questions.prompt: Describe the three-stage sequence for conducting Claude Code against the plan: what you do before asking Claude, what you do with what comes back, and when Claude may act.

rubric.text: Stage one: do the formulation work yourself (three candidates, pairwise results, the selection, and the interest it leaves out) before asking Claude.
Gives Claude Code the bounded objective and the exclusions and asks for a plan in the eight fields, saying explicitly that it should change no file yet; what returns is a proposal.
