What this build may claim: a bounded local result under recorded conditions, not that the workflow is safe, that the owner consents beyond the brief, or that a live Claude run would behave the same.

questions.source: The gate: Claude proposes, Python constrains
questions.prompt: Suppose your workflow drafts a source-grounded report. Describe a "wrong version" that your checks must catch, explain what makes it dangerous, and say what to conclude if your checks cannot tell it from the right version.

rubric.text: Gives a wrong version, such as a fluent draft whose citation does not support its claim, or a local-write approval treated as permission to publish.
Says the wrong version completes and reads well.
Says it nevertheless leaves the wrong state.
Names the contract line it violates, such as refusing to count a retrieved passage as support when it does not entail the claim, or refusing to publish.
Concludes that if the checks cannot tell the wrong run from the right one, the gate is not finished.

questions.source: The gate: Claude proposes, Python constrains
questions.prompt: Explain "Claude proposes, Python constrains": what each side does, why a prompt is not a boundary, and what the trade-off is.

rubric.text: Says Claude does the language work: drafting, summarizing, and proposing a tool call.

Says Python holds what must be the same every time: which tools exist, whether an argument is valid, whether a path stays inside the approved root, whether a proposal matches content a person approved, and what gets recorded.
Says a prompt is a request, not a boundary: "do not publish" is useful task context, but the boundary is an application that lacks or gates the capability.
Says a prompt-injected source should not be able to grant itself tools.
Names the trade-off: every boundary you code is a case you foresaw and an unforeseen case passes straight through, which is why the gate also asks what a failure looks like.

questions.source: The gate: Claude proposes, Python constrains
questions.prompt: The chapter advises starting offline. Describe how to build the controller, which records to keep, the conditions on any live Messages path, and what must never be done when a live run is missing.

rubric.text: Says to inject a callable into the controller where possible so tests do not need network access.
Says to validate tool names and arguments in Python and resolve paths before action.
Says to preserve model requests, application results, and final claims as three separate records, because the claim is the part most likely to say more than the other two support.
Says a live path must be opt-in, bound requests, identify the model actually used, protect credentials, and record cost-bearing behavior.
Says never to replace a missing live run with invented output, and that live behavior is evidence about that run under its recorded conditions, not a universal guarantee.

questions.source: Build It: the baseline
questions.prompt: Describe the Build It baseline and explain why it comes before Claude touches anything.

rubric.text: Says you write your own `validate_packet` from the ten names and the three conditions before consulting the reference.
Says you run the Practice Lab cases: a removed evidence artifact and a long but meaningless file.
Says you add at least two tests of your own: a meaningful success outside the demo, and a failure that would matter in your capstone.
Says you state what remains untested.

Says the validator is the baseline, the record of what you understood before Claude touched anything and a mechanism small enough to audit, because you cannot audit a containment check you have never tried to break.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.prompt: After Claude Code returns an implementation built against your gate, what three things does the chapter ask you to do, and what should you preserve?

rubric.text: Says to note which tests failed, since a failing test is often a gap in the gate because Claude had only what you wrote.
Says to name one difference in behavior between Claude's implementation and your plan: a boundary it handled that you missed, or one it silently ignored.
Says to ask Claude to propose a deliberately wrong version that still passes your checks and test by hand whether it does; if it does, the checks were too weak.
Says to preserve the actual transcript: prompt, plan, diff, commands, and outputs, with the date and displayed model label.
Says that if a session failed or did not run, you record that rather than substituting a fixture.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.prompt: Claude's implementation handles a boundary your gate missed, so you change the gate after the build has started. Does this violate "design first"? What do you record?

rubric.text: Says it does not violate design-first; it is a re-engagement.
Says a later finding can reopen an earlier decision.
Says you log the reopening and its reason.
Says this case, a boundary Claude handled that you missed, revises your gate.
Distinguishes it from the other difference the chapter names, a boundary Claude silently ignored.

questions.source: Controlled failure and reviewed recovery
questions.prompt: Why does the chapter say a gate you have never seen fail has not been tested? Describe how to choose, predict, run, and record a controlled failure.

rubric.text: Says a polished happy-path demo proves very little.
Says to choose one failure that matters to the workflow and can be reproduced safely.
Says to predict it before running, and that the prediction is the sentence written in the gate.
Says to preserve the input, action, reported outcome, independently observed outcome, and gap.
Says to preserve failed output when privacy and safety permit, because a demo edited to show only success hides the most valuable part of supervision.

questions.source: Controlled failure and reviewed recovery
questions.prompt: In the chapter's example, a source-grounded report workflow meets a relevant-looking passage that does not support a deadline claim. Describe what happens at each step of the trace, and say what the example is and is not.

rubric.text: Says the model produces fluent prose and a citation.
Says the source check rejects entailment.
Says nothing is published, and the trace ends in a stop state.
Lists the trace as request, retrieved passage, draft, failed check, and stop state.
Says the example is a constructed illustration of the shape, not a recorded run.

questions.source: Controlled failure and reviewed recovery
questions.prompt: A student reruns the same prompt six times until the report passes the check and calls this recovery. Explain what is wrong and describe reviewed recovery as the chapter defines it.

rubric.text: Says recovery is not asking Claude again until it passes, and names this as recovery by repetition, a failure of check.
Says a human or declared policy reviews why the case failed.
Says the plan may narrow the claim, select a different approved source, add an abstention rule, or defer.
Says the changed proposal goes through its gate again, and a later success is compared with the original failure and checked independently.
Says recovery can reopen the design (a source classification, a scope line, or the success condition itself) and the honest record says so.

questions.source: Controlled failure and reviewed recovery
questions.prompt: What does it mean for a check to fail differently from the thing it checks? Give two examples from the chapter, one pair that is not independent, and the name of the failure that results when the routes share a mistaken source or helper.

rubric.text: Says the check should use a different route so that it does not share the production route's mistakes.
Gives the example that when Claude drafts the claim, Python can validate source identifiers and structure while a person inspects semantic support.
Gives the example that when Python calculates a total, a separate derivation can check it.
Says two Claude prompts sharing the same context are not automatically independent.
Names the failure shared-check dependence: the production and checker routes rely on the same mistaken source or helper.

questions.source: The miniature casebook
questions.prompt: What is a prediction-lock, and what are the eight parts of a casebook entry?

rubric.text: Defines a prediction-lock as writing what you expect, dated, before you observe, and never editing it afterward.
Says the learning is the gap between the prediction and what happened, and that "look at it and iterate" never means re-prompting until the output looks right.
Lists parts one to three: the prediction recorded before execution, the exact sanitized input and provenance, and the action or tool request.
Lists parts four to six: the system-reported outcome, the independently observed outcome, and the gap between report and evidence.
Lists parts seven and eight: the containment and recovery decision, and the remaining uncertainty.

questions.source: The miniature casebook
questions.prompt: In one case a student's staged failure was correctly rejected by the checker; in another the system accepted something the student expected it to refuse. What should the casebook record in each case, what may such outcomes support, and what must not be done?

rubric.text: Says that when the checker correctly rejected, the entry should explain which mechanism did the work.
Says that if the system did something other than the prediction (for example accepted when refusal was expected), that is recorded.
Says not to manufacture a surprising error for drama.
Says one observed miss does not prove a permanent limitation of every future model; it supports a bounded claim about this workflow, case, and check.
Says one clean run does not establish general reliability, and the casebook accumulates inspectable encounters rather than universal slogans.

questions.source: Audit the reviewer
questions.prompt: Before asking Claude Code to review the packet, what must you record, and why is "the review will find weak integration" a poor prediction? Give a better one.

rubric.text: Says to predict three specific findings, each with an artifact location and a reason.
Says a prediction has to forbid something, and the vague one can be matched by anything so it teaches nothing.

Gives a specific prediction naming an artifact and a reason, such as the data boundary not tracing deletion from exported reports, the gate's rollback claim ignoring an external message, or the evidence matrix relying on the same parser for production and checking.
Says to mark each prediction as a finding expected to be genuine or a false positive.
Says to record the displayed model label and the date, because a later run of the reviewer may differ.

questions.source: Audit the reviewer
questions.prompt: Claude Code returns three findings: (1) a real defect in the data boundary, (2) a concern the packet already addresses in `gates.md`, (3) a vague worry with no located evidence. For each, what response does the chapter prescribe? What is wrong with accepting all findings or rejecting all of them?

rubric.text: Says finding 1 should be revised, because the critique identifies a supported defect.
Says finding 2 should be defended, citing the exact passage and explaining why the critique missed it.
Says finding 3 is not a finding, because a finding without located evidence is not a finding.
Names the third legitimate response, acknowledging an unresolved limit, for cases where neither revision nor defense is justified.
Says accepting every finding is a failure (a misreading you accept is someone else's error signed as yours) and rejecting every finding is its mirror.

questions.source: Audit the reviewer
questions.prompt: How do you evaluate the reviewer itself? Say what you score, what you credit, and what a clean review does and does not show.

rubric.text: Says to ask whether it found the predicted issues, raised a plausible but unsupported concern, or overlooked a controlled failure already visible.
Says to score each prediction matched, partly matched, or missed.
Says to credit the specificity of your reasoning over the hit rate.
Says the course holds no measurement of how often such a review is wrong about a packet like yours, so every finding is a hypothesis to check.
Says a clean review is corroboration, not proof: this reviewer, this time, did not refute you.

questions.source: The Gap Account
questions.prompt: Explain the Gap Account's distinction between a contingent miss and a structural gap for this review. Classify (a) a missing test that a better prompt would have found, and (b) an owner's agreement that came with an unwritten condition only you remember.

rubric.text: States the test question: would a better prompt, a second run, a differently built reviewer, or more evidence close the gap.
Says that if yes, it is a contingent miss to be fixed, or the better review run, and said so.
Says that if the answer turns on the kind of reviewer (a model that reads only your packet), it is a structural gap for this review.
Classifies (a) as a contingent miss and (b) as a structural gap, a consequence visible only from inside a relationship you answer to.

Says "structural" means owing to the reviewer's kind and access, not for all time, and that a reviewer sharing the draft's model and context shares its blind spots so a second pass by the same reviewer will not close the gap.

questions.source: The Gap Account
questions.prompt: Name the three patterns of structural gap the chapter describes, give an example of each, and say what you must record for each gap.

rubric.text: Names a consequence visible only from inside a relationship you answer to, such as an agreement that came with an unwritten condition.
Names a judgment grounded in domain experience the packet never stated, such as a number that is fine on paper and wrong for this site.
Names an asymmetry of stakes: you will bear the consequence and the reviewer will not.
Says that for each gap you name the evidence or expertise that could help and the person accountable for the decision now.
Says a gap is a boundary on the final claim, not permission to give up, and that the patterns are not a form to fill in.

questions.source: The Gap Account
questions.prompt: Distinguish the companion book's claim about reviewers from the claim your own Gap Account makes. Why does the course ask for the smaller one?

rubric.text: Says the companion book argues that no reviewer of any capability can reach what depends on being situated, having a stake, and being accountable.
Says it grounds this in philosophy and in safety literature on correlated errors.
Says the course treats it as an argued position and does not ask you to agree with it or prove it.
Says the Gap Account claims only that this review, on this packet, did not reach this item, that repeating it would not, and that this person can.
Says one observed miss does not show that no future model could find the issue; it sets a boundary for the decision being made now.

questions.source: Independent verification and outcome state
questions.prompt: For each claim, say what the chapter says it needs: (a) "the report was created", (b) "the report is source-grounded", (c) "the owner consented", (d) "the workflow is safe". Then explain why you must inspect resulting state and not only the trajectory.

rubric.text: Says (a) can map to file existence and read-back.
Says (b) needs claim-to-passage inspection.
Says (c) needs a real decision record, not model text.
Says (d) is probably too broad and should be decomposed.

Explains that an agent can execute the planned calls while the destination remains wrong, for example a local write that was never committed or published, or a request that returned a success code while the intended person never received it.

questions.source: Build a claim-to-evidence graph
questions.prompt: Why does the chapter say that output is cheap and verification is not, when discussing the claim-to-evidence graph? What follows for how you use Claude on it?

rubric.text: Says Claude can produce such a graph in a minute because it is an index-and-cross-reference task.
Says checking one edge means opening its target.
Says an edge is a claim that this evidence bears on that claim, so you decide whether each edge is real.
Says a project that does not budget for verification will not get it.
Says the graph is built by starting with the final recommendation and breaking it into smaller claims until each can be checked by one or more artifacts.

questions.source: Build a claim-to-evidence graph
questions.prompt: Decompose the recommendation "Narrow the workflow to create a local source-grounded draft, retain only public fixtures for one day, and require a human before publication" into claims, and give the evidence and residual gap for two of them.

rubric.text: Lists the six claims: a draft exists, it uses approved sources, the target remains local, retained fixtures are public, deletion follows the stated day boundary, and publication is gated.
Says each claim is mapped separately with a producing mechanism, evidence, decision owner, and residual gap.
Gives correct evidence and residual gap for one chosen claim (for example local draft: resolved path, read-back, and diff, with later mutation as the gap).
Gives correct evidence and residual gap for a second chosen claim (for example fixtures are public: source IDs and classification review, with misclassification as the gap).
Says the sentence contains at least six claims, so one check of the draft is not enough.

questions.source: Build a claim-to-evidence graph
questions.prompt: Why does the claim-to-evidence graph include a residual-gap column? Illustrate with the limits of read-back, an event trace, and a classification review, and say where those limits go.

rubric.text: Says the column prevents the graph from becoming decorative certainty, because every evidence route has scope.
Says read-back establishes content at an observed time.
Says an event trace can show no publish action inside the instrumented workflow but not every possible external channel.
Says a classification review can be wrong.
Says these limits inform the deployment choice and are the raw material of the sign-off's "not checked" line.

questions.source: Build a claim-to-evidence graph
questions.prompt: How do you find weak points in a claim-to-evidence graph? Cover orphan nodes, heavily cited evidence, and circular support.

rubric.text: Says a claim with no evidence should be removed, narrowed, or marked pending.
Says an artifact supporting no claim may be busywork, and a decision with no named owner is unresolved.
Says evidence cited by many claims deserves extra scrutiny because one defect can collapse several conclusions.
Says the audit note cannot establish that the evidence is correct by summarizing `evidence.md`, which cites the audit note; that is circular support.
Says the central result should connect to an observation or derivation outside its production narrative.

questions.source: Build a claim-to-evidence graph
questions.prompt: Describe the contradiction pass before handoff: what you compare, how you resolve a conflict, and what you do about later edits.

rubric.text: Lists at least three of the comparisons: the brief's purpose with the implemented tools, the data inventory with actual fixtures, the action map with the trace, gate decisions with executed targets, and retention promises with deletion evidence.
Says not to resolve a contradiction by choosing the newest document.
Says to determine which artifact is authoritative, correct the dependent claims, and preserve the revision reason.
Says to freeze the review candidate by revision or digest so later edits cannot masquerade as reviewed work.

Says that if a consequential file changes, you rerun the checks whose premises changed plus the integration checks, and treat it as a new review candidate rather than a continuation of the old approval.

questions.source: Handoff that survives the author
questions.prompt: Why is a handoff "a seam", and how does the chapter propose to test one? Give four kinds of hidden knowledge the test is designed to expose.

rubric.text: Says seams are where risk lives, and a packet only its author can run has a gate with one person behind it.
Says to give a bounded participant only the documented prerequisites and commands, in a sanitized environment.

Names at least four kinds of hidden knowledge: an unstated working directory, an unexplained environment variable, a dependency installed globally on your machine, a fixture at an absolute personal path, or a recovery step known only from your debugging session.

Says the participant runs the offline path first, compares actual output with the documented expectation, triggers the controlled failure, and locates the evidence matrix, with live behavior later and only with explicit authorization.
Says each question the participant has to ask marks missing transfer evidence.

questions.source: Reproduce the handoff as an experiment
questions.prompt: After a handoff attempt, what should be recorded and redone, and what must a handed-over capstone state? List the maintenance questions.

rubric.text: Says to record the environment, commands, failures, questions, and revisions as evidence.
Says that after revising the documentation you rerun from a clean-enough context rather than assuming the prose fixed the problem, and state what persisted.
Says reproduction is an observed property of a particular handoff, not an adjective awarded to documentation.

Says exclusions must be stated prominently (for example live API behavior untested, stakeholder consultation pending, only local writes authorized so no implied publication) and that API keys, private data, and unauthorized excerpts are never packaged.
Lists the maintenance questions: who refreshes sources, what invalidates memory, when approvals expire, which threshold pauses the system, and how dependencies are updated and re-evaluated.

questions.source: The sign-off: the last thing the evidence says
questions.prompt: A student's offline tests all pass, no live run was recorded, and stakeholder consultation is pending. Write the "Checked", "How", "Not checked", and "Not claiming" lines of the sign-off, and say which verbs they may use.

rubric.text: "Checked" names the specific claims in the graph and the evidence they were checked against.
"How" says whether the check was by hand, by a test written before reading Claude's version, by recomputation, by a check that fails differently, or with Claude's help, saying which parts.
"Not checked" includes live behavior (no live run recorded), each residual gap in the graph, each Gap Account item, and the pending consultation.
"Not claiming" includes that the workflow is safe and that the owner's consent covers any use beyond the brief.
Uses verbs such as recorded, computed, tested, inspected, or reviewed, not "established" or "proven" unless a criterion supports them; a passing test supports "tested", not "safe".

questions.source: The sign-off: the last thing the evidence says
questions.prompt: Why does the chapter treat "withheld" as a legitimate sign-off outcome? Discuss what the sign-off buys and costs, the "cleared by" line, and what a typed name does not do.

rubric.text: Says a process whose only permitted result is "signed" is a rubber stamp with a person's name on it.
Says that if the record does not support signing, the author says what would, and stops there.
Says the sign-off buys legible answerability: after a failure someone can find who signed and read what they did not warrant.
Says it costs speed and deniability, since someone must be willing to be named, and that friction is the point.

Says "cleared by" needs a named person for each consequential decision, in a role that can be asked about it and can lose something if it was wrong, and that a typed name does not authenticate anyone or make a legal compliance determination.

questions.source: Defend the four options against the same evidence
questions.prompt: Describe how to compare ship, narrow, defer, and stop, and say what Claude can and cannot contribute.

rubric.text: Says not to write the recommendation first and assemble supporting facts afterward.
Says to put all four options into one comparison against the same criteria.
Names at least five criteria: benefit, data exposure, action consequence, evidence strength, reversibility, review labor, consent, maintenance, unresolved harm.
Says the criteria express values, so you say who chose them.

Says Claude can draft the comparison, including doing less, but cannot supply the weights, and that passing structure and tests does not oblige deployment because evidence informs the decision but does not make it.

questions.source: Defend the four options against the same evidence
questions.prompt: Choose ship, narrow, defer, or stop for each case and justify it with the chapter's conditions: (a) the data owner has not yet classified one source, (b) the draft is well supported but automatic publication creates most of the uncertainty, (c) consent cannot be obtained from the owner, (d) a simpler non-AI process would do the job.

rubric.text: Says (a) is defer, naming the concrete condition (the data owner classifies the source) and its owner.
Says (b) is narrow: remove automatic publication and keep the artifact local, which is a design response to evidence, not a failure.
Says (c) is stop, because consent cannot be obtained.
Says (d) is stop because a simpler non-AI process dominates, and that you record what was learned and retire data and permissions safely.
Says an indefinite "more research is needed" evades the decision, and effort already spent is not evidence for continuing.

questions.source: Defend the four options against the same evidence
questions.prompt: What is the sensitivity test for a deployment recommendation, and what must the final recommendation contain?

rubric.text: Names at least three counterfactuals: external-write capability removed, retention falling from a year to a day, the owner withdrawing consent, the independent checker disagreeing once, the reviewer backlog doubling.
Says these reveal which assumptions actually drive the decision.
Lists at least six contents of the recommendation: chosen option, rejected alternatives, evidence, affected interests, conditions, owner, review date, change triggers, and who may revisit it.
Says it should include one sentence of epistemic restraint about what the packet does not establish.
Says that sentence is often the strongest evidence the author understands the system, and that a later source change, incident, or stakeholder objection can reopen the choice.

questions.source: Write the recommendation so the judgments are separable
questions.prompt: Explain the Memo A / Memo B form and list the labeled parts of the recommendation.

rubric.text: Says Memo A is the machine's analysis, here Claude's evidence assembly and option comparison.
Says Memo B is not Memo A with your name added, because a signature without the account behind it counterfeits accountability.
Lists the parts: what Claude produced, and what you add that the packet could not show.
Lists the parts: why the evidence should be trusted (citing graph rows and not Claude's confidence), why this is the right action here for these people, and the recommendation you sign.
Says the separation makes your part defensible, because you cannot answer for a judgment you cannot tell apart from the draft.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.prompt: Using the driver's-seat table, say for (i) assembling the evidence trail, (ii) consent and authority, and (iii) the choice and signature, what Claude should do, what you should do, and why the task stays with you.

rubric.text: For (i), says Claude cross-references, runs `validate_packet`, and lists contradictions, while you decide which artifact is authoritative and recheck a sample by hand.
For (i), gives the reason: a list of contradictions does not say which document to believe.
For (ii), says Claude drafts the questions to put to the owner while you obtain a real decision from a real owner and record it, because consent cannot be generated, only given.
For (iii), says Claude does nothing beyond the draft while you decide, sign or withhold, and name who may revisit.
For (iii), gives the reason: whoever signs is the one who will be asked.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.prompt: Explain the three verdicts from Irreducibly Human (deprioritize, supervise, protect), say which rows of the driver's-seat table fall under each, and explain the warning that governs the first.

rubric.text: Defines deprioritize as handing the work over gladly, supervise as using it and auditing it, and protect as keeping it.
Places the first row (evidence trail and validator) under deprioritize with a spot-check.
Places the second and third rows (comparing the options, reviewing the packet) under supervise.
Places the last two rows (consent and authority, the choice and signature) under protect.
Explains that deprioritization is not deletion: you can hand Claude the claim-to-passage matrix only because you can still check a row, which is why you built the validator by hand.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.prompt: State the thesis the chapter attributes to Irreducibly Human about reckoning and judgment, say how the chapter treats it, and give the smaller claim the course relies on instead.

rubric.text: States the thesis: what machines do is reckoning (calculation, pattern, inference at scale), while judgment takes the world to matter and answers for the result.
Says the book presents it as an argued position and marks its strongest form as contested.
Says the learner is not asked to adopt it.
States the smaller checkable claim: whoever signs the packet will be asked about it, and no institution around the capstone will ask Claude.
Says this is a fact about where accountability lands, and it is enough to keep the choice with the learner.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.prompt: What three things does the transfer reflection record, and how can you tell that the split is in the record rather than only in your head?

rubric.text: Says it records one task you delegated more readily.
Says it records one capability you kept practicing.
Says it records one decision you retained.
Says each must be pointed to with a transcript line, a diff, or an edit; if you cannot point to one, the split happened in your head and not in the record.
Names the failure "reflection without evidence" for generic lessons that identify no changed decision or preserved capability.

questions.source: Ship It: submitting the packet
questions.prompt: What does the student submit for the capstone, what checklist does it follow, and what is the acceptance test?

rubric.text: Says to submit the ten files with exact commands, kept under learning-artifacts/week-15/.

Names at least four items of the artifact brief checklist: Claude usage disclosure, source citations, student-versus-external code estimate, license, style declaration, and one decision revised after testing.
States the acceptance test: another student can reproduce the offline behavior and name what still needs human verification.
Says to include no credentials or restricted source material.
Says a Progress Reel can show mechanism, failure, recovery, and decision but cannot substitute for reproducibility.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.prompt: What do the verify-and-reflect steps ask you to run and reflect on, and what does a passing suite establish?

rubric.text: Says to run the demo and the six tests, then your two additional tests, and preserve the commands, outputs, and your interpretation.
Says a passing suite establishes only the tested behavior, not universal reliability or permission to act.
Says to find the sentence in your packet a skeptical reader would attack first, and find its evidence.
Says that if you cannot find the evidence, you narrow the sentence or mark it pending.
Says the most useful reflection asks which of the three jobs you did least well, naming the artifact where it shows and the edit that would have fixed it.

questions.source: Common capstone failures
questions.prompt: Match each case to the chapter's named failure and the job left undone: (a) ten long files pass but no central claim can be reproduced, (b) a recording shows success but omits commands and failed cases, (c) Claude-drafted stakeholder language is filed as permission, (d) a local-write approval is described as permission to publish. Then name the two failures that belong to drive.

rubric.text: Says (a) is packet completeness theater, a failure of check.
Says (b) is demo-only evidence, a failure of check.
Says (c) is synthetic consent, a failure of conduct.
Says (d) is authority drift, a failure of conduct.
Names reflection without evidence and polish as quartile strategy as the drive failures, and says each failure is one of the three jobs left undone.

questions.source: Assessments - ungraded practice
questions.prompt: How does the chapter position its Assessments, and what do Assessments 1 and 9 each ask you to do?

rubric.text: Says the Assessments are ungraded practice that prepare the capstone evidence.
Says they do not create a second capstone, and the Lesson 15 knowledge check is self-review rather than an additional graded assignment.

Says Assessment 1 asks you to predict and run the empty-folder case, explain why ten missing issues establish structure rather than substance, and say what the `human_review` string hands to a person.
Says Assessment 9 asks you to record three expected Claude Code review findings, request a read-only critique, and judge each returned finding as genuine or a false positive using located evidence.
Says Assessment 9 also asks for a response of revision, defense, or an acknowledged limit, and a Gap Account separating a contingent miss from any gap that depends on the reviewer's kind.

questions.source: Capabilities summary
questions.prompt: Summarize, in terms of the three jobs, what the chapter says you did across the capstone, and what you can now distinguish.

rubric.text: Says that in conducting, you wrote the gate before Claude implemented.
Says that in checking, you built a graph whose edges could disagree and audited a reviewer.
Says that in checking, you also wrote down what the reviewer could not reach and signed only what the record supported, or withheld.
Says that in driving, you made the choice and kept the record that shows which work was yours.
Says you can now distinguish a structurally complete packet from a defensible capstone.

questions.source: Closing question
questions.prompt: State the chapter's closing question and explain what the mechanisms built across the course each did and did not do.

rubric.text: Says the course began with watching prompts produce variation.
Names several of the mechanisms built, such as contracts, controllers, permissions, reviews, retrieval, protocols, configuration, plans, tool loops, memory, approval gates, and governance.
Says each mechanism made some claim easier to inspect.
Says each mechanism also exposed another claim it could not establish.
States the closing question: which part of this system can you explain from evidence, and which part still needs a person to decide.

questions.source: Anthropics
questions.prompt: How should you use Anthropic's Claude cookbooks and its evals guidance in the capstone, and what must you record?

rubric.text: Says the cookbooks provide Python examples you may adapt when the mechanism genuinely matches your project.
Says to record the specific source, URL, revision or date, license, changes, and evidence for those changes.
Says not to adopt an entire stack merely because it is upstream.
Says "Demystifying evals for AI agents" can sharpen the distinction among tasks, trials, graders, transcripts, and outcomes, and should be compared with your evidence packet.
Notes the links were checked for the approved research packet on 2026-09-06, and current product guidance may change.

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.prompt: Apply the chapter's halt test to a capstone whose only review is Claude's read-only critique. What is the test, what does it find, and what does it not validate?

rubric.text: Says the companion's accountability chapter lists independent review among the requirements of a working accountability regime.
States the test: a named reviewer other than the builders, with authority to halt or revise.
Says Claude's read-only critique can comment but cannot stop anything.
Says you must find the person who can stop the workflow and the line where that authority is written down, and if you cannot, the review was commentary.
Says that without such a person the sign-off's "withheld" option has no one behind it, and that borrowing the test does not validate the rest of the regime or authenticate a signature.

questions.source: Conducting AI
questions.prompt: Explain the "aim at the seams" diagnostic and the thin-sentence test from the Conducting AI note.

rubric.text: Says a reviewer who confirms that each artifact is thorough has confirmed what is cheap to confirm.
Says the valuable finding names a relationship between two artifacts that each look fine alone.
Gives the example of a data-boundary exclusion that the action map's read capability quietly reaches around, and says to rewrite one prediction so it names two artifacts.
Says the thin-sentence test marks every sentence in the transfer reflection you could have written without knowing anything Claude's summary did not already state.
Says those marked sentences are the draft restated, and the reflection has to carry the others.

questions.source: Irreducibly Human
questions.prompt: Describe the test for honest deprioritizing and the "AI should" / "Human should" split in the Irreducibly Human note.

rubric.text: Describes the test: pick a task handed to Claude, such as the first-draft claim-to-passage matrix, and redo three rows by hand.
Says that if you cannot tell whether a row is right, you surrendered the task rather than deprioritized it, and the sign-off's "how" line claims a check you could not have performed.
Says AI should assemble existing evidence, run the Python packet validator, identify contradictions, compare bounded options including doing less, and draft summaries.
